Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the likelihood of someone obtaining a federal job?
Answer: US Government: I can’t speak for today, but in 2012 when I started, the odds were slim. None of my classmates could figure out what to do to land a phone call, let alone an interview. I probably uploaded my resume to the federal government website and applied to thousands of jobs before even netting just a few calls back. Then there was an interview, and an on-boarding process (to include background checks, reference checks, and a probationary period). Even having veteran’s preference and finishing my master’s degree didn’t get me very far ahead of the field. Some of it was just luck and sheer number of resumes sent out. This was all to land a GS-7 position, but my career ladder lead me to GS-12 fairly quickly. I was only unhappy with my salary for a year or so, then I got overtime which meant an almost insane amount of money for a government employee at times (plus bonuses). There is also huge potential for investment profits if you invest your TSP intelligently with generous government matching. Of course, the job outlook is a general statement. Some specialities will have no problems obtaining a government job like doctors, nurses, and some engineers. These fields are pretty much always in demand.

Question: What do you love to do the most that gives you peace?
Answer: For me it is going for a run, especially on a morning that is cool, but not too cool. Of course, this is after a few cups of coffee and listening to music. Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are your opinions on pacifists?
Answer: Some days ago I went to the Saturday market in my part of town. I didn’t even buy anything but a coffee. I was out walking and decided to drop in. Outside there was a line of people with signs calling for peace and “co-existence.” I rolled my eyes just a little bit. Sure! You can hold these signs up over here in a relatively safe part of town, go over to Kinsman and preach that shit. Let’s see how long before you’re robbed at gunpoint. Which leads to my point. You see, in the real world, as it actually exists, there are robbers. Because there are robbers, we must also have cops to catch the robbers. Those cops are armed and willing to do violence to keep our society safe. In a country, even one as powerful as the United States, we understand there are areas of our own cities where law and order exists only marginally. Those of us who are upstanding citizens don’t even go to those parts of the city unless absolutely necessary. From my perspective, lawlessness and chaos is the default state of man. We are just barely evolved primates. Pacifists would have you believe that humans are really peaceful and that our tendency towards war and disorder can be socialized away. However, from what I have seen of the world, that is just not true. The great majority of people will behave as others do (morality), a few will be against any use of violence, and yet another few will be willing to engage in the most extreme and heinous types of violence. A pacifist society automatically gives all the cards and negotiating power to those few willing to wield the most violence. Yet, none of this is to say that pacifists aren’t useful. In any sane and democratic society, it should be normal to have a group of people in opposition of war. If everyone is doggedly pro-war then it’s probably not a country in which it is worth living.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do Western powers care about us (Taiwan and Philippines)? They only gave us Cold War era weaponry. China would soon take us. We need F35s and F22s and as well as Abrams X tanks. There’s no way we can beat their 5th gen weaponry.
Answer: With Taiwan’s weaponry of today, I would still bet on Taiwan all by itself to win the conflict if China invaded. Am I saying Taiwan would win 100%? No. But I am confident enough in Taiwan that I feel it would be a good wager. There’s a reason the CCP has waited so long and amassed such a large military before openly declaring it wants to take back Taiwan by force. 1) The CCP doesn’t trust the Chinese military to take Taiwan based on skill, ability, and military competency. Therefore, the CCP is counting on taking Taiwan with superiority of numbers and technology. But the technological gap really isn’t that wide between Taiwan and China today. China’s technology is also untested and there aren’t any experienced battlefield commanders in the Chinese military. They’re quite disadvantaged as the aggressor against a mountainous island nation. 2) China can’t hide the staging of an invasion of Taiwan. Sure, if their stealth aircraft actually work, they could knock out some key infrastructure in Taiwan in the early stages of the war, but I don’t think stealth is as much of an asset here as people think it is. Will China’s stealth aircraft be the thing that assures victory when they still have to send soldiers to secure and hold Taiwan? We are talking about a full on conventional war against a near peer military. This means hundreds of thousands of soldiers having to be ferried over to Taiwan, during which time they’ll be sitting ducks. We’ve already seen how complicated it can be invading the country next door in the Russia-Ukraine War. The logistics of a seaborne invasion are probably too complicated for China to pull off successfully. 3) It’s certain that the Taiwanese government will leave a stay-behind element in place. If the Chinese invasion were to somehow succeed, stay-behind elements will likely keep the CCP tied down in a horrifying guerrilla campaign that would easily last 5–10 years. Too many of China’s only children will have to die to make a violent re-unification of Taiwan politically feasible. Even for a regime as controlling as the CCP. The CCP won’t invade Taiwan unless it has its back against the wall, politically. It’s too dangerous of a move with very huge downsides for very little real world benefit. (China has a full-scale replica of the Presidential Palace of Taiwan in the desert where it practices for an invasion of Taiwan. The above graphic features the shadow of the untested 5th generation Chinese J-20 stealth fighter. Photo credit: France 24.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What's the craziest bar fight or street brawl you've ever witnessed or been involved in?
Answer: Craziest bar fight I was involved in: I was living in Ann Arbor while finishing my undergraduate degree at nearby Eastern Michigan University. On an otherwise boring winter night, some friends and I decided to go to a nightclub we frequented. Once there, a big, burly man was making his way through a crowded dance floor at the night club. He must have weighed close to 300lbs and just started shoving people. Right in front of me he pushed down a tiny woman who was probably only five feet tall and weighing less than 100lbs. It was at this point that I knew I had to do something. I had a beer bottle in my hand since I was drinking. I grabbed him by the back of the collar of his shirt as he tried to make his way past me, then used my other hand to smash the bottom of the beer bottle into the back of his head. The beer bottle did not break like in a movie, but it did buckle him and he fell to the floor. I grabbed him again and gave him a few more stiff punches to the face for good measure. Soon, in a moment I’ll always remember, a pretty girl with an Afro looked me dead in the eyes and calmly asked “why are you hitting this man?” In the rush of adrenaline, I had not realized that by this time he was already stunned and unconscious. Somewhere in the melee I lost my glasses and had to run to escape security that had noticed the fight in progress. Although I could hardly see, I made it out of the back door to the alley and got away free. For the next few days I closely and nervously monitored the news in Ann Arbor. I never heard anything about the fight in the news, I can only assume the man was okay. (Downtown Ann Arbor, these days when I go there it really does feel like returning to the scene of a crime. Good times.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Reflecting on your cultural background, how has it influenced your identity and worldview?
Answer: First, my cultural background: American (USA): I am from the United States which influences my worldview to a great degree. Black: I have a very typical Black American background. Urban: I love communing with nature, but at heart I am a city-dweller. Veteran: I spent six years in the military and several years in government. That experience is still a big part of my identity. My worldview: So first, there’s that tried and true cliche of a word. Freedom. Of course, I am a big believer in it like any red-blooded American. I guess that makes me a liberal in the classical sense. More Jeffersonian than Ayn Rand though. However, my take on what freedom means is certainly different, if I am honest, than your average white libertarian. Many of whom I call friends. I like guns, I like marijuana, and I like that my gay friends can get married. I draw the line at saying we shouldn’t collect taxes though. My experience, both as a veteran of the US military and as a person that grew up in a violent city, inform my view that the world is a naturally chaotic place. The world isn’t divided into groups of good and bad people, but there are those generally trying to do good and those generally trying to oppose it. Both are actually small groups of people. The majority of people will go with whatever is fashionable at the time. As objectively as I can say it, I still believe America and the West, more generally, is still on the right side of history at the moment. Of course, we all know, mistakes were made (Iraq War - Wikipedia). From what I can tell, all societies will always (quite logically) put the needs of the many before those of the few. If you are a minority in your respective country or region you always have to take this into account. Also, you should never take your freedoms for granted just because you have them now. One day the mood of society can change and you can lose those freedoms. Rights can erode quickly when people become apathetic. This is why I see the world the way I see it. (Captain America. Image credit: Marvel).

Question: Why is it difficult for young men to get older women to date?

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What was the most messed up punishment(s) you received as a child?
Answer: I received the same punishment whenever I misbehaved, got bad grades, or said something I shouldn’t have to an adult. I was whipped with a leather belt. This was very typical of the time and place in which I grew up and not at all considered child abuse. I was often told how lucky I was to only receive a beating with a leather belt. My parents’ generation, I’m told, could be beaten with anything within reach, but especially with tree branches (often called a “switch” in the south). The leather belt in our household hung ominously from the coat rack. It was there to say goodbye when I left home in the morning, reminding me to behave in school. If ever there was a bad report from my teachers or I received a bad grade — what occurred next would be no mystery. Although sometimes, if I was lucky, I’d get grounded for a couple of weeks. This was maybe if I got a “C” or two on my report card in school. Today, I am often told how Black parents in America are soft on their children and let them misbehave. My experience growing up in the 1990’s tells me differently. Black parents, where I came from, gave their children excessive discipline that would get parents thrown in jail in the suburbs. If the police had thrown people in Detroit in jail for whipping their kids, our jails would have overflowed quickly. (Old trusty. Image source: LL Bean.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How many veterans work full-time while going to school on the GI Bill?
Answer: I started college then stopped to go to the military and then went back to college, including graduate school. I worked part time during undergrad, but I didn’t work a single day, except for my reserve duties, during graduate school. It was great, actually. I had only 3–4 lectures a week that were just a few hours apiece. This left plenty of time for studying and whatever else I wanted to do. For my first year of graduate school I had so much fun with my spare time. My girlfriend was a nurse and had four days off a week and so we had lots of time together. Most of my friends were college dropouts that worked menial jobs around Ann Arbor and Ypsilanti. This meant lots of time to hang out and party. It was all an idyllic situation and I will always fondly remember those times. My second year of graduate school was dedicated nearly entirely to conducting research with a police department and helping them to analyze crime statistics. My spare time was applying for government jobs. Overall, going to school as a veteran is a better than average college experience. I can say this with confidence as I went to school before joining the military and after. You won’t have to work hard as a veteran student, you can dedicate most of your time to studies because you will have plenty of money coming in. (Ann Arbor is already a really amazing place to live. Living there as a veteran student and being able to afford it makes it even better. Photo source: Getty Images.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you currently or have you ever worked a minimum wage job?
Answer: I have worked exactly one job for minimum wage and it was my first job. Both my twin sister and I, got our first job at Burger King on the exact same day. It was September of 2001 and we were 16 and juniors in high school. We worked evenings after school and weekends. The pay was $5.15 to start. Almost immediately, I did not enjoy it. I scrubbed dishes non-stop for hours, swept and mopped floors. Worked under incredibly hot conditions loading burger patties into the automatic broiler, and exposed myself to biohazards cleaning shit-covered bathrooms. Amongst all of this I had to deal with the acerbic attitude of my dipshit manager and my colleagues who were either young students or old burnouts, including a few convicted felons. After a while I hated showing up and started looking for work elsewhere. In a few months I’d secured a much better job at Domino’s, which paid a whopping $1.35 an hour more than my old job. Looking back, the only positives of working at Burger King were that I quickly tired of eating fast food and even today, I am not a huge fan of burgers. Secondly, there was a pretty assistant manager from Puerto Rico who had no problem showing a 16-year-old teenager what a grown woman looked like naked. We’d disappear into the walk-in freezer for a while when work got slow. I don’t think anyone ever noticed. (Burger King on Vernor Highway in Detroit. My first job. Photo source: Google Maps.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: If you were rich, would you live in NYC or Rio de Janeiro?
Answer: As long as no one has to know I am rich, then I am picking Rio — hands down! I really don’t know NYC very well. I have only been there once and it has been over a decade since then. I know that it’s centered a lot more around business and finance, which is really the role of São Paulo in Brazil. I love Rio though and it’s already where I spend part of my year these days. It’s a city and it is also home to millions of people, but it does not feel like a city in much the same way as New York. There is the ocean and mountains that surround the city. Incredibly beautiful sunrises and sunsets each day, world class dining, and an infinitely interesting night life. The pace of life is much slower than even the Midwest city I am from. I often enjoy long lunches in Rio chatting with other people on vacation or people taking a long break from work. It’s always as if time is of very little consequence in Rio. I would choose a rather simple apartment near the ocean in Ipanema and a second home in calmer, but nearby, Tijuca. No one would know I was really rich. I would dress in a T-shirt and shorts as many Cariocas do. I would still wear my Casio watch and pay for things using a credit card. I would enjoy life in one of the places where people from all of the world come to vacation. It’s not such a bad deal. (My Quora profile picture is of me in Rio. This should have given you a clue as to how I’d answer this question. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Since no civilization can last forever, how much longer do you expect the United States to last and what will ultimately be responsible for the downfall?
Answer: Barring some extinction level event, the United States is probably closer to its beginning than end. I think we could see the United States “split up” within the next century, but its geography and shared culture make too much sense, so it will probably reunite with any separatist regions eventually. We need only look to China. It has contracted and expanded over the last couple of thousand years, but it is still the same civilization. Completely destroying the US could happen, but it would likely only happen in an extinction level event (same with China). The US probably won’t be destroyed in the way that you’re thinking. Rather, we will see different iterations of the US over the next few hundred years, but it will remain, fundamentally, the same civilization. No different than what we see with most of the much older countries in the world.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are your thoughts on traveling? Do you ever get tired of it or does it never get old for you?
Answer: Traveling is good for the soul, the ego, and the mind. Yet it can still be tiring and hard on the body. Inevitably, living out of a bag or two always begins to suck after enough time. The experience of exploring new and interesting places never gets old to me though. I have spent most of the last five years traveling and living in just one region of the world and there is still so much I haven’t seen or done here. I can’t imagine the desire to travel, to explore, ever fully dying out in me. That’s how I know I’ve found a passion. (A day spent exploring cenotes, or sinkholes leading to underground rivers, in Yucatán region of Mexico. There are thousands of them, so I’ll never see them all. It won’t stop me from trying. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What movie absolutely scared you when you were a kid?
Answer: The Ten Commandments. Growing up in puritanical America in the 1990’s with sky high teen pregnancy, drug use, and gang violence, we could always count on Charlton Heston’s The Ten Commandments to put us back on the straight and narrow. One Nation, Under God and all that stuff. The Ten Commandments was shown once a year on television, always around Easter. And every Easter I had the unpleasant assignment of watching it along with my twin sister. This movie has all kinds of terrifying and scary shit going on: Moses turns the Nile into blood. Moses turns his staff into a snake. Moses uses wizardry to part the Red Sea, then uses it to kill his enemies. The God of Moses possesses terrifying power that no man can directly witness. Most terrifyingly to me, an ominous Black Smoke kills all of the first born sons of Egypt. Only those who paint their doors with —and I’m not kidding here — a sacrificed lamb’s blood will survive. Ultimately, the movie is scary and confusing for a child. I recommend showing it to your child if you want to scare them away from all organized religions. If you don’t want your teen daughter to get pregnant, show them a short film about safe sex, not The Ten Commandments.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: A genuine question for Americans who have actually travelled out of their country. How do you really find the food that you try in other countries? Is it better, on a par or worse than you have back in the USA?
Answer: This is an incredibly difficult question to answer, because it means giving such a general answer in that one must speak for the entirety of the United States. Generally speaking, this is a foolhardy endeavor. Your experiences in this country are very different across a number of variables including geography, ethnic background, income, class, etc. You get the point. The food in the US is above the world average, but not the best in the world. You can find good and high quality food in most places, in most cities. There can be an insane amount of choice in many grocery stores. For things you can’t get there, there are specialty stores and shops that will sell your favorite niche items (locally raised grass fed beef, anyone?). Furthermore, fine dining in the US isn’t too much different from other major world cities, which is the norm. That’s to say, if you like fine dining, you probably won’t suffer in places like New York, San Francisco, Las Vegas, or Miami. You might in smaller cities though, of which there are dozens, since America is a big place. So, I don’t find that American food is bad, but sometimes I have to travel far to find the food I want. (Lunch at the famous A Casa do Porco in São Paulo, Brazil. Comparing food by country is often pointless. Instead, take part and enjoy the culinary scene in every country in which you travel. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you agree that everyone is a hypocrite?
Answer: Yup. Every single group you can identify or put a label to. Every person that has ever walked the earth. Take for instance, motorcyclists. Here in Middle America they represent freedom, independence, and the American spirit. When you think of patriotic American values you often think of these guys that ride Harleys with the American flag. But where is the American value of personal responsibility when it comes to safety? I see that ever since they’ve changed the laws to allow people to ride sans-helmet, bikers seem to love it. The same people that say “look twice, save a life” don’t really seem to value their own lives enough to protect their noggin. Now how the hell am I supposed to care about your life more than you do? For some reason, a person’s commute to work becomes more virtuous because it is on two wheels. Even though it is known by riders to be more dangerous than simply driving a car or taking the bus. Whenever there is an accident between a motorcycle and a car, the people always look and say it was the “cager” who is at fault. “He was probably on his fucking cell phone!” they say. But you know who else is responsible for motorcycle accidents? Motorcyclists! If you’re going to go 20 miles over the speed limit without wearing a helmet while riding down a main avenue, you don’t get to then blame motorists when bad accidents happen. And yes, I know it’s not all motorcyclists, but it’s enough where people really notice and write articles about it on Quora. Of course, I’m just as much of a hypocrite as motorcyclists. I often write on Quora on my mobile phone while walking down the street. If I am hit by a car, it certainly isn’t my fault. (American Bad Ass and hometown hero, Kid Rock, out for a cruise. Image source: Pinterest.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Lloyd Austin refused to donate A-10 Warthogs to Ukraine with the justification that they would be a “squeaky target” for Russian defenses. Is Austin correct? If so, then why does the US continue to utilize A-10’s? Will the US never fight Russia?
Answer: The A-10 was designed for an entirely different conflict in an entirely different era. As the only dedicated close air support (CAS) platform in the Air Force, it has no meaningful air-to-air capability, so it can only be used in its CAS role when air space is not contested. On the other hand, the F-16 is capable of the CAS role in addition to its air-to-air combat role. The US lost an A-10 against the relatively unsophisticated Iraqi military in 2003, which didn’t even have a functional Air Force. It would be incredibly difficult to employ it in a CAS role near the front lines with Russia, which actually has an Air Force and much more sophisticated surface-to-air missiles. Moreover, as I discussed in a previous answer, Ukraine is actually lacking in pilots for the F-16’s already pledged to the Ukrainian Air Force. Any pilots in the training pipeline for the foreseeable future should be dedicated to training to fly the much more suitable and multi-role F-16. Trying to utilize yet another air frame for the Ukrainian Air Force right now would be an inefficient use of personnel and really isn’t even practical given training considerations (i.e. availability of A-10 pilot training slots) and availability of Ukrainian pilots for training. Dennis Watson's answer to How would the situation be if Ukraine had F-16's but did not have pilots to fly them? The trusty, but old A-10 is just fine in low-intensity conflicts like post-invasion Iraq and Afghanistan. However, it’s not so good against any country that actually has an air force or capable surface-to-air missile batteries in the 21st century. (Capt. Kim Campbell inspects her A-10 after a close call over Baghdad in April of 2003. The next day she flew another mission to support combat search-and-rescue of a downed A-10 pilot. Source: theaviationgeekclub.com)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: West Point is free. Why don't more people apply to West Point so they don't have to take out student loans to pay for tuition?
Answer: Ah, you make it sound so easy. Just a wave of the hand and BAM! You’re in West Point. Let me tell you, West Point already gets more applicants than are eligible. Only about 12% of applicants get into West Point right now and only about 85% graduate (and if you don’t graduate, you now owe Uncle Sam money). In addition to the high academic achievement needed to attend, you must be physically and mentally qualified to be comissioned as an officer in the military. Even relatively minor medical issues like allergies, asthma, and skin conditions can have you disqualified. You must also be physically fit and able to pass the entrance physical agility test. Most people aren’t cut out to go to West Point. Most people already in the military aren’t even cut out to attend a service academy. My training instructor in basic training used to say to us “you’re tired of folding laundry and making beds? In the Air Force Academy, cadets have to do this shit for four whole years! You can’t do it for six weeks?” Everything you do will be inspected and graded for quality. This is on top of the already rigorous academic program and mandatory athletics. If you think you got what it takes, you’re more than welcome to apply. You’d better be high achieving just to have a shot at going. (Soon-to-be Army officers. Source: ABC News.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What makes another unpleasant?

I dread catching up with her at all these days, because I know I have all of the above to look forward to. It’s a bit much. (Neighbors can make or break your desire to live in a neighborhood.
