Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is really ironic?
Answer: If you write for long enough on Quora, you’ll probably dislike your popular answers. They are the answers that will attract misanthropes weeks and even months later who will rage-post in the comments. It’s incredibly annoying, especially when you would have otherwise moved on from a topic weeks or months ago. Now you find yourself having to defend yourself yet again or at the very least read another hate-filled comment. Thus, after a certain amount of time, popular answers are the most likely to have comments disabled. (Pictured: a writer on Quora reading comments from a user in Belgium. The commenter hopes the writer’s children are born as mutants and that he dies in a house fire. Now have a good sleep. Just kidding, but you get the picture. Image credit: Healthline.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are (once) safe cities that are (now) dangerous?
Answer: From the perspective of a man that often solo travels in South America: Medellin. (Museo de Antioquia, Medellin. Photo by Author.) In just a few short years it went from a relatively safe hub for the digital nomad crowd in South America to a funhouse-mirror-version of a city. Now it is plagued with drugs, prostitution (some of it underage), murder, and violent kidnappings or druggings of foreigners. In addition, rents and home prices in expensive neighborhoods like El Poblado have become unobtainable for anyone except the richest of Colombians and foreigners. Simultaneously, crime is invading even El Poblado and the surrounding neighborhoods frequented by tourists. For a preciously small amount of time it still felt like a hidden gem, with a city barely visited except by the intrepid gringo, European, or Aussie, and people from other parts of Latin America. Rents were low. Drinks and joints were cheap. We mingled and shared freely stories about our travels throughout the rest of Latin America. Armed robbery or being drugged in a nightclub existed only as a peripheral threat on our radar. (The Medellin cable car system is praised throughout Latin America as an example of good, practical urban transport. Recently, an accident left 1 dead and 20 injured. Photo by author.) I visited for just a few short days last year. Sadly, the “vibe” of the entire city has changed for me and I probably won’t be visiting again anytime soon. Medellin is a place where the influx of rich foreigners has demonstrably harmed the city and the people. To make matters worse, the migrant crisis from neighboring Venezuela has added fuel to the fire since there is an adjacent network of drugs and human trafficking into the city. Medellin has, thus, become a “perfect” combination of things. A place where people interested in drugs and sex can go to meet people who readily deal in drugs and sex. Additionally, as a foreigner, you represent the opportunity for an enormous pay day to people in the city who are escaping extremely desperate conditions. It seems that every single Venezuelan you meet on the streets has a harrowing tale of poverty, death, and life lived on the fringes of civilization. Some of them are very willing to kill if it means not ever having to live like that again. (Medellin’s infamous Communa 13. Photo by author.) Seeing Medellin today is like seeing your struggling friend who finally got a job, a car that works, and a pretty girlfriend. Only to lose that job and have his car ruined in a crash that permanently scarred his girlfriend. I feel for you my friend. I miss our younger days before we knew the harsh realities of life.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How are older guys attracting younger women?
Answer: In my opinion, older men represent the ideal mate for many younger women. Attraction doesn’t work the same way for men as it does for women. That’s to say, men are least attractive to women when they are in their early 20’s. Maybe not physically, but certainly as someone with which to build a stable relationship (coincidentally, this is why you shouldn’t worry too much about dating success in your 20’s). A man that is graying, is in decent shape, and has money to throw around is dangerous in the dating game in a way that a young man is not. You may literally find yourself up against Batman. (The one and only. Image source: Newsweek)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is your biggest “only in the USA” moment?
Answer: After spending years of my life living and traveling to the tropics in Mexico and South America, I have become conditioned when going to the beach to always have currency. Last fall, I was visiting some friends in the Tampa Bay area and we went to Clearwater Beach for the day. At some point, I got too involved in conversation and noticed only at the last moment that I really had to pee. My friends pointed out to me that the restroom was near the parking lot for the beach. Instead of going directly to the restroom, first I searched my pockets and then my beach bag desperately trying to find coins or bills to pay for the bathroom. My friends were amused, asking what I was doing. Me: “I’m looking for money to pay to use the restroom.” Them: “what are you talking about?” Charging for public restrooms is not a thing in the USA. (Clearwater Beach. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What tiny daily habit could be life changing?
Answer: This morning as I practice this very tiny habit, I actually couldn't wait to share it. Maybe you’ve heard of it before, or maybe you haven’t. I didn’t start this practice at someone’s insistence or because of counseling. Or even because I read it on Quora. I started doing it because one of my friends was doing it and I said “what the heck, why not?”. It’s pretty simple. I write one sentence every morning saying what I am grateful for in a journal. Because really, who doesn’t have five seconds to devote to this practice? I felt there was nothing lost by doing it. Now, I don’t have 100% attendance on this practice. Sometimes I have skipped a day or two, but generally, yes. I remember to do it because I keep my journal somewhere visible and always with a pen nearby. I have a smaller journal that goes into my briefcase when I travel. How long have I been doing it? Now it’s already been nearly three years, I think. I go back and read some of them. Some of them I have actually avoided reading, because I can tell when I was going through a rough time. It’s at those times I keep my gratitudes to super basic shit, like “I’m grateful for life” or something like that. The point is that I at least have to do a perfunctory search for something to be grateful for, on even my worst mornings. How has it changed my life? Okay, I’m not going sit here and bullshit you guys and tell you that I went from homeless to Oprah rich overnight or something like that, but there are some very tangible results I have gained from this practice. I’ll just list them: Conlusion: I can’t imagine my life anymore without practicing this tiny habit that gave birth to other tiny habits that have made me a more grateful, focused, and organized person. My life is undoubtedly made better by it. Perhaps this is a reason to practice daily gratitude from a more pragmatic perspective. (I always keep something to write on nearby, whether I am at home or traveling. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What happened recently that you really didn’t expect?
Answer: I have gone back and forth on whether to write about this. I can delete it later if I want to? I went on a date. Not just any random date though, since I really haven’t been trying that hard. Last month I was leaving to go home to the US for the summer and under rather terrible circumstances. Randomly, I met another American citizen in Playa del Carmen on vacation. We discovered so many unlikely things that we had in common. We both served in the Air Force, we have both lived in Cleveland, we both like to spend our spare time vacationing in Playa Del Carmen, we are both divorced parents of teen daughters. Eerily, both of us had a parent that was murdered. Of course, we are close in age too. We even narrowed down that we had been at one air base at the same time during our careers. It was really weird, man. We exchanged numbers and agreed we would meet for dinner in the future. The only problem is that she lives in a completely different part of the country these days. But, a few a days ago I had a little time to myself and decided to take a flight to see her. Honestly, I kept my expectations incredibly low, but just saw it as more of an opportunity to feel like a tourist in my own country. Something totally unexpected happened in that we really hit it off and had a really fun couple of days together. This woman turned out to be really intelligent and with a really funny sense of humor. I remember pretty much non-stop laughter the entire time. It was great. Yesterday morning, however, things changed rapidly. We’d been sharing text messages every day for the last week or so and yesterday was no different. But things started off very differently. First, she sent me a Tik Tok video saying that monkeypox is essentially a conspiracy by the government to have all of us locked down again. I simply replied with an “ok” to this video. Then she started to share photos from her Ring camera and also screenshots of messages she sent in her neighborhood group chat. To my disgust, she’d sent some of the most virulently racist and sickening messages to one of her neighbors in an effort to get his dog to stop peeing in her yard. These were messages she sent in a group chat with her home owner’s assocation. All of her neighbors could see exactly what she said. Then, she was so proud of herself that she thought she would also show those messages to me. Her HOA blocked her from the group chat. She then asked me what I thought about the entire situation (by text). I told her that I couldn’t believe what I was seeing occur between two fully grown adults. Privately, I was incredibly disappointed that I didn’t pick up on the kind of person she was sooner. I’m still feeling very confused by it all, but I guess you really can’t get to know that much about a person in just a few meetings. I’m glad I know all of this now, but dating has once again made my faith in humanity dip a little bit lower. (Image credit: Ruffle Blog.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why do some kids say school is prison?
Answer: It’s so strange looking back at elementary school especially. I had a hard time sitting still. I was constantly distracted if I was in a classroom that had a view of outside. I would read things unrelated to the instruction I was supposed to pay attention to. In other words, I was a bad student. Even many years later I can still remember the guilt I felt as a child upon this realization. “Ms. Watson, I am afraid Dennis is always distracted, he rarely pays attention, and has to ask for questions to be repeated.” — Every Teacher I Had in Elementary School I can remember the scowls and promises of discipline I received at nearly every parent-teacher conference. What I have discovered so late into adulthood is that sitting at a desk indoors for eight or more hours a day is quite unnatural. I have never suffered from a lack of interest in learning or a desire for achievement in academics. However, it took until my teenage years before I could use sheer willpower to overcome my natural urge to be anywhere other than school. Indeed, school felt like a prison. (Webber Middle School in Detroit, a building I always wanted to escape as a pre-teen. Photo credit: homes.com)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Which type of stolen valor is more prevalent, non-soldiers pretending they are soldiers, or soldiers pretending they’re more important or heroic than they are?
Answer: Yeah, so it’s much harder to fake being in the military if you have never served. I’m not saying it’s impossible. But it’s nearly impossible for someone who didn’t serve in the military to pass for military around military guys for very long. It will all come apart fairly quickly. For a time I worked in private security and one of the other employees lied about serving in the military. This was quickly discovered by me when he didn’t know what a DD-214 was. Seriously, the most basic of military shit. You can’t make it up. To anyone not familiar, the DD-214 is the document that releases us from government slavery. Every single Iraqi Freedom and Enduring Freedom veteran EVER knows what a DD-214 is. However, verifying individual events or even units is much more difficult and you can’t really call anyone out on anything with certainty (unless you see their service record). At the same company, a guy swore that he served in SWCC in the Navy (the elite unit tasked with transporting Navy SEALS by boat). To us, he seemed like a really out of shape idiot with his head constantly up his ass. We more or less tolerated his stories, but always with a healthy dose of suspicion. If he was lying, it was kind of an intelligent lie. He didn’t say Navy SEAL because that might have been too unbelievable amongst a lot of veterans (and we may have taken the initiative to contact someone). SWCC, on the other hand, is cool, but not so cool we ever called him on his bullshit and asked him to show us his record. (Everyone with recent service in the US military knows what a DD-214 (military discharge document) is. There are even a few companies that make DD-214 blankets so veterans can sleep sound knowing they never have to deal with the military again. Photo credit: Amazon.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the best breakfast burrito you have ever had and where did you get it from?
Answer: My favorite place for a breakfast burrito is simply Filiberto’s. Filiberto’s (and its many imitators) can be found throughout the Greater Phoenix, Arizona, area (and Tucson). (A typical Fili-B’s in The Valley. Image source: Google Maps.) Depending on mood, I either get egg, cheese, and chorizo or I get egg, cheese, and steak. You can’t go wrong with either. No potatoes for me, thank you. The only problem is that their salsa isn’t spicy enough for me, so I add a little El Yucateco habanero salsa to it. (A breakfast burrito from Filiberto’s. Hopefully you have someone to share it with. Image source: Door Dash.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What meal from your childhood did you dread being served?
Answer: Hamburger Helper. When I saw this box coming out of the cupboard, I knew I had nothing to look forward to in the rest of my evening. I disliked nearly everything about Hamburger Helper. The ugly box it came in, the creepy anthropomorphic hand featured in the TV advertisements, and of course, the taste. At a young age, I preferred chicken to beef, I didn’t really like the texture of wet noodles, and I remember the flavor as an ill mixture of both savory and sweet that only highly processed foods can deliver. But it was always the stance of my parent that I should never complain if I had anything at all to eat, since she said there were children in the world with nothing. Even at a young age, I could only agree with her logic. Thus, I never ever complained about anything I ate. Still, to this day, I’m not sure my aunt knows how much I really hate Hamburger Helper. I’m glad it’s been over 20 years since I last had to eat it. (What do you call recollections of bad memories? I don’t think nostalgia is the right word, that’s for sure. Just seeing that box makes me shudder. Photo credit: Click Americana.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How does your reoccuring nightmare play out?
Answer: My reccuring nightmare usually plays out the same way each time. It is one I have had for many years now. I’m somewhere at a nice restaurant. The kind with white tablecloths and a piano in the corner. I start to eat my meal and my teeth begin to fall out. But I don’t stop chewing. For whatever reason, I can’t stop chewing. I just continue chewing as more and more of my teeth fall out and mix in with the steak or whatever I’m having. This continues until my mouth is completely full of my loose teeth. It’s a dream, but the unique texture of food and teeth about to be consumed always feels incredibly real. It’s a strange dream to be sure. I always wake up in a sweat at the part where I begin to swallow my loose teeth. I tongue each of my teeth individually to make sure they’re still there. They are. I have all of my teeth, even my widsom teeth. My recurring nightmare ensures I am diligent in how I care for them. (Image source: iStock)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why is the Francesinha the world's best sandwich?
Answer: A franscesinha is a good sandwich and can stave off both hunger and a hangover if eaten at the correct time during a night of drinking in Porto. However, it is not the best sandwich in this world. (Francesihna from Taberna de San Antonio in Porto, Portugal. Photo by author.) Late one rainy night in Montevideo, some Uruguayan friends introduced me to the chivito. It was love at first bite. A greasy sandwich composed of beefsteak, generous amounts of mozzarella, ham, bacon, and (usually) fried or hard-boiled egg. Supposedly there is some tomato and lettuce in it somewhere. I humbly submit it for consideration as the king of sandwiches. Or the sandwich king. Whichever you prefer. (Don’t visit Uruguay without having a chivito, unless you are a vegetarian, then stay away. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you think it is true that those poor people in the West do not live better than those people who make $1 per day in other countries?
Answer: I am originally from Detroit and have lived in and around Cleveland, Ohio, for many years. They are two of America’s poorest and most violent cities, but very typical of Rust Belt cities. As a born and bred midwesterner, I think of both cities as quintessentially American. Let me show you what the poorest parts of Cleveland look like: East Cleveland (Image credit: Bloomberg) St. Clair-Superior (Images sourced from homes.com) Goodrich-Kirtland (Image source: Cleveland.com) Now, are you really asking if the people above live worse than people in a nation like South Sudan, which had an annual GDP per capita of $422? (Image source: The Borgen Project) (Image source: The New Arab) (Image source: Welthungerhilfe) If you go to a poor neighborhood in the US a few things will stand out to you: There is a lot of poverty in the west, but it is relative. Not the kind of absolute poverty where people have to worry about their ability to survive for another day.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Does the USA view the EU as an equal or a junior partner?
Answer: Due to the egalitarian nature of our times, every couple when deciding on a life together profess a desire for a 50–50 relationship. That is where both partners are equals and all decisions are made with dual input. We all know things will not actually go down like this. This is just a pre-marital fantasy. In reality, the wife will be the deciding partner in the majority of serious life decisions. It is she who will decide where you will live, the color of the living room furniture, if you are allowed to ride a motorcycle, or if that tie you’re wearing looks stupid. Furthermore, you will listen when she has told you that you have had too much to drink and it is time to go home. Part of this is just me ranting. The other part is to drive home the point that any relationship, even one as loving as a marriage, will have a partner that has the upper hand. Both partners are always aware of which partner that is. The US is too large, both economically and militarily, for it not to be a part of the calculus in most aspects of the EU’s international decision-making. That factor alone leaves the EU on the disadvantaged side of the relationship. Both partners are aware of this. (General George C. Marshall. Post-WWII Europe was supported in part by the Marshall Plan. The Marshall Plan was not all together altruistic, but implemented with the goal of drawing Post-WWII Europe firmly into American ideological influence to counter the Soviets in Europe. To what extent this worked is debatable. However, the EU nations and the US are today still close allies. Photo credit: Britannica.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why do black people name their children such ridiculous things?
Answer: I have the blandest name ever, so from my perspective, most Black people have pretty normal names. In my family we are just like that. We all have rather anglo-sounding names, except for my daughter. Her mother is also Black, but has always been obsessed with all things Japanese, so my daughter has a Japanese first name. There wasn’t a chance I would have any say in her first name, so I chose her middle name, which is Spanish (which, reflected my obsession with all things Mexican). My daughter has gone on to live in Japan and is fluent in Japanese these days, so perhaps her mother choosing her first name was fortunate. However, it wouldn’t surprise me if many people thought her name is just a made-up ethnic sounding name. People draw their inspiration for names from all kinds of places. Even as a Black person I won’t pretend to know how other Black people arrive at choosing something so personal. I have enough decency to respect our differences though and call people by what they ask me to call them. We are a polite people ‘round these parts.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Which country has the best trained soldiers in the world? What makes their training superior to other countries?
Answer: This is essentially a philosophical question, since there really isn’t a right answer, just endless debate. My stab at answering the question would be one of the European countries with a smaller military, but good funding. (Swiss Guard. Image source: military history now) (Special Operations Forces of Sweden. Image source: Reddit) (Polish Special Operations Forces. Image source: Reddit) However, that doesn’t mean these militaries are the best in combat. Usually it means they have a lot of time and resources for training, but low deployment tempo. Good infantry soldiers also rank lowly in terms of military importance. They are easily replaceable compared to much more important military equipment and are usually not a force multiplier. Several things are much more important to military effectiveness, they include: (Reaper drone. Image credit: Wikipedia) This isn’t to say that soldiers aren’t at all important, but they are in reality a much smaller piece of the pie in militaries capable of combined arms warfare.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is the Earth a dangerous place to live without the help of people?
Answer: From what I’ve observed, I’d say so. I wrote in another recent answer how my part of Ohio experienced a number of tornadoes that knocked out power for several days. Late one night of the outage I couldn’t sleep. I woke up and looked out of my window at some of the very large and beautiful homes that sit along the lake in my neighborhood. I live several floors up, but in the otherwise quiet and darkness it was impossible not to see and hear a few things. I could not ignore the few homes which had lights on and the loud and distinct hum of diesel generators. In an outage that lasts just a few days these people are, of course, safe. However, in a real disaster these people would be in extreme danger. It would be clear they have the resources to survive a little longer than others and they’d become a target. This is why, if you are smart, in a disaster you will band together with those close to you. You will work as a group to obtain the resources, food, and protection needed to survive. Then divide those resources amongst yourselves. Going it alone is suicidal. People offer protection that even money can’t guarantee.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is there hazing in the military?
Answer: Yes and there always will be. Hazing is an inseparable part of military culture. All great military institutions engage in hazing on some level. It is something used to separate “us” from everyone else who isn’t “us.” Perhaps this is a bit controversial, but I think hazing has its place in the military as long as it doesn’t go overboard. I would not, for example, go to the Navy Seals or Marine Marsoc guys and tell them: please don’t do anything to these sailors and marines that might resemble hazing. To me, that’s a bit preposterous. We’re preparing these guys to operate in the most austere and dangerous environments known to man. Forgive me if I am not too concerned they might get an ass kicking at the hands of their teammates when they fuck up. Even SERE/survival school is, to an extent, institutionalized hazing and torture. We could simply show our soldiers with a movie what it is like to be sleep deprived, cold, hungry, and alone. We don’t do that because we know there’s an added benefit in actually experiencing it, with very little downside. However, outside of these limited circumstances and career fields, serious hazing of a physical or psychological nature is counterproductive and bad for unit esprit de corps. We usually try to stick to more funny gags. (Members of my unit captured a “terrorist” in our barracks. Later we sent him to our version of GITMO. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the best thing that has happened to you recently?
Answer: I’m home for summer and some days ago we had a few tornadoes pay us a visit. I’ve never seen any storm like this in the Midwest before. Extremely heavy winds and rains that downed several enormous trees throughout my neighborhood. The destruction was enough to knock out electricity for about 50% of the residents of my county. I spent a few years living in hurricane prone southern Mexico, so I’m no stranger to power outages or nasty weather. Still, it has been a long time since I went several days in a row without electricity. I also had a weak or nonexistent cellular signal. This was unexpected. Suddenly, without WiFi, reliable cellular service, or electricity, I found myself living in a different century, practically. What was remarkable was that with me having to take the stairs every day, throwing away all the meat and vegetables in my refrigerator, and eating picnic snacks for meals for a few days, I was pretty worry-free. No frequent updates from social media, work projects, Quora, or other stuff. It was just me and the outdoors. So, the best thing that happened to me recently was that I was transported back to a time before smart phones or internet, if only for a few days. And it was peaceful. (Image source: Pinterest)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why are Nordic countries usually ranked as the happiest?
Answer: They are ranked as happiest because the metrics used are arbitrary and inherently biased against developing countries (e.g. one metric is GDP per capita). What should be clear is that these surveys aren’t measuring emotional happiness. (Mexico, a country that ranked only 25th in the 2023 report. Photo by author.) The World Happiness Report uses GDP per capita, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom, generosity, and corruption as proxies for happiness. This isn’t the same as asking someone “how stoked are you about life right now, man?”. Look at the countries that top the so-called Happiness Report: (Source: World Happiness Report) Now here’s the list of countries that top charts in suicide (CLICK and ZOOM IN!): (Source: World Bank) So, you’re saying that seven of the top 10 happiest countries also rank in the top 20 list of nations that kill themselves? Yes. Now I am not saying that suicide rate is a perfect proxy for unhappiness, but people who commit suicide are generally pretty miserable. Also, intuitively, I don’t think anyone that has ever visited Iceland and then Spain can honestly say that Iceland is the happier place to live. You don’t see any retired Brits flocking to Reykjavik to buy a retirement home. The Happiness Index is really just measuring the factors that make life comfortable and, generally speaking, make one content with life. These societies lack extreme poverty, extreme violence, and extreme quality of life issues. That doesn’t make them a place I would look to live as an emigrant though. I’d much prefer better climate and food in a country like Mexico that ranks much lower on the Happiness Index, but which we all know is a happier place in real life. It’s why Cancun receives millions of visitors a year and many of us Americans can tell you about an epic night out in Tijuana or Cancun. Almost none of us have a cool story that started in Copenhagen.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: For dating, how important is it that a guy needs to be over six feet and makes six figures?
Answer: I’m a 5’8 guy. Based on personal experiences and observations, the height thing is a factor with very few women. Most women are open to dating a guy who is shorter than six foot, since most of the men in the world are not six foot tall. This is just a reality. I often see this six foot quote and I really think it comes from some incel-type dudes that want to tell themselves the reason no one wants to date them is because of their stature. The fact that they lack gainful employment, have a neck beard, own a collection of manga, and sit around watching internet porn all day is conveniently left out. You don’t need to make six figures, but you should be able to make enough money to take care of yourself before you get out there into the dating market as an adult. Some women won’t date you because you don’t make enough money. Some women won’t date you because you’re not tall enough. Others will reject you for other reasons. This is all very normal and although rejection stings, you just keep going. In time, the ones who rejected you will surely be outnumbered by the ones who didn’t. However, it takes a winner’s mentality to see things that way. You won’t find that in the kind of man who makes excuses because of his height or income. (The author, a “short king.”)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Can you live without a car in any American city?
Answer: For certain segments of the population, rather easily. The important things to keep in mind though: (Waiting for the Red Line in Houston, Texas, last weekend. The public transit in this city is okay, but extreme daytime temperatures discourage public transit use. Photo by author.) (Cleveland is very walkable, but the bus and light rail will get you to everywhere else you can’t go to by foot. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you travel to any country?
Answer: Nope, there is a list of countries I either can’t or won’t travel to due to either security issues or political reasons. They include places like North Korea, Russia, Chad, Venezuela, and China. I am open to visiting any of those countries if the security situation changes or the relationship between my government and their government changes. Until then, I’ll just dream of that day.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the most dangerous developed country you had ever been to? How about the safest country (whether developed or undeveloped)?
Answer: Most dangerous developed country is my home country of the United States. Our nation of ~330 million has about 20,000 homicides a year. Additionally, robbery and assaults are other common types of violent crimes. (The USA has a homicide rate more than double the OECD average.) At the other end of the spectrum, I have also been to Iceland, which is a country with a population of about 400,000 people. For the last year that I could find a statistic, 2022, four people were murdered in Iceland. This seems to be about average most years. This makes sense why it seems like such a relaxed country. I only remember seeing the police at the airport.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is it true that if you played American football in school or are a muscular man in America, you will be respected by those around you?
Answer: In my experience, no, not automatically. In the Air Force, where it is mostly men in a military police (security forces) unit, muscular men were valued, but not necessarily respected. In my unit we had one really tall and muscular non-commissioned officer, who was more or less good at performing the duties of a patrolman and had been improbably promoted to a supervisory position. He liked to powerlift and had massive, capable hands. Despite his senior rank, he was nice to have as a patrol supervisor because he would be great as backup if you needed someone who could smash someone’s head, rip someone out of a vehicle, or back you up on an alarm call. Basically, anything that required strength or aggression. He was unhelpful, however, in any situation that required subtlety or insight greater than that of a 12-year-old. He was a valuable member of our team, but not so highly respected because of his personality and intellectual shortcomings. Eventually he was discharged in connection with his steroid abuse. (He was built something like this AI created soldier. Image source: playground.com.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What’s a recent lesson you’ve learned?
Answer: You should always rewind your videotapes when returning them to Blockbuster. You never know when that shit will catch up to you. It could be twenty years later when you’re applying for a pilot’s license. Edit, shared in the comments:

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What's it like to have a twin?
Answer: Having a twin, first and foremost, means sharing. Everything. Your holidays, your birthdays, your schools, and nearly every moment of your parent’s attention. For my twin sister and I, it also meant we instantly had someone else to be compared to. We received our reports cards for the same classes on the same day. We would spar in the same martial arts tournaments. Who received the most medals or trophies would be obvious. I grew to love school, my sister hated it and rarely attended school as a teenager, eventually dropping out. I went to college, she did not. Still, my twin sister is strong in ways that I am not. Despite not having many advantages, she has made her life work and raised some wonderful kids. My niece will soon go to the same university I attended. She is a really intelligent and model teenager. My twin sister and I have lived radically different lives as adults and I have spent much of my life in places far away from her. We aren’t even especially close, but we have a mutual respect and loving for each other as any siblings. We have entirely different personalities and an entirely different outlook on life. (I have a twin, but not this kind of twin. My twin is a girl. Image credit: Smithsonian Magazine.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is it true that if you don't tip in the U.S., you get bad customer service?
Answer: Yeah, you will on repeat visits to some places. Wait staff, barbers, and pizza delivery guys remember people that don’t tip well. Even in the early 2000’s, we used to note in our computer at the pizzeria which addresses didn’t tip and which tipped well. A $5 tip at the time meant dropping everything else and taking care of that order first. At some places like bellhops at a hotel you’ll never visit again, skycaps at a random airport, and taxi drivers, you could theoretically not tip and get away with it. However, since it is traditional to tip these people, Americans think lowly of people who don’t. As Mr. Pink’s exposition in Reservoir Dogs will tell you, you could theoretically get away with not tipping. But if you are like many Americans who live in the same neighborhood their entire lives, you’ll definitely have trouble getting good service.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do you feel about immigrants in your country?
Answer: I think my views on immigration are about middle-of-the-road as they are with a lot of things. I have lived in Mexico and South America. I continue to spend at least part of my year in these places. The countries south of the border don’t seem all that scary to me, but like most people, I am for legal migration only. This is as a pragmatist. We should know who is crossing the border and why they’re here. This is to, as best as we can, keep the criminal elements out of the country that operate with impunity south of the border. I have seen what they are capable of. It’s not pretty. We also need to disempower the human traffickers and their wretched trade that takes advantage of some of the most vulnerable people on the planet. I am all for making it easier for both highly-skilled and lowly-skilled immigrants to come here, to do jobs Americans can’t or won’t do. Immigration for the United States has largely been a positive, but we have the right to choose who does and doesn’t get to come here like any other country.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What was your last memorable meal?
Answer: Last night was one of those rare nights both a friend and I had time to hang out. We went to a restaurant in my city that specializes in food from Singapore, but also has a few other regional dishes from Asia. I go to this restaurant about twice a year, usually with the same friend. For good reason — we both love it. It’s a small, humble little place with a few lopsided tables and chairs. Just a married couple runs the place. A woman from my city and her husband who is from Singapore. How their marriage survives running a restaurant together, I’ll never know. One problem here is that we always forget what we ordered last time (did we get the char bee hoon or char kway teow?). This means I usually end up eating something different each time. Last night I ordered something called carrot cake, which the proprietor explained to me doesn’t contain carrots and is not a cake. Instead it is a dish made with steamed turnips and stir fried with eggs and seasonings. There is a white and a black version, I do know the difference really, but ordered black which she said is sweeter, but would come with some spice. It would be the first of a couple of courses and dessert. Due to the lack of personnel, but great many orders, this restaurant receives, you can always expect to wait a long time to get any food. My friend and I had a lot of time to talk. Being the caring and good-natured person she is, she wanted to know how I’ve been doing with all that has gone on lately. Like many men, I find it difficult to be vulnerable in these situations, but I had nothing but time and hunger, which makes for an incredibly good interrogation technique. For the next hour I got to talk about my travels this year, some of the mistakes I made, and the loss of my little sister. Mercifully, our steaming hot appetizer came out right around the time I felt drained and tired of talking about myself and my emotions. Our meal was memorable because of the novelty of trying the sweet, savory, salty, and spicy carrot cake which does not contain carrots or cake. It was also memorable because I got to share it with a friend who cared enough to have dinner with me just to see if I am doing ok. (“Carrot cake.” Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: In what ways are you lucky?
Answer: So many things: (A pretty lucky guy with ice cream. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What were your favorite candies as a kid?
Answer: Candy corn. But especially the pumpkins! Who knows what this candy is made from, or what it’s supposed to even taste like. The important thing is that I loved it and a lot of other kids didn’t. More for me! (Source: Wikipedia) Chick-O-Stick. Hands down favorite. This combination of crunchy peanut butter candy with coconut, vanilla, and a dash of salt is the gold standard of candies. They always seemed hard to find, but when we found them, we were happy. (Source: Atkinson candy company) Laffy Taffy. This is the favorite candy of dentists too! It sticks to your teeth and is hard to get out, but delivers a kick of flavor that only artificial fruit, red dye #40, and high fructose corn syrup can deliver. As a bonus, there’s always a funny joke on the wrapper. (Source: Jack’s candy) Whoppers. The complex and rich flavors of the malted milk ball were the pinnacle of childhood snootiness. Only a real candy connoisseur like me could appreciate a candy like this. The other kids were perfectly happy with Skittles. (Source: Walmart) Toblerone. Only on special occasions like Christmas and had to be shared equally among all family members. You’d be skipped if you had been naughty recently. (Source: Pinterest)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How are college dorm roommates selected?
Answer: I was randomly assigned my roommate for my first year in college. This is not a good system. However, I didn’t know anyone living on campus that needed a roommate. If you know someone you can state your preference for that person, with most colleges you’ll likely get that person (as long as they’re the same gender). My first roommate was a strange guy. He loved to watch sports, but refused to use the common showers to ever take a shower. Similarly, he refused to do his own laundry, preferring to take it home on the weekends for his mother to do. Therefore, it wasn’t long before our room came to smell offensive. Even people in distant dorm rooms would comment on our malodorous living space. My roommate was too shy to eat in the dining hall of our college, so he made sandwiches that always included barbecue sauce from lunch meat he kept in a refrigerator in our room. We went through lots of ups and downs. Let’s just say that my roommate wasn’t very ready for the world, even the safe world of a college campus. He had a crush on a girl and we went over so many times what he needed to do. Some evenings he would just come back to our room and cry. We never really fought though except for one night he wouldn’t shut up while watching basketball. I yelled at him to shut the f*** up because I had an exam the next day. Of course, he ended up crying himself to sleep and I felt terrible. When the school year ended, so did any chance at friendship, but we survived it. Despite everything, I still recommend living on campus for new college students. This is your first chance to socialize as an independent adult. What you learn here is just as important as in the classroom. Please be courteous though and remember that minimizing body odor will increase your odds of successfully dating.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What can’t AI do, even given unlimited resources?
Answer: AI can’t tell you what it’s like to eat escamoles for the first time. Or what’s so special about the TV series The Wire. AI can’t tell you what it is like to rekindle a relationship with an old flame, only to have it again end in bitterness. AI, cannot possibly tell you which restaurant in Detroit offers a superior coney. Even given unlimited resources, AI cannot describe the utter embarrassment one suffers when learning to tango. Only I can do that, because I am a human. To hear or read those words from a computer is meaningless. This is what platforms like Quora used to be good for.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What do you think about Republicans refusing to admit that America has a gun problem?
Answer: Because of this simple reality: Republicans don’t live in places where gun violence is much of a problem. Republicans mostly live in suburban and rural areas of America and that totally changes your perspective on how you see gun violence. Of the 20 most dangerous cities (if you believe such rankings), only two are Republican lead cities: Miami, Florida and Stockton, California. 20 Most Dangerous Cities in America (2024 Updated) Republicans and Democrats see the issue of gun violence differently because they live in two different countries.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do we save western civilization?
Answer: A common project that unites the west in both ideology and motion. Millions of people working together with the belief a common good can be achieved. The Soviets understood the ability of grand gestures to galvanize and unite. Soviet ventures into space with man and artificial satellites were about much more than science. With the right project we can create new truths and even new myths that buttress our society. (Soviet space propaganda. Image source: PBS.) Creation of secular civic rituals for the irreligious and the differently religious. The 21st century is a diverse one and there is no going back. People of all ethnicities, races, and religions are living and working closely together. America did this the best in the 20th century. Everyone, regardless of background, was invited to pledge allegiance to the flag. The national identity took precedence over ethnic, religious, or racial identity. The multicultural west needs to forge a new common identity, reinforced by civic rituals in which all of us can take part. (Image source: Wikipedia) Abundant beauty. What we did for science in the 20th century, we should do for beauty in the 21st century. Our cities are optimized for function over form. Let’s not totally reverse that, but we have to acknowledge that humans need beauty in our lives and build the places we live accordingly. We are not ants meant to live in tidily organized rows in identical and ugly homes. A beautiful civilization is something to live for, even die for. (American suburbs. Image source: Medium.) De-emphasize the individual. At least for a while. Right now our society is too atomized and apathetic to care about the whole. Legally, we should protect the rights of all individuals. Socially, we need constant reminders of how much we need each other to survive as a civilization. Reconciliation and collective effort will move us forward.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What do you think other people notice about you first?
Answer: Usually, it’s my arms. Somehow, going into middle-age I managed to regain some of the athleticism of my youth by training really freakin’ hard. That and good genetics through selective breeding of my ancestors. I’m on the shorter side of average height, which really tends to emphasize just how big of an upper body I have. Additionally, I got an ill-advised tattoo on my left bicep in college that tends to draw people’s eyes to my arms. I know people notice this as sometimes they come up to me and say “damn man, you got some big arms!” Like I forgot or something. It has pros and cons. pros: Cons: (Daisy and me. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why did you decide to join the military, as well as your branch and occupation?
Answer: This is a funny story, because I think it says something about how you should be careful in raising your children. To put it simply, I didn’t join the military for one single reason, but for a few. The first was that I needed money. This was the primary reason I joined both the military and the Air Force, specifically. I’d just finished my second year of college. I had a full academic scholarship, but I’d lived on campus in the very expensive dorms. I had to pay for that through loans or grants. For whatever reason, I had a $2,000 bill left at the end of my second year. It meant I couldn’t enroll in classes or even get a copy of my transcripts before I paid the balance. $2,000 might not seem like a lot of money today, but it was more than I could think of getting ahold of in 2005, so I looked to the military. The military would give me money, a job, and contribute to my college tuition. Additionally, the Air Force was the most attractive because they were offering me a $10,000 signing bonus for the job I already wanted. Silly me, I thought I would get $10,000 the moment I signed on the dotted line, but my recruiter was honest and told me that it doesn’t work like that. I knew I wanted to be a part of the military police no matter what branch I joined. The reason was twofold. First, I was raised by my aunt, who always told me stories about my uncle being an MP in the marines. Once a year she would show me some of the pictures she had of him in uniform on duty in Hawaii. For someone that had never left Detroit, the pictures of my uncle in the tropics always stayed with me and stoked my desire or adventure. Secondly, I was never allowed to touch anything resembling a gun (including water guns) when I was a child. So, when I decided I was going to join the military, I definitely wanted a job where I could learn to use and play with all of the weapons. Be careful which stories you tell your children. And be seriously careful about which prohibitions you give to your children. It tends to backfire. (Forgetting any noise or light discipline in the desert and upsetting our boss: priceless. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: If a US citizen is living in Mexico and is wanted for a crime committed in the US, can a warrant be issued for their arrest with the Mexican authorities?
Answer: There could be a warrant in the sense that if Mexican authorities run a check on you against the Interpol database, it could show a Red Notice issued in your name. That’s if the agency that has a warrant for your arrest has contacted Interpol and they are provided with a warrant for a serious offense. Usually rape, murder, kidnapping. That kind of serious. Lesser, misdemeanor types of offenses do not qualify. About Red Notices A Red Notice itself isn’t technically a warrant, but it tells the police in any Interpol member nation that you’re a wanted fugitive and to apprehend you.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is Ohio a good place to live?
Answer: Provided you can answer just one question, Ohio can be a great place to live. Will you have a good job or good source of income in Ohio that includes good health insurance? If you can answer yes, you’re in a pretty ideal place to live in the US. The median salary in Ohio is on the lower end, at $36,000 per year. Low level professionals in much of Ohio will earn a salary at or above this wage and mid-level professionals, substantially higher. Let’s take a look at my city using a website I often use to compare cost of living in various cities around the world. The Earth Awaits - Cleveland, OH, United States With the cost of living calculator, I can make adjustments based on family size and lifestyle (very lean, lean, modest, ample, and opulent). (Cost of living calculator. Source: The Earth Awaits). Let’s just choose the opulent level, which takes a normal cost of living and multiplies it by a factor of 1.75. For a single person, it calculates that an opulent cost of living would be $ 4,038.36 or about $48,000 a year (net). I think that amount is really accurate. That would be the take home pay of someone earning between $60–$70k. That’s enough to live in a nice and safe neighborhood, own a decent car, buy groceries at good grocery stores or farmer’s markets, dine out 1–2 times a week a decent restaurant. Take at least one international vacation, a domestic vacation, and a few long weekends every year. All for $60-$70k in earnings a year for an individual or (according to the calculator), a household net income of $78,000 for a household of three. (Cleveland has good or high metrics in almost every category except crime. However, crime is highly dependent on neighborhood and in reality, applies mostly to the inner-city and not to suburbia where most professionals will live. Healthcare is great, but expensive without good insurance.) In other words, in Ohio you can still have the American dream for a fraction of the cost of just about anywhere else. All on a salary that’s obtainable in just a few years in a white collar position or as a professional tradesman. Yes, Ohio is a good place to live as long as you have a good income.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why do so many Americans have a problem with alcohol?
Answer: Drinking is a large part of adult culture in the United States. Although I have gone long periods of my adult life without drinking, I have never given drinking up completely because I have realized it makes social situations more awkward. Some people get really uncomfortable if they are drinking and not everyone else at the table is drinking. It’s also a time-honored tradition to conduct certain business meetings in informal sessions that sometimes feature drinking. Additionally, sports, holidays, and cookouts usually involve alcohol. In my family, this isn’t a problem really. A few weeks ago we had a family gathering and a close friend came with me. She remarked how no one in my family drinks at all or does any drugs except me. First of all, survivorship bias is apparent. Secondly, because there have been so many people with substance abuse issues in my family, drinking or smoking marijuana, although perfectly legal, are nearly taboo. Our family gatherings are usually completely devoid of alcohol, because nearly everyone in my close family gave up drinking in any form years ago or never developed an interest. We never tell our guests one way or another that they can’t bring drinks, but if they do, they’re usually the odd man out. Although I used to be a nearly daily drinker, these days I no longer prefer to drink as the main way I relax after a rough day. Increasingly, I am not the only one. Many young people are putting aside alcohol in favor of more holistic hobbies that don’t take such a toll on the body and mind. Going to a local adult arcade or bar and ordering a mocktail or alcohol free beer isn’t that unusual around here these days. (Cigar, whiskey, and sports! There was a time when I thought this was all there was to life. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Where do wealthy people who live in the Midwest go on vacation?
Answer: Popular places with midwesterners, but definitely not in order: Basically, people who have money vacation where everyone else from the Midwest vacations (if they have enough time and money to go on vacation). (Mackinac Island’s Grand Hotel in Upper Michigan. This isn’t a place to visit if you’re cheap. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Will Venezuela face a mass exodus similar to the one that took place on the border with Colombia over the past decade?
Answer: A mass exodus is already ongoing. People have been leaving Venezuela as quickly as they can for over a decade due to the harsh reality of life there. Many of the Venezuelans remaining are those that haven’t gathered the resources to leave or must stay due to other life circumstances. I don’t think anyone was really counting on a free and fair election in Venezuela, least of all, Venezuelans. Maduro already demonstrated that by doing everything he could to trip up his opposition before the election. (Maduro dines at a Salt Bae restaurant in New York. Photo source: CNN).

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What was the biggest scandal at your high school?
Answer: I am not sure if scandal best describes the situation, but let’s just say that vicious rumors occurred. My senior year, just weeks before our graduation, one of my classmates was killed in a car accident. It was actually on a day that most of us were skipping school (Senior Skip Day). This was a tradition and rite of passage for graduating seniors in Detroit public schools. People that had cars would go out to one of the large parks out in the suburbs or to Belle Isle, an island park in the middle of the Detroit River. My classmate, Juan, along with friends and girlfriends, decided to visit a park out in the suburbs. Juan had a nice, shiny, black pickup truck that was bought for him by his parents as a graduation gift. The rumor was that his girlfriend was in the passenger seat while Juan played with the steering wheel and that she attempted to grab the wheel to stop Juan from joking around. In the process, she caused the accident that resulted in Juan being ejected from the vehicle and dying. Whether it was true or not, didn’t matter. Juan had been an incredibly popular kid in our school and to some extent, his girlfriend was blamed for his death. It all happened so abruptly it shocked all of us. It was a little terrifying how someone so young, intelligent, and promising could be taken away from us so soon. In the wake of his loss, his girlfriend was unjustly made to suffer.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is it currently safe to travel to Peru with the state of emergency in place?
Answer: I have a friend, a fellow veteran, that sometimes travels with me to dangerous places. Last month he returned from several weeks in Peru, completely alone. He said it was interesting for the hiking, otherwise unremarkable and boring. His feelings largely mirror my own. If you travel to Peru right now you’ll almost certainly be safe. Avoid areas where protestors may gather. Stay alert to the changing threats by monitoring news and travel alerts. Register your location and phone number with your embassy. Most importantly, only drink bottled water. Other than that, you should be okay. (Riding ATV’s in the Peruvian countryside. Photo by author). I’m not sure if you are a US citizen or not, but the US embassy in Lima does a good job at posting alerts when there are planned protests or a change in the security situation. Currently, they are not advising against travel to Peru, and the US embassy tends to be the most paranoid.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How many flights are there to Mexico City?
Answer: Mexico City airport is the busiest airport in all of Latin America. It’s an important airport that connects Mexico to South America, the United States, Europe, and Asia. There are about 1,000 aircraft movements (departures and arrivals) each day for flights coming and going from all over the world, but especially from South America, the United States, and Caribbean. You’ll easily find non-stop daily flights to New York, Miami, Havana, Bogota, Buenos Aires, Panama City, Madrid, and Tokyo. (Boarding a flight to Cancun from Mexico City. Photo by author).

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: People who grew up poor then entered the middle class as adults, what changes did you notice the most?
Answer: I noticed that most aspects of life are easier, but not all of them. I have been middle class for nearly all of my adult life, but grew up in urban poverty in Detroit. I think that living in America’s middle class is a very fortunate place to be in society, especially when compared to life, globally. However, I think it’s interesting that America’s middle class comes across as the most worried and anxious in life, but maybe that’s because they make up most of the population. Or it could be my opinion because these are the people with which I am most familiar. When I was poor we had worries, but in some ways we worried less, because we had less to lose. Middle class Americans live very similar lives in that we are college educated or work in a trade, live in the suburban areas of large cities (with a few exceptions), often work Monday - Friday types of jobs, take yearly vacations, and own our own homes. The biggest problems faced by the middle class are: (1) the price of admission into a middle class life has risen steeply. Particularly, college and professional education. (2) For most middle class Americans, their health insurance is tied to their job or small business. Long term illness can be a very real threat to your way of life, should you encounter it. Those two things cover probably 70% of the worries of middle class Americans. Just two issues, but they’re both incredibly expensive issues. Living around other middle class people means hearing them complain about these issues all of the time. Keep in mind though, most middle class people are from middle class homes. To them, the world seems worse, because they don’t have the same lifestyle their parents had at a similar age. For those of us from poverty that are middle class, we have a much different outlook on what it means to be middle class. We are usually much more grateful.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What's it like to live in Mexico City?
Answer: Intense. Loud. Exhilerating. Delicious. It’s cloudy a lot. Doesn’t get too hot, doesn’t get too cold. No two days are ever the same. I had an international group of friends. Mexicans born and raised in the capital, Mexican-Americans returning to Mexico, gringos like me, people from Europe, especially former Soviet Republics. I think this is a pretty normal friend group for young professionals living there. There’s a million places to see, so you’ll never see them all in a life time. I still haven’t gotten around to seeing the place where Trotsky got whacked. With the dire water situation in Mexico City, I am terrified for the future of the capital. I wouldn’t choose to live there right now.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How has international travel changed since you started doing it?
Answer: I did not start traveling much until my mid-20’s (early 2010’s) and so much has changed in just the past 15 years. Some of those things obvious, some of them not so obvious. (747 landing at Maho Beach on the island of Saint Martin. Photo by author). Mobile phones were just expensive bricks once you left the United States. Purchasing international service was extremely expensive and not something done by a casual traveler. Instead, I frequently navigated the streets of places like Rome, Paris, and Athens praying that for Christ’s sake I could find someone who spoke English and could give directions. I missed buses, showed up at the wrong places, got ripped off by cab drivers. Because there was no Google Maps, you automatically identified yourself as a dumb and lost tourist all the time by holding up a map made for dumb and lost tourists. How humiliating. Navigation is now a cinch. Your phone gives you turn by turn directions in any large city on earth. As long as I have a signal I can order a taxi or rideshare, even if I don’t speak the local language. Google Maps is even available offline, if you download a map of the city you’re traveling to beforehand. Payments are much easier. Many more places accept credit cards now. You can also verify payment and conversion amounts immediately through mobile banking apps. You can settle payment disputes at the moment of occurrence, instead of waiting to see a statement after returning home. Hidden gems are mostly a thing of the past. Everyone can do a ton of research through Youtube, Trip Advisor, or right hear on Quora. The last frontier in travel is either to extremely distant, extremely dangerous, or extremely expensive places. Everything else is accessible to the common traveler. Language is less of a barrier. These days I find that many young travelers spend time learning at least some basics in language apps like Duolingo. There are language classes on Youtube, and you can watch foreign programming. Additionally, Google Translate is there when traveling abroad and also available offline. Airbnb or vacation rentals are mainstream. Before, this system was mostly the purview of budget travelers, much more informal, and required a bit of effort to book in advance. Today, I can book a vacation rental for several months, in just a few moments in an app like Airbnb. Both parties get certain assurances through a third party like Airbnb and a high level of transparency. Friends are easier to make. I use apps popular with nomads like Couch Surfing, Meetups, or Facebook to find other nomad meetups.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are the pros and cons of globalization?
Answer: Globalization Pro: common prosperity. Clean drinking water, access to medications that treat or prevent diseases like cancer, malaria, polio, and HIV/AIDS in even the poorest of nations. Even in the developing world, most people will live to see the age of 70. Con: common prosperity. We’re using more of our earth’s resources than ever. Many years ago, this sin was the domain of the developed world. Today, nearly all of humanity contributes to the proliferation of single use plastics, extraction of rare earth minerals, and carbon emissions. Almost every aspect of modern life requires, at least in some small measure, extraction of a resource. Something that is not infinite. That goes for that cup of coffee you sip or the power generated so that you can read this very sentence, thousands of miles away from where it was written. (The real breakthrough of the 20th century was not the atomic bomb or space travel. It was containerization of cargo. Photo source: Logitude World). Pro: sameness. I travel a lot. One thing I hate is having to carry this big clunky thing that allows me to plug my laptop or mobile phone into an outlet, no matter what country I am visiting. That’s about it though. I can expect most aspects of my day-to-day life to be the same in cities the world over. I can use an app to order food, or find a McDonald’s or Starbucks nearby. I can order a ride-share in an Uber or something similar. I can stay at an Airbnb or chain hotel with similar levels of quality. Con: sameness. It has made traveling the world more predictable than ever! People rebel from the predictability of the modern world by venturing even further off of the beaten path. New places are exposed as being authentic and interesting. Tourism thrives, but the majority of locals see little difference in their standard of living. Sometimes they are pushed even further out of city centers. Traditional ways of living give way to economic considerations. (Quick, what city is this? Philadelphia? London? Could be any modern city on a river. Globally, even the boldest architecture still leaves our cities looking alike. Photo by author). Pro: outsourcing of labor. This gave us the world for cheap. Cheap blenders, refrigerators, and televisions. Now developing nations are not just the source of such goods. Most developing nations actually import consumer goods, because even the people in developing nations can afford such things. Con: outsourcing of labor. In the world of cheap and efficient containerized shipping, it matters much less whether your clothing is made in China, Vietnam, or Bangladesh. The manufacturer will go where labor is cheapest. This is a race to the bottom. Today, the people who make our things still work in deplorable and slave-like conditions. This isn’t a secret, so much as it is something hidden from view through a complex supply chain and intermediaries. The modern world doesn’t just outsource labor, but also outsources pain and suffering to the lowest common denominator. (Trash on a beach in Indonesia. Source: Green Queen).

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the reason behind the majority of Black migration to the East Coast rather than other parts of America, such as the West Coast?
Answer: It’s quite simple, you see. The area known today as the Rust Belt, was at one time the Steel Belt. There were jobs in industry there, which were uncomplicated and could be worked by people with minimal training and skills. In the Mississippi Delta, where my grandparents all came from, the only jobs for black people were in poorly paid agricultural jobs that were incredibly hard on the body. My grandfather would move from Mississippi to Detroit in the late 1940’s, he would go on to work on the factory line assembling cars at Ford. On his single salary, he was able to provide for his entire family of six, which included my grandmother who was a stay-at-home mother. (A black family heads north. Source: Getty Images). The promise of such a lifestyle is what drew millions of Black Americans north in a process that lasted several decades known as the Great Migration. Great Migration (African American) - Wikipedia

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is life like after getting a government job?
Answer: US government perspective: interesting. Very interesting. My first position after finishing graduate school was a lowly position with Veterans Affairs in Phoenix, Arizona. It would be the first of several positions in different federal agencies. Pay: sucks for your first few years. At least your base pay. If your position is in an expensive market you will have a long commute or live in a dangerous neighborhood if your office is in a downtown. Crime: if you haven’t committed a federal crime at this point in your life, you will now! You will unknowingly or willfully commit a crime by violating an agency rule or federal law. You will accidentally leave confidential information in a place it shouldn’t be, violate the privacy Act, or just ignore a dumb fucking rule you shouldn’t have to follow. Others resort to committing financial fraud and falsifying records. Your level of exposure to federal prosecution depends on how closely your agency wants to look at you. I saw a few careers end in federal prison or suicide. Stressful: my first position meant dealing with veterans in difficult situations who were sometimes homicidal, suicidal, or both. Sometimes we had to take time from work to deal with a federal investigation involving threats against the government. Nearly every position I worked had difficult metrics to hit to receive a favorable review or bonus. Pay: gets much better in mid-level positions, especially relative to the work you’re doing. I have observed that the more you’re paid the easier your job gets. You’ll be responsible for more things they can blame on you if shit ever goes tits up though. You’ll also have a pension and generous defined contribution plan. Many ordinary federal employees become millionaires due to shrewd investments here. By the time you reach senior levels you’ve seen how things work from the inside. If you’re competent in the least you’ll leverage this financially. Location: usually big regional offices are in city centers which can actually be nice if you make enough money to live downtown. If you work for a large agency you can transfer virtually anywhere in the country with time and patience. Veteran: friendly. The government strongly prefers to hire veterans in most entry level positions. This could be a good or bad thing. On one hand it meant we had a common bond and pretty politically incorrect work environment. It was bad for the same reasons too. We also brought along the drinking culture from the military. More than a few times I had to go bail someone out of jail over the weekend. Drugs: positions are either drug testing designated positions or not. If your position isn’t covered by drug testing, you can get high all you want (as long as you’re not caught at work or arrested). I had never tried any illegal drugs until I worked in government. After that, I usually bought drugs from other federal employees. Many young people smoked weed or did hallucinogens, but a few were into coke and pills. Special assignments: you’ll sometimes get to travel or work from different offices. These assignments are highly coveted by young and single people. They require at least some ass-kissing. Sometimes the postings are all-expenses paid trips for months at a time to places like DC, Seattle, Europe, and Asia. You’ll be living out of a decent hotel or nice government quarters. Most of us ate at Subway and spent our per diem on booze during official travel. Benefits: pretty good. All government owned or leased buildings I worked from had a gym. One leased office even had a restaurant and bar where we could get beers on lunch breaks and after work at a discounted price. I had lots of time off from work to travel both domestically and overseas. Medical and dental benefits are decent. (You probably won’t get to live the life of a spy. Your work will be dull and uninspiring, but your life can be interesting if you work at a good office with a good team. Image credit: Tailors With Love.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Are there really people who are unlucky?
Answer: Yes. Telemachus Orfanos was killed in a mass shooting at a bar in Thousand Oaks, California, on November 7, 2018. Although of little comfort to anyone, statistically, the odds of being involved in a mass shooting are extremely low. What made Telemachus Orfanos particularly unlucky? He’d already survived another mass shooting a year earlier in Las Vegas, that killed 58. His mother, Susan Orfanos, clearly still reeling from the tragedy that took her son, went viral in a news segment where she attacked gun ownership in America. Later, she received death threats for her anti-gun stance. (Telemachus Orfanos is pictured on the left. His mother during the news segment that went viral. Photo credit: The Christian Post).

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is the United States in decline?
Answer: A search of Google reveals that the Fast & Furious franchise has brought in a total revenue of $7 billion dollars since its initial release in 2001. Lesotho, a landlocked nation in Africa, home to over 2 million people, has an annual gross domestic product of about $2.2 billion dollars. Lesotho has the 184th strongest economy in the world. It is close to the bottom, but it’s actually not in last place. Lesotho’s entire economy could fit safely within the revenue of the Fast & Furious franchise, even if it tripled in size. Keep in mind, this is just a single media franchise. What’s even more interesting about the Fast & Furious film franchise is where it makes most of its money. That is, outside of the United States. More than $5 billion dollars of the $7 billion dollars in revenue was brought in from international ticket sales, of which the most important market is China. China, the country said to be America’s greatest geopolitical rival, is also the largest consumer of American pop culture. So, I don’t know, questioner. Is America in decline and if so, relative to who? (I suspect that once the US is in decline the global appetite for these dumb fucking movies about cars will be satiated. Until then, there is no hope. The cinema, dominated by American corporatism, is not a joyful place. Image source: IMDB).

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why were 100 flights cancelled at Frankfurt airport because climate protesters glued themselves to the runaway, when these protesters weren't big enough to stop planes weighing many tons?

This can result in millions of dollars in damage and pose a risk to the lives of everyone onboard an aircraft. I have worked at both military and civilian airports. Posters like the ones below are common in buildings exiting onto a flight ramp. Guarding against FOD is the business of everyone who works at an airfield. Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is an interesting fact of history that most people don't know?
Answer: Colombia’s participation in the Korean War. Just after the outset of the Korean War, conservative president Laureano Gómez, won election in Colombia. He sought closer ties with the United States, which was now fighting a war in Korea. The United States requested that several countries in the Americas send troops to aid in its efforts, including Mexico and Brazil. Only Colombia answered. (Soldiers of the Colombian Battalion with an American army officer. Photo source: Wikipedia). Colombia sent approximately 5,000 soldiers (Colombian Battalion - Wikipedia) and three frigates to Korea to assist United Nations actions in Korea in 1951, spearheaded by the United States. Given the relative smallness of the Colombian military, this contribution was significant. The Colombians fought honorably and with distinction, earning several awards from both the US and Korean governments including numerous Silver Stars and Bronze Stars for valor. (Colombian soldiers with the insignia of the Colombian Battalion on their ascots. Photo source: Wikipedia). Of particular note, the Battle of Old Baldy, was the single deadliest battle for the Colombian Battalion, which suffered 97 men killed in action. Approximately 20% of the unit’s fighting strength at the time. The Colombians returned home after the war ended in 1954. They suffered approximately 200 men killed in action and several hundred more wounded in action. (A statue paying tribute to Colombia in South Korea. Source: South Korea - Colombia - Korean War Memorials). Today, in most of the world, Colombia’s particpation in the war is all but forgotten. In Colombia, there are monuments and plaques in several cities displaying Colombia’s contribution to the war effort and acknowledging the sacrifices of their Korean War veterans. The other legacy of the war; South Korea quickly established diplomatic ties with Colombia. A few Koreans later immigrated to Colombia, particularly the capital. Today, there is a tiny, but very present Korean community in Bogota. Of course, there are several tasty Korean restaurants too.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why didn't Hitler just accept Stalin's offer to join the Axis and invade Allied occupied lands instead?
Answer: Bolshevism, in Hitler’s view, was a Jewish political philosophy. At its foundation, it was antithetical to national socialism. Still, Stalin somehow managed to be caught with his pants down during Barbarossa, despite signs invasion was imminent. (Nazi propaganda poster “Bolshevism is Judaism.” Image source: Wikipedia.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why are Americans so inhumane?
Answer: Besides the death penalty (in some cases), excessive traffic deaths, firearms deaths, a multi-tiered healthcare system, one of the highest incarceration rates in the world, and unavailability of euthanasia, I assure you that Americans are quite humane. Both dog fighting and cock fighting are illegal in all 50 states. Animal cruelty laws are particularly harsh and judges and juries unforgiving. Anti-cruelty laws have some of the highest approval ratings among the public in the United States. In 2023, Oregon was the 1st ranked state in terms of animal protection laws, According to the Animal Defense Legal Fund. 2023 U.S. Animal Protection Laws Rankings Additionally, states like California and New York have sought to make the sell and production of the French delicacy, foie gras, illegal. Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump?
Answer: TLDR: No. My friends from New York have a perfect saying in these situations; you’re being “gassed up.” (Source: Urban Dictionary) I don’t care what any polls say or how positively the media tries to spin the nascent Harris-for-president campaign. Harris would have to win in places like Ohio, Michigan, Minnesota, Georgia, and Arizona convincingly over Trump. Intuitively, I just don’t think she will be able to pull that off.
