Today, Harris, who really isn’t that young as presidential candidates go, looks vigorous and energetic. I think that’s all that’s in her favor. She won’t win the presidency against Trump for a combination of reasons including her politics, public persona, personal and professional history, the state she is from, and a not insignificant amount of lazy -isms to include sexism and racism that exist with John Q. Voter. Anyone who says otherwise has you gassed up.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: I am visiting Bogota on 7th and 8th August, Is there anything that I need to be aware of from a safety perspective? Protests, big events etc. Any parts of the city that I need to be steering clear of?
Answer: I don’t think so. I watched one of the Bogota news stations this morning, Noticias Caracol. I didn’t see or hear anything about planned protests. It is Independence Day and some roads places and roads may be closed. You can keep with news in the capital on Youtube or by “expat” groups on social media like Facebook. Bogota is a pretty safe city for visitors, in my opinion. A few tips to stay safe: (Watching the evening traffic jam from a coffee shop in Bogota. Traffic in Bogota is horrifying during peak hours. Try to stay close to the places you need to go in the city. Photo by author.) The most dangerous crimes that affect tourists will be pickpocketing, robbery, druggings (particularly of unaccompanied men), and much more rarely, express kidnappings. None of which are likely to result in your death if you cooperate. Or in the case of drugging, can be avoided all together by not going out drinking alone or inviting strangers to your place. Remember that if you are confronted for your valuables, always give them up and quickly. Be judicious using your mobile phone in public. The water is safe to drink in Bogota and there are many pharmacies, hospitals, and physicians there if you should need help during your stay.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: For poor people who went to elite colleges, (Ivies and others) was that the only time you felt elite? How did your life change or not?
Answer: I attended a so-called “Public Ivy” as a graduate student at the University of Michigan. Keeping in mind that by this time I was a veteran and receiving veteran school benefits, so I was never lacking in money to take care of myself. Attending an elite unversity will not make a person raised in poverty feel elite. It’s quite the opposite. You will realize how poor your upringing and education actually was compared to others in your cohort. Public Ivy - Wikipedia Your life changes because people tend to adapt the lifestyle and mannerisms of those with whom they spend time. Like my classmates, I spent part of my summers in Europe or the Caribbean. Ate at trendy restaurants, learned to refine my style of dress and diction. Graduate school isn’t just about academics, it’s also a finishing school that prepares you to conform in the way that corporate America or mid-level and higher government bureaucracies expect you to behave. The collegial atmosphere means that you won’t be excluded or bullied for being from a poor background, but people expect you to act with a different level of sophistication. Most of my fellow graduate students were from an interesting diversity of backgrounds. Lawyers, doctors, bank presidents, philanthropists, and even a mailman. I was the only Iraq veteran that I can remember. A lot of my fellow students had questions about my experiences in the military. My professors had worked for presidents, senators, or were high level managers at federal agencies like the State Department or Congressional Research Service. It was great to get not only their knowledge, but perspectives on the issues of the day. (At Michigan we often joke that Harvard is the east coast version of Michigan. Pretty arrogant. Photo source: Etsy. So, no. I never felt elite. Most of my fellow students and all of my professors had backgrounds that were much more impressive than mine. If anything, I felt humbled.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Be honest. What is your assessment of the current American culture?
Answer: America is having an identity crisis. Americans, as a people, are at their best when faced with a grave external threat. Today, no such threats exist. The 9/11 attacks were 23 years ago. Russia spent most of its military power to fail at conquering a nation smaller than Texas. Americans have some vague notion that China poses a threat to Taiwan, but it’s not clear we’d even get involved. It’s at these times that America becomes introspective. Closes its borders. Re-tools. Right now the political factions in the US are like the married couple that have been meaning to have a talk, because slowly things have started to change. But they’ve been too busy dealing with work, raising kids, and caring for elderly parents. Now it’s finally time for that chat. America isn’t headed for divorce, but it does need relationship counseling. (President George Bush gives a speech after the attacks of 9/11. Bush’s approval rating shortly after the attacks would be the envy of any president today. Although the events of 9/11 were undeniably a tragedy, the aftermath of the attacks would be the high water mark for American patriotism and unity in the first quarter of the 21st Century. Image credit: The History Channel.)

Question: Do you think a man and a woman can become travel buddies and even share the same room on a trip, and it not become romantic?

It was going to be the first time either of us would go to carnival in Barranquilla (I highly recommend). I don’t think we took at all into consideration that we were different genders. Question: Why didn't Joe Biden quit earlier?

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why is downtown in US cities often considered unsafe after dark, when it's normally the safest areas in European cities?
Answer: I don’t know that this is true. Crime isn’t likely to happen to you in most downtown areas of the US. Crime happens mostly in residential areas. Downtowns tend to be business and entertainment centers where violent crime, in particular, is exceedingly rare. Let’s take a look at two violent American cities I know very well. My hometown of Detroit and adoptive hometown of Cleveland: I have outlined the downtowns in red. Darkly shaded areas have the most crimes reported. (Detroit, neighborhoodscout.com) (Cleveland, beighborhoodscout.com) Neither city’s downtown has high crime compared to neighborhoods where people live. However, if you look closely at both maps you can see how much crime can vary just from postal code to postal code in American cities. Both cities have neighborhoods that are directly adjacent to downtown that do have high crime. Both are home to low income housing projects. Visitors or the few people that live downtown in these cities aren’t likely to wander there.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the quality of life like in Miami? Is the cost of living high compared to other cities? Are salaries in Miami comparable to the cost of living?
Answer: The quality of life is high as long as you have a high income. Yes, the cost of living is expensive compared to most cities in the United States except for a few places like San Francisco, New York, and Boston. The median salary in Miami is $60,000, significantly higher than the national median salary of just $48,000. The median home price is $655,000, so home ownership is unaffordable by someone earning the median salary. (South Beach, Miami. Photo by author.) To live comfortably in Miami, I’d want to have a minimum salary of at least $150k, but higher than that would be better and will mean a shorter commute, if you have one. I love Miami and it is the place where I love to spend a lot of time in the U.S. However, the decision to live there would be difficult in comparison to other parts of Florida or the Caribbean for those of us that live location independent lifestyles.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What was the best thing about being a child of your generation?
Answer: We were the last generation without social media during our childhood. Facebook was brand new just as I hit college. Although bullying was a problem in the 1990’s, it was mostly limited to school hours or day camp (during the summers). There was no fear of missing out. The only way to know what your friends were doing during summers and weekends was to be there with them or have them tell you about it when they saw you again. Even taking a lot of pictures was rare since film was still expensive and photography still an art. (Images like this automatically induce anxiety in 90’s kids. Source: Washington Post.) Entertainment for kids sucked in comparison to today. Sure, I think our video games were pretty fun, but they didn’t offer realistic and immersive worlds like they do today. Even if you could play for more than 3–4 hours at a time, eventually, the sun and sky would call and seem more appealing. Video games were best left for rainy days. More imaginative entertainment would take place during summers. You’d also occasionally read books. Many of the things that are health risks today weren’t considered during my childhood. On one hand, it meant that child car seats weren’t a thing and no one cared about secondhand smoke. On the other, it meant that we ate lots of candy, drank lots of soda, had fried foods, and occasionally, were given alcohol by adults. It never occurred to either us or our parents that our generation would end up fat and unhealthy. This ignorance was bliss.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: If you were to choose to move to a South American capital, which one would it be, Brasilia (Brazil), Buenos Aires (Argentina), Santiago (Chile), or Montevideo (Uruguay)?
Answer: Damn. You’re really going to make me choose Buenos Aires! While Argentina is not my favorite country, I think it has the best capital city out of the above choices. (Santiago, Chile, photo by author.) Santiago: I love Chile, but I don’t find there to be anything charming or especially interesting about the capital city. I’d totally live in Chile, but I wouldn’t want it to be here. Brasilia: I’ve never had a reason to go to this city, although I probably will someday, I’m not in a hurry. All of my acquaintances that have worked in the Brazilian government leave this city the first opportunity they get. People describe it as culturally dead and boring. I’m positive I’d never want to live there. (The name of this small chain of stores in Montevideo cracked me up a bit. Photo by author.) Montevideo: for a city of over a million people, it feels sleepy and a little boring. Sure, I love chivitos and I love legal marijuana, but I can get those things in Punta del Este too. I love you, Uruguay, but I would not want to live in your capital city. (Puerto Madero, Buenos Aires. I like this neighborhood, it offers apartment living, nice views, and walkable streets. Photo by author.) Buenos Aires: again, I would rather live in other places in Argentina than the capital, unless I had to. However, Buenos Aires is the one capital from the above that has a decent combination of safety, healthcare, transportation, value, and things to do and see. It beats the other cities hands down.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Surveys: What was your college experience like?
Answer: Overall: awesome! I was the first of my family to go to college, so I didn’t really know what to expect. I received an academic scholarship, but would have to find a way to pay for room and board. It was expensive to attend a private Jesuit school, but the first two years of college especially, were incredibly fun. As a freshman, no one really expects too much out of you. You’ll have a lot on your plate between sports, social, and academic activities. For kids from working class or poor families like mine, we also had student jobs (almost all were insanely easy). (Detroit Mercy, where I spent the first two years of university before joining the military. Photo source: Association of Jesuit Colleges and Universities). My university was small by US standards. Only about 5,000 students. Practically all of us freshmen that lived on campus knew each other. We’d spent two weeks hiking, camping, and playing games during summer orientation. A few of us freshman had already established relationships with people over 21 on campus. This guaranteed we’d have a steady supply of alcohol. None of my male friends had a girlfriend nearby except for my friend, Chuy, who I actually knew from high school. I had promised my high school sweetheart that we’d keep going steady, but she was two hours away at Michigan State. On weekends I was either fencing, drinking heavily with my friends, visiting my girlfriend, or in rare cases, studying. Sometimes a combination of all of the above. (Épée fencing at Detroit Mercy. Source: University of Detroit Mercy). I remember very little about my studies other than to say it was fairly rigorous compared to life in Detroit public schools. Still, I didn’t take my studies serioiusly. I often skipped or showed up late to classes and had friends hand me their notes. I was the complete opposite of myself as a high school student. I knew that in the long term my grades wouldn’t really matter. Overall, I received slightly higher than average grades. Nothing special. I think that only my GMAT score allowed me to attend graduate school. Graduate school was different in that it was a much more serious environment. Missing an assignment just isn’t something that graduate students do. You’re also expected at every lecture unless you have a legitimately good excuse. Basically, your professors want you to behave like an adult. Some of your classmates are also much older than your average college student. When I graduated with my bachelor’s I was old for a college student. At 25 in graduate school, I was about average age, maybe slightly younger for once. Still, my friends and I would often show up to class after serious drinking sessions in a bar near campus. Weekends were still spent partying in and around Ann Arbor and Detroit with more funds (read: student loan or veterans’ benefits) than people in their 20’s should reasonably control. I think my college experience was about average for people my age that went to college in the 2000’s. We partied a lot, learned about life through relationships, studied as little as possible. Us guys fantasized about girls much more than we actually got to share our bed with them. Our activities outside of the classroom were sometimes foolish, dangerous, shameful, and reckless. As I said, about average.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What aspect of everyday modern life is underrated?
Answer: I can think of so many, but here are just a few of the best: Travel: going just 10 miles used to be quite a journey just over a hundred years ago. Today, such a journey is routine. Even the worst modern cars are more comfortable, quieter, safer than the very first generation of cars. Since we have cars, we don’t have to find places in our cities to dispose of horse shit. Leading to my next point… Smell: most of us rarely deal with unpleasant smells on a day-to-day basis in the modern world. This was not the case for many of our ancestors. (Indigenous people using a smartphone. Photo credit: National Geographic). Communication: with nearly anyone, anywhere in the world. Instantly. Just 30 years ago calling people outside of your region or state was a pain. Almost no one used email yet. Today, cell phones make us anxious if we see someone has gone ten minutes without reading our message. Safe food and water: although not everyone in the world has guaranteed access to these things, the percentage that do is higher than ever. We shouldn’t take this for granted. Choice: we have the ability to choose from an ever-increasing variety of foods, flavors, hobbies, careers, destinations, and romantic partners (thanks to the reach of dating apps). We don’t talk enough about how unusual this is in human history. Travel 2: the distances we can travel in less than a day. A few days ago I was in a completely different climate zone, with people speaking a different language, eating different food while listening to different music. Most of the people also had a different appearance. Later that day I was thousands of miles away on a different continent with different weather, language, food, music, and people. Sometimes the rapid change in scenery and climate actually messes with you a little bit. For most of human history this journey would have been impossible. 400 years ago it would have been a dangerous proposition that would have taken months. (Richard Westall’s Sword of Damocles. Wikipedia). What do we pay for all these glorious benefits? Humanity has the power to destroy life as we know it in a single afternoon. Compared to our ancestors we live like kings and queens. But above the throne on which we sit hangs the sword of Damocles.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What kind of firearms training do people receive in the military? What is the training like?
Answer: Generally, you receive training on all the small arms needed to do your job. For the great majority of people in the Air Force, this means the M16 or M4 series of rifles. As a security forces airman, however, my training included many more weapons on a course that is timed and scored for accuracy. I did such training with the M16 rifle, M4 rifle, M249 squad automatic weapon, M240 machine gun, M203 grenade launcher, and M9 pistol among a few others. Our training on the pistol range was memorable and I had the absolute best instructor teach me how to shoot a handgun for the first time. Later, that very same day, I qualified as a pistol marksman. I simply had no bad shooting habits to do away with. (An airman in the firearms training simulator (FATS). Image source: US Air Force). The same couldn’t be said of one of my classmates. Not only did our firearms training consist of live fire training, but training on a firearms simulator that consisted of “shoot/don’t shoot” scenarios. The idea of such training is to teach airmen when the use of lethal force is appropriate. These simulators were fun in that they use the actual firearm, but it is modified with a CO2 charge that cycles the weapon and produces simulated recoil. It isn’t loaded with any ammunition, but instead works as a fancy, but realistic, laser pointer. The system works in conjunction with short films that are projected on to a screen. The projector shows the location of any shots the officer fires by marking the screen with green dots. When it was my turn, I had accidentally caused the entire class to erupt into riotous laughter. I’d been given a shoot scenario where a man pulled a gun and pointed it at me. I rapidly fired off two shots. The scenario then froze and showed the location of my pair of shots on the perpetrator’s body. I’d shot him two times squarely in the genitalia. Being immature, everyone, including myself, doubled over in laughter. At least I didn’t miss! (“Fanning” in cowboy action shooting. Photo source: Dinosaur Cowboys). After we composed ourselves, it was then the turn of another airman. The first scenario played and he drew the pistol from his holster. It was a “don’t shoot” scenario, so he didn’t have to fire. The only problem was that he was drawing the pistol like a cowboy. While bringing the weapon up with his right hand, he was using his left hand to simultaneously cock the hammer so that he could fire the pistol in single action. Something that is quite obviously stupid. Our instructor told him to “knock it the f*ck off” and not do that again. The next scenario played and he did the exact same kind of cowboy draw of the pistol. This time it was a “shoot” scenario. While drawing, the airman simultaneous cocked the hammer with his left hand and then fired. It brought the hammer of the pistol down on the fleshy outer portion of his left hand and tore off a bit of it. He let out a shriek, dropped the pistol, and started bleeding everywhere. Everyone laughed even harder this time. Our instructor called him a “f*cking idiot” and sent him to medical.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why is rent being raised everywhere?
Answer: It’s a good question, because it does indeed seem to be a thing in most parts of the world right now. How can rent be going up everywhere all at once? I have a property that I rented to a young couple in my relatively small midwestern town. This was in 2019. They stayed for nearly four years. At the beginning I charged them what I thought was a slightly below market average for rent, because I just wanted the property occupied, but preferably by good tenants. They turned out to be exactly that, thus, I never raised their rent. They paid me on time every single month and handed me the property back without anything broken. How lucky! By the time they moved out to buy their own house, the market rate for rent for the property had risen approximately 40%. That’s a huge jump in a short amount of time. I think their case demonstrates what’s going on, at least here in the US. They bought their own first home at around age 30. I think that millennials that are around 30–35 or so are the people moving the property market because they have now saved up enough money to buy. Here we don’t have a problem with Airbnb since we don’t have tons of tourists. But places where young people actually want to rent or buy are seeing the hottest rises in prices around here. The older folks are all moving down to Florida.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Are there any countries in South America where it is possible to live on $1000 a month or less?
Answer: I would say probably every single last one of them. You could. Heck, I know people, personally, that live in the United States on that kind of money. The question is, would you want to? You could live well outside of the top metropolitan areas of Brazil, Colombia, Argentina, Chile, Peru, etc., and even the relatively expensive country of Uruguay. Now, I have never been to the Guayanas or Venezuela, but I’m going to bet you could manage in those places too, but I am going to assume you don’t really mean those countries, since they really aren’t very popular. (Taking the cable car over a community in Medellin. No one here makes anything remotely like $1,000 a month. You can live well in Colombia on $1,000, but you’ll want to stay away from big cities like Medellin to get the most for your dollars. Photo by author.) I’d say that if you want to live a decent life, Colombia would be my top choice because you will probably get the best combination of quality of life, value, security, and healthcare than the other countries. Especially in smaller cities like Armenia or Manizales, which are safe and have good healthcare options. Argentina, a country I’m really not even that fond of, might be my second choice. Chile is the more expensive choice, but offers the highest standard of living on the continent. You’ll have to hunt to make your money stretch, but it’s feasible. Especially if you’re not the type to dine out or do a lot of things that cost money. (Chile ranks highest in South America in HDI, only a couple of places below Portugal. It is ahead of its neighbor Argentina and even the oil rich nation of Kuwait. Chile offers excellent value. Source: Wikipedia.) The thing is, no one can really tell you these things ahead of time in my experience. While it is possible someone could live rather comfortably on that amount of money in much of South America, your ability to do so depends on your personality. Personally, I could not and would not live in anywhere in South America with that kind of budget. There’s not a lot of room with that much money in the case of emergencies that will arise from time to time.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Where do ultra rich people live?
Answer: Here’s one perk the wealthy definitely don’t want you to know! They don’t really live in one place. At least not in the sense that regular people would know it. For example, I have an acquaintance who runs his own IT consultancy. He’s at a point in his career that he wants to slowly hand over the reigns of the company to someone else. His people can reach him when he’s on the go at any time by phone or teleconference. His address, if you bothered to look, says that he lives in Idaho. We met through a mutual American friend who lives in Rio de Janeiro for part of the year. My acquaintance travels frequently, but likes to spend most of his spare time in Colombia, another country I frequent. He will stay there for weeks or months at a time and sometimes even commute back to his office in Idaho for part of the week before returning to some city in South America, or ocassionally, Asia, and Europe. We’ve hung out in several places because we just happened to be somewhere at the same time. Unlike even the modestly wealthy people we meet in Bogota, my friend doesn’t ride around in an armored vehicle with bodyguards. When we eat at a cafe there no one has any idea he is the founder and CEO of a company worth many millions of dollars. A nomadic lifestyle offers anonymity, safety, and freedom from pesky worries like bad weather or terrible beaches. Residency or citizenship in multiple countries can also come with tax benefits, something of particular interest to the wealthy. Where do ultra-rich people live? They live in an ever-expanding network of cities all across the globe, for as little as months, weeks, or days at a time. It is a shockingly small network of people, who are almost all in some way connected to each other through business, familial, or friendly relations. (The Clube Naval in Rio de Janeiro literally has a moat to separate it from the rest of society. In the nearby neighborhood of Leblon is South America’s priciest real estate. However, many of the luxury apartments are empty for much of the year. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What do you miss about the 90’s?
Answer: I have written before about the chaos of living in Detroit in the United States in the 1990’s. I didn’t touch on a lot of the good things. Particularly, I remember the mid — late 90’s being the best years of my childhood. I was finally a teenager and approaching my most formative years. We children were very indpendent. We didn’t have mobile phones yet. The most our parents could hope for was a call when we got to where we were going. On weekends we rode our bicycles clear across Detroit, or if the weather was bad, we’d take the city bus. We could take the bus to the suburbs to watch a movie or buy some silly gadget at the mall. Sometimes we’d go very, very far from our neighborhoods. We’d all agree to a lie about where we’d been so that we were on the same page. We never felt endangered by strangers or adults. From the age of 11 or 12 our parents would leave us home alone for an entire week or more if they had work or something else to do. (Gorbachev in a Pizza Hut commercial is perfectly emblematic of the mood of the late 1990’s. We Americans had defeated communism. Now it was time for all of us to gather around the table of a capitalist multinational pizza restaurant and celebrate freedom.) Eating food from a restaurant was rare. Maybe once or twice a month and it would almost always be fast food. Otherwise, we cooked at home. Certainly nothing like Uber Eats existed. A very fun, but ocassional treat was pooling our money as kids and going to Pizza Hut. We could sit down there. A waitress would come and take our order and treat us as if we were grownups. 15 minutes later a big, hot pizza would come to our table! We’d drink unlimited coca cola and play video games. Almost always any gratuity was left in dimes, quarters, and nickles that we carefully counted. We were blissfully ignorant about the world. 24/7 news coverage like CNN was a totally new concept. In the 1990’s we mostly watched our local news for an hour and then a national news program like NBC Nightly News with Tom Brokaw. It was rarely political and we only got trickles of information about global events. Therefore, our knowledge of the outside world was much less than it is today. This meant that our day-to-day lives rarely featured anxiety over tragedies happening half a world away. Conflicts in Kosovo and Somalia registered only as blips on our radar. America was confident. We had Bill Clinton as president, we’d soundly won the Gulf War in the early 1990’s, the economy was rebounding, and people had money. Furthermore, America had seen the disintegration of its main geopolitical rival, the Soviet Union, on live television. The first president of Russia, Boris Yeltsin, was seen as western-friendly. We no longer had to fear nuclear annihilation. The internet and Silicon Valley were becoming an important part of the American lexicon. None of us had ever heard of Osama Bin Laden, the Taliban, or even the nation of Afghanistan. Our parents and teachers told all of us that our generation would be the ones to make the world even better. There could be no doubt about it. The internet became commonplace by the late 90’s. This lifted the veil on the outside world somewhat. We didn’t have an abundance of websites or online encyclopedias like now, but we could actually talk to people in far away places. My aunt in San Francisco, whom I would usually send letters to, started to prefer that we mostly correspond by email. At first this meant taking a trip to the local library, but eventually we got our first desktop computer. A giant hulking thing that cost a ton of money that we had to pay for in installments. Make no mistake though, it was an incredibly exciting time since we looked at the internet as a miracle that gave us unlimited reach and knowledge.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are some unfair things about life?
Answer: A lot, perhaps even most things about life are unfair. Here are the most striking examples of unfairness in life: Youth are called on to make some of the most important decisions of their lives when they are young and very inexperienced. In most places, around the age of 18. College, military service, or entering the trades are all options. How can someone know if any of the above are for them before actually experiencing it? Choose wrong and you could spend multiple years correcting a mistake. Meanwhile, life still comes at you fast. The learning curve of life is steep! Life is expensive. Shockingly few people around the world are able to afford all the costs of daily living, yet people produce more value than at any other time in human history. There’s something inherently unfair about that. No Guarantees. You can do everything right in life and still end up in a shit situation. A friend of mine came from a difficult family and managed to go to college and dental school. Later she joined the Air Force and became an officer. Her life should have been good. However, she ended up in a relationship with another officer who abused hard drugs and gambled to excess. It nearly ruined her both personally and professionally. Time only goes forward. In life, there are no rewinds. That mistake you made 15 years ago not asking out your crush or passing up a job in that startup that is now worth hundreds of millions of dollars. Sorry, you’ll be living with that for the rest of your life. Where you’re born determines so much about your life. Even within developed countries this is true. Sometimes we can make predictions about someone’s life based on the very postal code in which they grew up. The person born in Libya will not have the same opportunities in life as the person born in Switzerland. Education is a key building block of life. Yet, our educational sysems are disparate in many, if not most parts of the world. The gap between elite schools and public schools is enormous, but we have high standards for all children, even if their education was insufficient. Health is vital to life and quality of life. Some people are born healthier than others. Modern medicine elliminates some, but not all disparities. There’s still much to be done in this area around the world.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the best way to waste time?
Answer: I like to stay busy. I am prosperous when I am industrious. Yet, everyone deserves a break. If not for days, even hours or minutes will do. Some things that are an excellent waste of time: Watching a sunset or sunrise on a beach. Sunset is better because it doesn’t involve getting up early. A caipirinha or tequila based drink is encouraged. Light music is a good addition. Not at all overrated. (Thousands of people await the sunset on the beach in Ipanema, Rio de Janeiro. Photo by author.) Getting dressed up and going out for dinner and wine with interesting people. In a world where everything is so casual, throwing on a jacket and a nice pair of shoes can feel like stepping into a different world. I’d argue that it’s precisely what you are doing. A time to dine and drink voraciously, while throwing around ideas, no talk about work or politics. (capturing star trails in Arizona. Photo by author.) Hiking and camping. Out in the wilderness, under the stars. Only a cell phone with no signal and your thoughts to keep you company. Best done solo if you really want to unplug from it all for awhile. Reading. Nothing serious. Many of us who still read, read technical knowledge in their field of expertise, history, or great works of literature. I’m not talking about that kind of reading. I mean wasting your time reading for pure pleasure like fantasy or detective novels, or the newest release of a celebrity gossip magazine. Good stuff. (Sailing the Caribbean Sea. Photo by author.) Any time spent on a boat. Today, almost no one is on a boat for business reasons. Being on a boat means leisure. Leisure is a “waste” of time, but boating or sailing is a glorious way to do it.

Question: Why the Bogota El Dorado airport treat their tourists, that are bringing money to the economy, with immigration and departure lines of up to 2 hours and 20 minutes? What can be done to improve the situation?
Answer: I haven’t found customs at Bogota to be much worse than other airports in Latin America or even compared to some airports in the United States and Europe. Depending on where you’re flying from, you could fly directly into Medellin or Cartagena and go from there. I just don’t find wait times to be much better at either of those airports. Long wait times are a reality of visiting Colombia right now. (Waiting for a flight at El Dorado, Bogota. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are the best steps we can take to recreate the glory of America in the 70s?
Answer: You can stop looking at the 70’s with rose-tinted lenses. For part of the 70’s there was still the Vietnam War, the rapid rise of crime in America, the oil crisis, proliferation of drugs, broken homes, dismantling of the Apollo Program, Three Mile Island, the beginning of de-industrialization, and urban decay. The Cold War was very much still ongoing and people lived under the threat of nuclear annihilation. People didn’t wear seatbelts, airfare was more expensive, life expectancy lower, and industrial accidents much more common. How good were the 70’s, really? (70’s fashion was also terrible. Image Source: New Idea Australia)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How big is the United States of America?
Answer: To give context, let’s compare just one state, Ohio, to a nation of the European Union, Ireland. By many standards, Ohio is an American backwater. A state composed of farmland and a few, mostly unimpressive, metropolitan areas that foreigners haven’t even heard of (Columbus, Cincinnati, Cleveland). Ohio has a population more than twice that of Ireland and has a land area one and a half times that of Ireland. By the numbers: Population: Ohio: 11.7 Million Ireland: 5.1 million Land Area: Ohio: 106,156 km2 Ireland: 70,273 km2 Gross Domestic Product (nominal): Ohio: $872 billion (7th in the US) Ireland:$516 billion (25th in world) GDP Per capita: Ohio: $74,080 (28th in the US) Ireland: $101,509 (2nd in world) Gun Ownership Rate: Ohio: 40% of households Ireland: 7% of households Percentage of residents covered by public health insurance: Ohio: 38% Ireland: 100% (Ohio is only one state. But it’s bigger than a lot of European countries in both population and size. Source: mylifeelsewhere.com.) If you had to choose between the two, where would it be? Why?

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do soldiers deal with or prevent body odour (considering their strict training routines?)
Answer: US military perspective: we take showers. We shower after morning physical training and again at night before bed in basic training. Sure, you’ll be doing a lot of marching during the day and might sweat, especially if your training was in Texas like mine. This is usually manageable to the point where most people’s body odor doesn’t get out of hand. In the field, everyone packs baby wipes and deodorant and many changes of socks. If you’re lucky, you get access to a lyster bag (portable field shower). However, the fact is that you’re going to begin to stink after a few days of living in the same uniform and boots. It sucks, there’s no other way to put it. After a while everyone just agrees not to say anything. There are always one or two guys who smell much more than average though and they are made fun of mercilessly. Body odor and lack of sleep are the way of life in the field. (I’ll pack Pampers if I am in a pinch, but I prefer Huggies. Photo credit: Amazon).

Question: Why do migrant farm workers come to America to put food on Americans' tables when Americans supposedly don't value migrant farm workers?
Answer: I think the obvious answer is that America does value them. In fact, it values them so much they come to the United States for wages American farms are willing to pay. That sounds like the very definition of capitalism. Of course, the workers have no protections, poor working conditions, no pension, or disability insurance. If they come illegally, they may be shuttled across the border by coyotes, some of whom are the scum of the earth. (Waiting to cross the border into the US from Nogales, Mexico. This will be a point of entry for many migrant workers. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What's an unexpectedly good travel experience you've had?
Answer: Some years ago, I decided to embark on a trip in the Southwest United States to a few different national parks. After visiting Sedona and the Grand Canyon, I wanted to go to Utah for the first time to visit Bryce Canyon and Arches National Park. With it being my first time in Utah, and particularly in Southern Utah, I was a little nervous. For those that don’t know, a lot of people in this region are Mormons and they’re not known for being particularly friendly to outsiders. Especially someone as much of an outsider as me. I was all alone in an SUV with camping supplies, food, and my mobile phone. I drove through miles and miles of mountainous switchbacks, open desert, and forest. Although I’d lived in Arizona before, I’d never seen this area. It was amazing how quickly the biome changes with distance and altitude. It was stunning. (Sedona, Arizona. Photo by author.) Unfortunately, as I passed from Arizona into Utah, my mobile phone signal became weak, then completely non-existent. I pulled into Bryce Canyon City, thinking I was somewhere near my campsite. I went into a small motel, hoping I could get directions. This would be my first interaction with anyone in Utah. Inside was a middle-aged man wearing a cowboy hat with red tinted lenses, a middle aged woman, and a little girl. All were white. They greeted me warmly and asked how they could help me. I explained to the man that I was looking for my campsite near Bryce Canyon. In a drawl I have never heard before, he replied “now you’re in Bryce Canyon City, you want to get to Bryce Canyon. That’s a different place.” He began to draw a map and write detailed directions, while the woman called the campsite and let them know to expect my arrival in 15–20 minutes. The couple then gave me their business card and assured me I could return and stay for the night if I needed to. I thanked the family profusely for their help. We all said goodbye with warm smiles on our faces. They were so kind that a few weeks later I sent them a gift in the mail. (Bryce Canyon, Utah. Photo by author.) Sure, I did encounter some jerks in Utah that week, but thankfully, it was not the majority of people that I met.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What should a young person know and consider before joining the military?
Answer: Whether you plan to make a 20+ year long career out of the military, or just a four year term of enlistment, young people should consider what it is they want to do after the military. Sooner or later that day will come and you’ll want to have a plan. Even for those who believe they’ll serve for 20 or more years, your ability to do so isn’t a guarantee. People get injured, fail course requirements for a promotion, get RIF’d, have sick loved ones, or other problems of life that may mean cutting your enlistment short. When that day comes, what will you do? Who will you be? You’re just another social security number to Uncle Sam. He’ll help, but you have to take the initiative to enroll in college, technical training, vocational rehabilitation, or other veteran’s benefits. Where will you live? Will you retire completely after your 20 or will you want to get a civilian job in government or the corporate world? Have a plan, write it down, then stick to it. (My squad practicing building clearing. You’ll need to develop new skills to be useful in the civilian job market. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Can enlisted soldiers give orders to lieutenants or higher-ranking officers in certain situations?
Answer: Yes, in several instances. One is if you are a member of a military police unit and you encounter an officer in the course of your duties. I can order anyone to, for example, identify themselves or to get out of a vehicle during a traffic stop. Those things I can do at my discretion on base. However, it certainly wouldn’t be wise to do it without reason. Even within the police squadron, rank doesn’t matter if you catch a superior violating the law. For example, one night a lieutenant in our police squadron had hatched a wicked plan. Recently, the army barracks on our base had relocated. As a result, the army mess hall was shut down permanently. Our lieutenant had family nearby that ran a restaurant or two. He decided that he would “tactically acquire” the industrial stove out of the closed army mess hall for use in his family’s restaurant. He was caught in the act by someone who then called the police. When one of our enlisted policeman arrived, he ordered the lieutenant to put his hands behind his back and arrested him. Our lieutenant was later dismissed from service. (Judge Dredd, how military police see themselves. Never use the phrase “sir, please don’t mistake your rank for authority” when dealing with officers. They always consider this rude. Be gentle with officers and other small children. Image credit: IMDB.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is Mexico a dangerous place? What are the different perspectives on the safety of Mexico and why do they differ?
Answer: Mexico is a dangerous place in the way that the United States is a dangerous place. Danger is usually restricted to certain geographical areas, within the country and within a city, for example. Just as the vast majority of people in the U.S. do not experience or witness violence, it is the same for Mexicans. The level of violence tends to get gruesome quickly when dealing with cartels, however. It’s not unusual to hear cases of kidnapping, torture, and executions by various methods. Violence can and does spill over into the more civilized parts of society, but its probably more rare than you think. The only violence foreigners visiting Mexico are at all likely to experience, provided they stay away from clearly dangerous areas, is robbery. So, ultimately, the perspectives on safety will differ based on where someone lives in Mexico and within particular cities. People from places like Merida, San Miguel Allende, and Queretaro have different opinions from people that live in Ciudad Juarez, Mexico City, and Tijuana. In places like Merida, violent crime isn’t a concern at all. In Juarez it’s probably best to be constantly vigilant, but better if you don’t visit there at all as a foreigner. (Tepito, Mexico City. If you live in this neighborhood, your perspective on crime is different than someone in Condesa, although they are just a few miles apart. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: In the USA, if you are poor, can you study but not go to a university?
Answer: In the US, anyone can go to college, regardless of your ability to pay at the moment. You will need to apply for federal grants and student loans to cover the cost of your tuition. Taking out a student loan means one day you should expect to have to pay it back, although there are a few ways to get out of paying the full amount, such as working in the public sector. You can study outside of universities such as in vocational training, certificate programs, or from the internet. The issue with the latter is that employers in the US do like to see a piece of paper saying you’re good at something. It helps them weed people out very quickly. If you don’t have a degree or certificate and want a job that usually requires one, you’ll need to be good at greasing palms and selling your skills to convince someone to give you a shot. (“Hash Bash” on The Diag, University of Michigan. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the possibility that the "attack" on Trump was a GOP staged false flag?
Answer: Zero. Trump came incredibly close to being killed. No sniper is so talented as to purposely miss his target by a few centimeters. By November, it will be a distant memory, because several more tragedies and political upsets will occur between now and then. This is terrible timing for such a false flag operation. Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the typical "military type" of person, or is there such a thing?
Answer: Instead of focusing on whether there is a military type, let me give you some perspective from inside. I have found that nearly all military units I have been with have people who possess similar traits. This is my perspective as an enlisted airman in the US Air Force. The people you meet in the military are as follows: Lifer: generally squared away, but is not the sharpest nor the dullest in the shed. He is in it for the long term. Lives and breathes the military, because that’s all he has. By year 15 of his career he is either solidly married or twice-divorced. A bit overweight. Swears when he needs to, doesn’t go overboard. Drinks hard only on the weekends these days. Jaded Senior NCO: an asshole. He hates you. He hates your ugly wife. He hates your family, especially the mother that created you. You cretin. He has only 2–3 years to retirement. Barely gets a word out without swearing and telling you that you and your entire squad are “fucked up like Chinese money.” Is definitely twice divorced. When he retires he will pick up a civilian government job closely related to what he used to do. Is actively an alcoholic. Drinks every day. Bible Thumper: the most boring guy in your unit. He has a large bible as well as a small bible with a camouflage cover. The small bible is always in one of his pockets. We only hang out with him if we need a designated driver from a bar or strip club. Doesn’t drink, doesn’t smoke, doesn’t swear. Doesn’t believe in pre-marital sex. Single and a virgin. See…like I said, boring. Womanizer: this is the guy who always has a new lady on his arm. Sometimes they are civilians, sometimes he poaches the base population. There are always whispers about him. “I heard he banged the supply sergeant with big tits!” “Bro, I heard it was the new squadron XO!” Always has a fresh haircut and sharp uniform. Fun to hang out with after duty. Swears constantly, especially when talking about his sexual escapades. Real hedonist. Binge drinker on the weekends, just beer on the weekdays. Occasionally, a line of coke. Teetotaler: is actually a cool guy, but he had to give up drinking because he was out of control when he was a young airman. He actually likes hanging out with the guys, he just won’t drink. He comes to work and does his job. Keeps a neat appearance, but the goal is to stay under the radar. Goes home to an Asian wife and kids who actually enjoy having him in their life. Only swears when telling stories about the good old days. Nerd: today you see a lot of this personality type in the military. These are the guys who joined up to pay for college. They can make the worst airmen, since they do tend to have a lot of book smarts. They question orders where others woud not. His uniform and appearance could use some work. Swears a lot, especially when talking about which Star Wars is the best Star Wars. Is single. Drinks daily, but drinks weird shit like Pabst Blue Ribbon. Jaded Black NCO: is from a place like Philadelphia, Baltimore, or some southern town you’ve never heard of. Swearing is a part of his personality. He hates the military and secretly and sometimes not-so-secretely hates white people. Motivation for military service is simple: he wants to get every buck out of Uncle Sam that he can. For lack of more stable options, he is also a lifer at this point. His uniform and haircut are always sharp. One of his auxillary duties is to pull aside all new black unit members and give the lay of the land. He has a wife, kids, and a couple of girlfriends. Drinks some weekends and on special ocassions. Attends church. The lieutenant has recently asked him to stop using so much profanity, especially when people from other squadrons can hear him. Alcoholic: in an organization that loves heavy drinking, those labeled alcoholics are the absolute heaviest of drinkers. They frequently are too ill to come to work, show up for duty drunk, or get caught driving under the influence on the weekends. If the person is a senior NCO or officer, they’ll almost always have someone to cover for them to protect their careers. For senior NCO’s, they’ll be put in a position where they can’t hurt anyone or break anything until their time is up in the military. Divorced. This person is profane, untrusthworthy, and usually disheveled in appearance. Patriots: this personality is the rarest of them all. These are people who join the military with their main reason being to serve and fight. They are often religious. They come from a long line of men who served. They are conservative, already well-versed the use of firearms and living off the land. Neat uniform and appearance. Rarely swears, drinks socially. Knows a lot of racist jokes. Spends his off duty time hunting, fishing, and driving a big fuckin’ truck. Has a pretty blonde girlfriend he is thinking about marrying. American dream. Future divorcee, Jaded NCO, and alcoholic. Commanding Officers: are so stereotypically the same, you can substitute one for another. All went to a four year university or a military academy. They always have an impeccable appearance and uniforms that are starched and creased in all of the right places. Usually fit. Their activities both on and off-duty mystify enlisted men. We don’t know what he does on duty besides sitting behind a desk with a computer with big stacks of paper. Off duty, he has weird hobbies like tennis, triathlons, and chess. In a stable marriage with kids. Only uses swear words sparingly, and then only “damn” or “hell.” Only has a couple of beers in front of the men to show his face. Is secretly having an affair with his clerk. (My squad doing land navigation training, Fort Bliss, El Paso, 2009. Photo by author.) Edit: this could all be based on memories, horribly offensive stereotypes, or both.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is America still the land of opportunity?
Answer: Yes. America is the country where several people have become millionaires due to their companies that make plastic testicles for the trailer hitch of pickup trucks. Would this be possible in a country like France, Germany, or Japan? I think not. Next question, please. (No matter your inclinations or political affiliations, there is a pair of Truck Nutz for you. Image credit: Reddit.) See also:

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What do you think of the attempted assassination attempt of President Donald Trump moments ago?
Answer: I think the only reason Donald Trump is alive is because he got lucky. It looked like a complete failure of our security services. I hate to think of what may have happened had Trump been killed. (Photo credit: CNN.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do you see life? What's your philosophy about it?
Answer: I see life itself as a journey. How else could it be described? Life has a beginning, middle, and end. Dying is the great equalizer. No matter what we do in life, we will all go to the “undiscovered country” that is death. While we are here, we should love intensely, find something to be passionate about, follow our own instincts, make our own decisions, live with what life serves us. Never give up. (Cemetery in Yucatán region of Mexico. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is it possible to build muscle with isolation exercises alone, or do you need to incorporate compound movements like squats and bench press?
Answer: Is it possible? Yes, in the same way it is possible for humans to fly. The yes comes with a lot of caveats. Isolation exercises are good at working out individual muscles or muscle groups. They can give decent results in terms of hypertrophy, but strength gains will come slower and hit a maximum. Compound lifts are hard, especially squatting. But sooner or later, if you’re at all serious about being a strength or hybrid athlete, you’re going to need to incorporate compound lifts into your routine. They’re incredibly efficient and good at building stabilizing and core muscles. You’ll see your isolation lifts advance faster with compounds as a part of your routine. When you finally compound lift the only regret you’ll have is that you didn’t try them sooner. Otherwise, you’re leaving gains on the table.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What would happen if the Mexican Mafia overthrew the Mexican government and took control of Mexico themselves?
Answer: Why would they do that? It’s far easier to bribe a government official than to run a government. Government means rules, diplomacy, and even restraint. The cartels are interested in money, domination, and unbridled hedonism. Running a government is a job. Running a cartel is an art, but much more than that, it’s a lifestyle. Even if it’s bigger brother, the US, didn’t mind a cartel having control of the fourth largest oil producer in the Americas, they’d pressure them to hold free and fair elections, eventually. Cartels don’t care about democracy. They murder their opposition completely, thoroughly, just to gain power. Besides, the power of the cartels already rivals the power of the government in many parts of Mexico. A lot of places are safe, not because the police or government make them safer, but because one of the cartels has declared an area a “safe zone” where violence shouldn’t happen. The government doesn’t have that kind of power, the cartels do. (Genaro García Luna, former secretary of public security of Mexico. He received millions of dollars from the Sinaloa Cartel to ensure the protection of their drug shipments. Mexico is corrupt at the very highest levels of government. Luna was so hated by his own government that Mexico willingly extradited him to the US for crimes committed in Mexico. He faces up to life in federal prison. Photo credit: Fortune.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are the risks of crossing the U.S.-Mexico border without a coyote? How much does a coyote usually charge for their services?
Answer: The risk is that you’ll accidentally go to some area that is controlled by a gang, that you’ll cross at a dangerous point and die in the desert or drown in a river. Almost no one crosses the Mexico-US border alone, because to do so is at serious risk of life or of being caught. Coyotes will charge what they think you can pay. If you’re Mexican, Colombian, or Venezuelan, they’ll charge less than if you are Chinese or Arab. They can charge anywhere from a few hundred dollars to thousands. They’re very unscrupulous people to deal with, and they may decide to rob, rape, or flat out murder you if it’s to their advantage. (a recent documentary on some Chinese citizens’ journey across the Darien Gap and later, the US Border.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is something that people commonly think is true, that is actually a myth?
Answer: That they’ll save money by moving to a developing nation. I have seen this fallacy time and again. Sure, theoretically, you could. But people don’t live like that in real life. They think that magically they’ll end their spendthrift ways and settle for a simple, humble abode. Dinners at home prepared with fresh ingredients from the local market. This almost never happens. Just like when Americans move from an apartment to their first home. They’ll say “I have been wasting all of this money on rent, when I could have been paying a goddamn mortgage! “ When they buy their first home though, it’s almost always a huge lifestyle upgrade over their apartment. Now they’re stuck with a mortgage and utilities that are nearly double what they were paying for rent. And so it is when you move abroad. People don’t want a simple life. Instead they want to leverage every single dollar or euro they have to give them every luxury and advantage they can get. Moving abroad can save you a ton a money, but only if you live like a local. People from the developed world rarely want to do that. (One of the nicest McDonald’s restaurants I have ever seen, Parque 93, Bogotá. An acquaintance recently sold his home in the US and moved to Bogotá. He’ll pay substantially more for a home here than his old home, but it will be bigger and with a nicer view. How quickly gentrification becomes corrosive.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is it safe for tourists to visit or move to Mexico City? Why do some people advise against it?
Answer: Yes and yes. The thing about Mexico City is that you’re never really safe from being robbed. Even in a very nice neighborhood (or sometimes especially). This might be even more true if you definitely look like a foreigner (like I do). If you take the right precautions you’ll be ready for this possibility. Such as carrying only the essentials when traveling in the city and taking the metro. If you’re robbed at gun or knifepoint remember — don’t resist! Give up your things immediately. Take a backup cell phone if you can, something cheaper than the newest iPhone. Don’t wear anything of value, you will see some locals in nice neighborhoods doing this, but you’re not them. Overall, you’re not likely to have these things happen to you if you just dress plainly and are careful with your smart phone. But be prepared. (A day on the canals in Xochimilco, Mexico City. Photo by author.) The only other problem with Mexico City is that the air pollution is some of the worst in Latin America. I was sick for my first several months with a respiratory infection. Mexico City is well worth visiting. Living there is a tough decision right now, especially with the ongoing water crisis. Living in Yucatán, we received a steady influx of people from the capital who wanted to escape life there. Teleworking during the pandemic allowed them to finally do it. It’s not the nicest place to live in Mexico if you don’t have to, but that’s just my opinion. (Waiting for the metro in Mexico City during non-peak hours. Peak hour traffic is horrendous and not for the faint of heart. It’s also incredibly hot down there and it’s one of the places you’ll have your things taken. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What types of weapons can the American military mount onto its vehicles?
Answer: I can tell you the absolutely coolest weapon system I saw mounted on a humvee during the War in Iraq. A freakin’ minigun! (Special Operations personnel usually had their humvees set up something like this in Baghdad.) This thing can fire between 2,000 and 6,000 rounds per minute up to maximum range of about 1,000 meters. An absolute beast of a weapon to unleash on the ground. A runner up: Common Remotely Operated Weapon Station (CROWS). CROWS was brand new when I deployed to Iraq, so it’s probably old hat by now, but to us it was something out of the future. It allows a weapon to be fired from inside the protection of the vehicle, without exposing the gunner. Gunners were almost always the first to be injured or killed in battle or by roadside bombs, since they’re exposed. CROWS changed all of that. (Two soldiers with the CROWS system. Image credit: Wikipedia.) (Vehicles equipped with CROWS on convoy duty, Baghdad. Image credit: Wikipedia.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is it like living in America? Why do people tend to ask about other countries instead of their own?
Answer: In 2024, things are interesting. I just returned to the US after eight months abroad. It’s always so interesting to compare how things are in the US to life elsewhere. This is my perspective as someone from the Midwest United States and who spends much of his time in the “global south.” Here’s what it’s like living in the US: Convenient: we can make things like groceries, furniture, and musical instruments appear at our door within a short amount of time with just a few pushes of a button. This almost seems like magic. We can send something in the mail and know with a huge degree of certainty that it will get to its destination. Traffic is bad on the coasts, but here in middle-America, our commutes can be quite reasonable. It’s also not completely impractical to use public transportation, walking, and biking, as I do. (Edgewater Park, Cleveland. Cleveland is a very typical American city in almost every dimension. Photo by author.) Political: the environment everywhere in America is politically charged. New people you meet will quickly put out feelers to see where you live on the political spectrum. If it doesn’t match up closely with their own beliefs, usually, you can’t be friends. Lazy: native-born Americans often go without any strenous activity whatsoever throughout the day. We seem to abhor it. You see all kinds of weird things like people practically fighting to get a parking spot 20 meters closer to the door of a grocery store. (Pictured: Miami Beach. Even a bustling city like Miami isn’t quite the same as it was before COVID yet. Photo by author.) Boring: if you’re looking for a good social scene outside of a few large metro areas, life is tough. Covid killed off a lot of things, and cities still haven’t completely bounced back. Dating in the US is kind of a hellscape, because dating apps allow a few shady people to completely wreck the dating ecosystem. (Percentage of income Americans spend on food, compared to other nations. Source: ourworldindata.org.) Cheap: I must be crazy, right? Seriously though, I know there are things like medical expenses that are a huge burden to some, not to mention the cost of a college education. However, things needed on a day-to-day basis actually cost us less as a percentage of our income. Food in America is insanely cheap, even imported stuff. Same with gasoline (comparatively). We also don’t have crippling tariffs on everything imported, which makes buying imported things like electronics, Italian cheese, and foreign cars much cheaper than in other places. Big: of course the people are big, the food is big, but the thing that kind of shocked me recently: our cars. I was standing in the parking lot of my local park the other day. It was shocking how many of us drive trucks, SUV’s, and big sedans. A lot of the rest of the world drives much smaller cars. Anxious: almost all Americans have serious worries about some key aspect of their life. Whether it is about politics, healthcare, the job market, economy, or the price of real estate. You don’t have to talk to any of us for very long before we let loose with a deluge of problems. Substance abuse/addiction/mental illness: from my perspective, it’s rare that you meet someone who does not have some kind of substance abuse disorder, is not taking drugs, gambles too much, or eats too much. Others will have been diagnosed with anxiety, depression, bi-polar, or other conditions. Meeting someone who has a “clean” resume in all of these categories is incredibly rare. Trust: despite everything, Americans still have a rather high degree of trust in its institutions and political system. People still actually believe that social and economic problems can be solved through voting. People still believe the resurgence of America is just a few years off. Even in my native Detroit, a city often used to showcase the decay of urban America, people say that the city is coming back. Detroit is the story of America.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Should we travel abroad or not?
Answer: I think this is a good question to ask in this day and age. There are some that will insist that we should all travel, that we should all get to know other countries, especially us Americans. However, the truth is that travel is not desired by everyone. It won’t suit everyone. It’s difficult to write a prescription for all of humanity. (Trying to find a boat to take me out on the bay, Puerto Escondido, Oaxaca. Photo by author.) There are also ethical concerns of travel like the effect of carbon emissions on climate change and gentrification. Of course, there are methods of travel that mitigate these problems, but are often impractical or much more expensive. I don’t see travel as essential for everyone that wants to be a well-rounded person. Besides, it’s not as if traveling is a panacea when it comes to ignorance about the world. Plenty of people go to all-inclusive resorts in Mexico, never leave the resort, and behave like assholes. This kind of person has been abroad, but it was hardly an educational or transformative experience. You can get what you need out of life where you are, or abroad. Which kind of person you are depends largely on which decision you should make. Are you curious, are you an explorer? Do you want to learn new languages, and eat foods you have never even heard of in your native country? Are you good at being alone? Traveling long term, as in more than a few weeks, almost always means traveling alone. (Lunch alone at OCI.mde in Medellin, Colombia. Photo by author.) Remember that travel is only one form of exploration. If you do decide to go abroad, be kind to the locals, it makes things easier for the next citizen of your country that comes after you.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What American foods do you recommend to non-Americans?
Answer: Hot dogs: not a regular hot dog on a bun, but the more exciting stuff. Each major city has its own take on a hot dog or sausage. (Sonoran hot dog, El Guero Canero Restaurant, Tucson, Arizona.) (Half smoke, Ben’s Chili Bowl, Washington, D.C.) (Hot dogs with crazy toppings at Happy Dog, Cleveland, Ohio.) Tex-Mex: especially in the Southwestern, United States. Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona all have fairly different takes on Mexican food. (Tex-Mex tacos, homemade.) (Carne asada fries, Filiberto’s. Phoenix, Arizona.) Barbecue: America has a few different styles of barbecue. My favorite barbecue is from Texas, especially brisket. (Hard Eight Barbecue cooking ALL of the meats. This is a fine alternative if Pecan Lodge is too full. Dallas, Texas.) (North Carolina style at The Pit, Raleigh, North Carolina. North Carolina style is my least favorite. Just my opinion, nobody shoot.) Philly cheesesteak: it’s best to eat this in Philadelphia, of course, but you can find some decent ones in other places. (Jim’s Steaks, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.) Fried chicken: there’s a lot to choose from here and so many styles. Go wherever the locals go though. (Stir fry with a side of chicken fried in duck fat. Slurping Turtle, Ann Arbor, Michigan.) (Chicken and red velvet waffles with a side of grits. Zanzibar, Cleveland, Ohio.) Alaskan King Crab: It doesn’t get much better than this! It’s good in most restaurants, but even better if you get some shipped to you on ice from Alaska or at a friend’s seafood boil. (Alaskan King at the Nauti Mermaid, Cleveland, Ohio.) Burgers: So, I am not the biggest fan of burgers (boo, I know), but if you’re going to eat them, the US is a pretty good place. (Mile High Inn and Grille (now defunct), Jerome, Arizona.) (In-N-Out makes a better than average fast food burger. Ask for the animal style fries. All over California and Southwestern US.) Desserts: try one of our absurdly huge desserts. (Lulu’s Bakery and Cafe (now defunct), San Antonio, Texas.) Note: all photos are my own.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What will be the most important resource by the end of this century?
Answer: People. Below is a population pyramid with a relatively normal population distribution: (Nigeria’s population pyramid.) Now here is Russia’s: Here is China’s: Here is the United States: Finally, if you want to see something really fucked up, this is Qatar: Humans are the frog in a pot with the water temperature slowly rising. Right now, most of us can’t tell we’re in a crisis, but once it becomes apparent, it’ll already be too late. Most countries have low fertility rates with no replacement population possible. Humans will become the ultimate commodity. It’s likely that many governments will sooner or later restrict the movement of talented people and fight desperately over importing those they need. AI or robots won’t save us from this fate. It’s already too late. Image source: Wikipedia

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are Millennials doing right?
Answer: By no means is it all Millennials, but it’s some Millennials. Particularly those I meet while traveling. It is the same with some I meet from Gen Z. I see a paradigm shift from my parents’ generation. Millennials and those younger, aren’t that interested in trading their time for money, if they don’t have to. A lot of my friends or people that I meet, would rather not take that promotion if it means working more than 40 hours a week. Others won’t take that promotion if it means having to give up telework and go back into the office. Others, would rather make less money and be their own boss if it means more freedom and taking a vacation whenever they feel like it. (The road to success looks a bit different for us Millennials and Gen Z. We’ve re-defined Middle Class aspirations as an age cohort. Photo by author.) I think they’re right. Not only because I write these words, but because I am one of those people. I think that our generation realized the idea of working for that promotion to buy that big house, to then buy a vacation home, and jet skis was a false idol. We saw our parents’ generation work themselves into mental and physical illnesss, largely to buy things they didn’t need. In doing so, they forgot to actually live. As their children, we thank them for their sacrifices, but we don’t want to live like them.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Which branch of the military has more power and authority: Army or Air Force?
Answer: Army and Air Force have the same amount of authority. The Air Force clearly has more power. It’s not even close. We have the majority of fixed wing air craft. Army Airborne troops can’t really get anywhere without us. (Air Force C-17 dropping US army airborne troops.) Without the Air Force, they’ll have a hard time getting their helicopters close to the battle space. (Helicopter being loaded on a USAF C-17.) We have hundreds of aircraft capable of dropping precision guided munitions on formations of ground troops and armored columns. (A-10 Warthog. Even your best tanks don’t stand a chance against one of these guys.) But even on the ground, we have these guys: (Special Tactics Airmen.) And these guys: (US Air Force Security Forces. We’re kind of dumb, but there’s a lot of us. Photo credit: US Air Force.) And if that’s not enough, we make up 2/3rds of the U.S. military’s nuclear assets. (B-52 armed with air launched cruise missiles.) (Minuteman II control center blast door. The Air Force can radically alter the fate of humanity in the time it takes to deliver a pizza. The Army can’t do that.) The US Army is more powerful than an Air Force…but that air force is the Air Force of Bolivia. Technically, you can call Bolivia’s Air Force an air force in the same way that you can put pineapple on pizza. Technically, you can, but that don’t make you right. Photos: US Air Force/US DOD

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the hardest thing to deal with being in the military?
Answer: That a job must get done no matter what. That means if it is hotter than hades outside, or if it is cold, or if it is raining, or if there is a sandstorm, you must still go to work. A rather humorous example is from my life as an airman, while deployed to Camp Sather, Baghdad Airport. The airport had a mix of Iraqi civilian air traffic controllers and U.S. Air Force air traffic controllers. Although our air traffic controllers were armed with an M9 pistol while on duty, these guys weren’t really trained for shootouts and how to conduct security. They were, understandably, worried about their Iraqi counterparts and if one of them should smuggle in a weapon or worse into the air traffic control tower. Consequently, an airman was assigned as security for our personnel inside the tower, 24/7, in the event of an attempted insider attack. In reality, this air conditioned posting was posh and we loved being there. There was a desk with a computer and internet connection, movies that could be watched on the computer, and even a DSN line to call back to the United States as much as you wanted. Even the Iraqi controllers were quite pleasant to be around and they all spoke at least some English, per their job assignment. Also, since the posting was outside of the camp’s defense perimeter, you would have food from the cafeteria delivered to you. No waiting in line! (Baghdad Tower, photo by author.) The only downside: The elevator in the control tower often broke. But that doesn’t mean you don’t have to go to work. That meant climbing up 14 floors with your vest, helmet, NVG’s, rifle, pistol, and spare ammunition. What a bitch! Nothing could make you go from loving how lucky you were to draw this assignment, to hating it in mere seconds. When you made it to the top, the person you would be relieving would always have a bottle of cold water waiting on you. By that time you were huffing, puffing and drenched in sweat. Tough life in the Air Force.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What factors contribute to São Paulo's lack of popularity among foreign tourists compared to other Brazilian cities like Rio de Janeiro and Florianópolis?
Answer: I can think of a few. São Paulo doesn’t have beaches like Rio de Janeiro and Florianopolis, but instinctively, I would say it lacks the sex appeal. São Paulo is the business center of Brazil, while Rio is the fun center. Florianopolis is for peace and tranquility away from the larger cities. (View of Rio de Janeiro from Botafogo. Photo by author.) When we gringos think of Brazil, we think of Rio as fun, sun, and beaches. When we think of São Paulo, we think of it as a concrete jungle with endless rows of tall buildings and skyscrapers, not unlike our New York. The number of us that want to go see a city like New York in Brazil is much less than those of us that want to see a city like Rio, which is more like Miami, but on steroids. (View of downtown São Paulo at night. Photo by author.) That said, the idea that São Paulo is a boring city is a huge misconception. It’s one that even other Brazilians perpetuate, especially those from Rio. São Paulo alone actually is worth a visit to Brazil. To me, it woulnd’t be a stupid choice. They are only an hour apart by air and seven hours apart by bus though, so I would encourage anyone visiting Brazil to visit both.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How would the situation be if Ukraine had F-16's but did not have pilots to fly them?
Answer: That exact situation is the reality, actually. A total of 20 Ukrainian pilots are expected to graduate F-16 flight training this year. Denmark, Norway, the Netherlands and Belgium alone are slated to send 60 F-16’s to Ukraine by the end of the year. That’s three airframes for every one trained pilot. The ideal ratio is almost the reverse. It would benefit Ukraine to have at least two trained pilots for every airframe, since people get tired before aircraft. (Zelensky and Danish Prime Minister Frederiksen sit in a F-16 fighter jet. Photo credit: Politico.) Unfortunately, both European and American F-16 schoolhouses are at capacity with only a few slots given to foreign pilots each year. In the case of the U.S., foreign pilot training is typically scheduled years in advance and the U.S. can’t easily change its obligations to train its own pilots as well as those of allied nations. That said, Europe, the US, and defense contractor, Lockheed Martin, seem to be making every effort to adjust to the new reality. Additionally, Ukrainian pilots must learn English before they begin pilot training, which also takes time. What it means is that we’re still looking at another year and a half before Ukraine has even one fully operational F-16 squadron. Until then, we can’t hope to see these fighters making much more of a difference. The major hang up for Ukraine’s Air Force right now isn’t aircraft — it’s trained pilots.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do Americans ever leave the US in pursuit of a better life even though many immigrants immigrate to the US for a better lives?
Answer: Yes, I was one of them. It’s important that you define “better”, though. If by better, you mean a decent salary, low prices of imported goods, better healthcare, lower corruption, and great educational system, few other countries on earth are going to offer something better than in the US. For the most part, you’ll need to go to places like Canada, Western Europe, Scandinavia, and a few in Asia. Generally, they have rather strict immigration requirements with a few notable exceptions like Portugal and Spain. For the vast majority of the world, you’ll find that most of the quality of life factors are kicked down at least a notch or two. However, there is the opportunity for arbitrage if you still earn money in U.S. dollars or if you possess a skill that is rare in the country you are immigrating to. This is the situation where immigrating to a developing nation can vastly improve your day-to-day life in at least a few ways. For the vast majority of the people from the US who immigrate to other countries, it really boils down to this though: they’re looking for a little excitement and need a change in geography and/or a change in pace. This is the most common theme I see among US citizens living abroad. The one thing I can guarantee you if you move to a new country is that it’s going to be a while before you feel bored again. (Out at one of my favorite restaurants in Meridá, Mexico. More interesting food is a totally legitimate reason for moving abroad too. Photo by author.)
