Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you think Barcelona's plan to phase out all short-term rental leases by 2028 is a good idea or do you think it will have unintended negative consequences?
Answer: I don’t have a real opinion on whether Barcelona should or should not ban short-term rentals. I think that is for the people of Barcelona to decide. There are two things I feel relatively certain about: It’s interesting how these proposed bans never get implemented. However, it could be that I am being too cynical. (A photo of me taking a photo. Barcelona, 2023. Photo from author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do American people respect or love Muslim legal immigrants who obey American cultures at all?
Answer: I think in general, yes, but in my case, definitely yes. I grew up in a city with many immigrants from Islamic countries. Our nearby suburb, Dearborn, had the largest concentration of people from the Middle East in North America. I went to school with many muslims, I served with a few muslims, and my military unit had an interpreter who was muslim and was himself from Dearborn. I also had a doctor perform a life-saving surgery on me; that doctor was a muslim and wore a hijab. I thanked her profusely for the good work she did on me. (Islamic Center of America, in Dearborn, Michigan. Photo credit: Detroit Historical Society.) My favorite memories with muslim friends come from taking Tae Kwon Do at a martial art school in Dearborn and from my time working at a pizza parlor in a mostly Arab part of town. Most of my friends were from good, but stern homes. Many of their fathers ran their own businesses, while their mothers inevitably stayed home to attend to their children. I learned that my muslim friends suffered from the same problems non-muslims do. They think about sex, are tempted by alcohol, and drugs. Experience puberty, have silly notions about the world, use profanity, and a few were actually having sex. The image I previously had in my head of muslims being an extremely pious people was forever ruined. Needless to say, I think most immigrants from Islamic nations will adapt to American culture. If not in their own generation, their children’s generation.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why should you respect a veteran?
Answer: I think, collectively, as a nation it is good to both respect and honor our veterans that make countless sacrifices and give years of their life to the military — often times — the best ones. This is doubly so when we talk about veterans who have fought in combat, have been wounded or captured, and other heroic deeds. They represent some of the finest human beings I have ever had the pleasure to be around. The ultimate respect a nation can give veterans is to ensure they have the support they need when they return home, and that they have the tools to build a stable life, if at all possible. (John McCain, after returning from Vietnam where he’d been a prisoner of war in the infamous “Hanoi Hilton” prison. To me, John McCain is an example of veteran who was undoubtedly a hero for his nation, but your feelings may differ, especially based on your political outlook. Photo Credit: AP.) I am opposed to, however, the idea that each person, individually, needs to go out of their way to show respect to most veterans. My libertarian leanings also require that I mention it becomes a little creepy when patriotism bleeds into the area of unconditional hero worship. Most veterans are fallible human beings, with a wide diversity of political beliefs, backgrounds, mores, and even sexual preferences. There’s a non-zero chance that if you meet some of the people you call your hero, you may not even like them. Lastly, most of us didn’t see much combat. We probably had jobs that were tough compared to the average person, but so does a lumberjack.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do you deal with difficult times and uncertainty in your life?
Answer: This has been on my mind lately with everything that has happened in my life. I am apt to give the usual advice: one day at a time. It’s such great advice, because it’s true. I don’t know if time heals all wounds, but it certainly makes them smaller. When tragedy strikes, I tend to either mope around or completely throw myself into my work and any pursuit worthwile. Though I had a period of listlesness recently, I have decided on the latter. Don’t misunderstand me, however — I’m not saying you should ignore your emotions or try to forget them altogether. But if you’re angry, resentful, spiteful, etc., I think a person ought to use that as fuel. You’ll be surprised by how much more you can get done when you’re really pissed off. No moping around. (This picture, from a few years ago, was on one of the worst days of my life. I’d traveled to Cancun, so I could get a flight to the US, when I lived to Mexico. I’d just lost someone close to me. It also marked the beginning of one of the most productive periods of my life. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How are you today?
Answer: Dude, I’m tired. Like really fucking tired. I have been on a week long bender. This morning I am at the airport in Cancun. I am going home so that we can bury my little sister. Words I never in my entire life expected to say. I am crushed, but what can I do other than go with it? (Cancun airport. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why do people think Americans are bad at geography?
Answer: It is just another stereotype that America-bashers can hurl at us on Quora. We all rarely travel, we eat terrible cheese, don’t have healthcare, and shoot each other. Any other narrative about Americans is completely false.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Men, what traits in women are you attracted towards the most?
Answer: Femininity with intelligence. I like women who are as smart as a whip, I am not ever or at all intimidated by intelligence. I highly prefer it and I am endlessly fascinated with intelligent women who can speak with me on a variety of topics in a couple of different languages. So. Hot. 🥵

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Would you rather receive one million US dollars or flip a coin for the chance to win one billion US dollars?
Answer: Yeah, so…a million dollars isn’t enough money to substantially change my life as it exists today. So, I’m going to go for broke, baby! If I don’t get the billion dollars I think I would be quite satisfied knowing that at least I tried. If I do get it, I’ll buy Lichtenstein or some other small country. “Yesterday we were an army with no country. Tomorrow, we have to decide which country we want to buy!”

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What were the most significant turning points in World War II, and why?
Answer: Do I need to say something as glaringly obvious as Operation Barbarossa? After Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June of 1941, and engaged in a large scale war of attrition, it ended up eating away at much of the Third Reich’s men and materiel. Operation Barbarossa included the largest battles in human history and caused millions of casualties for both the Soviets and the Axis Powers. By the beginning of 1942, it became clear that Germany no longer had the advantage and was fighting the war on its heels. (Hitler and Field Marshal Walther von Brauchitsch. Photo credit: Wikipedia.) However, there was never a real possibility that the Germans would simply give up. Even though their eventual defeat was probably apparent to much of the Nazi high command, there could be no going back. It was all or nothing. Unfortunately for the Nazis, Hitler’s ideology left no room for the peaceful coexistence with a communist USSR. His decision to invade the Soviet Union was his greatest folly.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What happens to the equipment of soldiers when they leave the army?
Answer: In the US we say that we get to keep everything that touches the skin. That means, boots, t-shirts, uniforms, physical training gear, hats, etc. This isn’t to say that we never get to keep some military gear, however. Before deployment I was issued a compass, 5 pistol magazines for my M9 Beretta, and 8 STANAG magazines for my M4, flashlights, a Gerber multi-tool, and a glass breaker. I also got a few olive drab bags. Somehow, none of this gear was ever logged and I never had to turn it in. (Out of all the things I got to keep, the heavy duty bags are my favorite. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What’s your relationship with alcohol?
Answer: Complicated. I go weeks, months, and sometimes even a year without drinking, but then I will go on a complete bender that will last weeks. Sometimes it’s enjoyable, sometimes it’s not. The last few weeks have been rough. I had a couple of really horrible experiences in Rio de Janeiro and I decided to leave Brazil at least for a while (I still love you, Brazil). I ended up in Playa del Carmen, Mexico, just so I could wind down and decide if I wanted to go home to the United States this summer (I was leaning against going). Unfortunately, I received news that my sister died a few days ago. So, I will be going home shortly. Since then I have been in a constant drunken stupor. I made some horrible decisions and even burned a few of my friendships here in Mexico, because I just couldn’t behave myself. I pretty much never drink when I am in the States, so I know I’ll be fine soon. Sometimes I wish I wouldn’t drink so much when I decide to. (Spanish non-alcoholic beer. Sometimes I drink non-alcoholic beer because I miss the taste. I’m better when I don’t drink though. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What will happen to Mexico City if the water issue is not resolved?
Answer: I fear that Mexico City in its current size is simply unsustainable. What worries me most is what would happen if Mexico City is dealing with a water crisis and it simultaneously gets hit with another major earthquake. I think there’s the potential to unleash an enormous amount of human suffering due to poor oversight and poor foresight vis-a-vis the water situation in the capital city. Mexico City either needs to solve the water situation or it needs people to leave, it’s as simple as that. Life will go on in Mexico City, but it won’t go on for everyone. (Downtown Mexico City. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the most interesting item in your house?
Answer: This is actually difficult for me to guess, but maybe it is the Russian nesting doll given to me by one of my Russian friends. It has every Russian/Soviet leader from Tsar Nicholas to Boris Yeltsin. I certainly cherish it and it is one of my favorite things that adorns my home. It always sits on my desk. (All of the Russian and Soviet leaders up to Yeltsin. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What if there was no war in the world?
Answer: Let me tell you something my friend. War will always exist as long as humans exist. War is needed to reset political realities that can’t be easily negotiated over a table. There will always be aggressors and those who are susceptible to being trampled upon by those who have great power. What we can do is what has been done in the last 80 years since WWII. We can discourage such actions at every opportunity. However, eventually, our modern order will collapse. It’s not a matter of if, but a matter of when. You should know that the last 80 years have been the exception in human history, not the rule. Fundamentally, human history is rife with examples of incredible bloodshed. It will only be natural that we again devolve to such levels of cruelty. We are not at the end of history. In fact, we are teetering on the precipice of the most violent era humanity has ever seen. (During WWII powerful nations used industrial capacity to wipe out fellow humans at an unprecedented rate. That was 80 years ago, imagine what we can do with the technology of the 21st century. Photo credit: the D-Day Story.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are some weird facts about your house?
Answer: As an American there are two weird things about my house in the United States. There is no car parked in my parking space and inside there is no television. To most Americans this is unbelievable. It’s not like I don’t have a laptop, tablet, or mobile phone though. I also have a respectable book collection. Isn’t this enough to keep me entertained? The problem is that, slowly, over the years I outgrew television and wanted to do more things outdoors. After having worked in front of a screen for many years, now that I don’t have to, I actually don’t have the patience to sit in front of a screen for a couple of hours to watch a movie or tv show. You won’t catch me binging Netflix or any silliness like that. I don’t have a car because I don’t need one. I live in an urban area. I have a grocery store, restaurants, bars, and pharmacies close to my home. Whenever I am home (which is usually just for the summer) I can get everywhere I need to go using public transit, walking, biking, or if I am in a pinch, I can take an Uber. A car is seen by me as an unwanted burden. (To me, this is my anathema, not my idea of a dream. Photo credit: Yahoo Finance.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Which moments, either good or bad, do you still remember from your childhood?
Answer: I remember when I received the worst beating of my life from my drug-addicted mother. I must have only been 7 or 8. I somehow found one of her prescription pill bottles and not only that, I’d managed to open it. She walked into the bedroom of our shitty apartment and found me playing with the pills. I hadn’t taken any of them, thankfully. She decided it was time to teach me a lesson…never mind that she took zero responsibility for leaving dangerous prescription drugs within easy reach of a child. She took a thick leather belt and beat me until she was sweating and gasping for air and I had welts, and even cuts over my body. The entire time she swore and cursed my existence. I suppose it was effective. Not only would I never touch her things again, but I harbored a healthy amount of fear of her for the rest of my life.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are the differences between Canada and Mexico? Why do people prefer to move to Canada instead of Mexico?
Answer: For US citizens this isn’t actually true. There are almost three times as many American citizens living in Mexico than in Canada. I think world-class beaches, tequila, and tacos influence this decision. Americans aren’t chomping at the bit to retire in cloudy Nova Scotia. (Source: world population review.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Mexico, with gun control stronger than the UK, has a crime problem magnitudes worse than the UK. Is gun control the problem and not the solution?
Answer: Having lived in Mexico, I wouldn’t say that gun control is stronger than in the UK. You can, for example, still buy handguns, but they must be in a caliber not used by the military or police. (The Glock 42 is a popular pistol in Mexico for legal gun owners since it is chambered in .380, a caliber not used by the military or police. Photo credit: Glock.) As I understand it, guns like this are nearly completely out of reach for the gun-owning population in the UK. That said, the process of owning a gun in Mexico is long and arduous. There are also only a couple of gun stores in the country from which you can buy a gun. The problem with enforcing the law in Mexico is that there are huge parts of Mexico where the law and government hardly exist. It’s also relatively easy to smuggle guns into Mexico from the US, which is exactly what is done in many cases. The problem with Mexico isn’t gun control or any other laws, it’s really that there exists a state of lawlessness in many parts of the country that is not easily understood from someone from a place with firm rule of of law like the US or UK.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What "poverty food" is actually really delicious?
Answer: While I have rarely eaten it as an adult, I have fond memories of Spam as a kid growing up in Detroit. The characteristic sizzle it makes when in the frying pan, along with the smell of my aunt cooking it let me know that good things were to come. We always ate it on white bread that, as my aunt’s willing sous-chef, I covered in Miracle Whip and perhaps a slice of American cheese. A glass of Kool-Aid washed it all down. Bon appetit! Given our diet, it was probably a minor miracle we lived to adulthood. (Here is shown a very typical preparation of Spam. Photo credit: The Art of Manliness.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What can you take home from a trip to The British Museum?
Answer: A sense of awe and amazement!! When I went to the British Museum I had no idea that I would see this baby inside: (The Rosetta Stone in the British Museum. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the most ridiculous reason for which a flight was delayed?
Answer: I don’t know what started it, but a few years ago I was on a flight from Cancun when a fight broke out between two American passengers onboard the plane during boarding. We had to wait for the police to come arrest them. As the police were taking the two miscreants off of the airplane, one of the passengers quipped “I hear it’s a good time of year to go to jail in Mexico.” But no, it wasn’t. It’s never a good time of year to go to jail in Mexico. (Cancun airport. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why do Americans say that they are a classless society? Don't they have a middle class?
Answer: We have classes, but it’s based almost entirely on how much money someone earns. You cannot, for example, discern someone’s class in the United States from their manner of speaking, their dress, or where they went to school. (The Obama’s home on Martha’s Vineyard. Image credit: Homes and Gardens.) There are also no real barriers to anyone becoming a member of the highest strata of society, except money and your ability to earn it. If you are a talented athlete, actor, or invent a smartphone, all the velvety ropes will part for you. You can be Jewish, Black, White, or the son of a Lebanese or Cuban immigrant. These things are trivial compared to your wealth and your ability to access the power structures of our nation. Sure, it hasn’t always been this way, but that’s life as it exists currently in 2024. However, the few wealthy people that I know are incredibly relatable. Part of it is that there’s an enormous pressure on wealthy people in the US to play the role of every man. This is because one of the foundational myths of our nation is that anyone, literally anyone can become wealthy with enough hard work and ingenuity. (As we see in Spider-Man 2, even Harry Osborn, the scion of a wealthy family attends public school with our hero Peter Parker. This isn’t all together unlikely in America. Photo credit: Wikipedia.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you think it is fair for the New York Times editorial board to call for President Biden to exit the presidential election contest based on his debate performance?
Answer: Yes. Look, presidential debates, to a large degree, are about showmanship. None of us give a shit about the talking points either candidate is going to discuss. We’ve already heard them all. A significant reason we hold these debates is because we want to get the presidential candidates out in front of us where we can see them and get a good look at how they perform under a bit of pressure. If the debate was a test of those skills, Biden failed horribly. Terrifyingly. Sure, president Biden may have had a cold or other factors affecting his performance. But he is currently the President! Given the current state of our world today, at any moment he could be called on to make important decisions that not only affect Americans, but all of humanity. That is the kind of burden our president carries at all times. After seeing how he performed in a simple debate last night, do we really want to leave the fate of humanity up to this man? I think not. We need to do better, much better as a nation. The mere fact that the election is between these two grumpy old men is a testament to that. (Photo credit: AL.com)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Military members, have you ever been accused of Stolen Valor?
Answer: No, I tell people that I was in the Air Force and they automatically know I haven’t stolen anything. People who steal valor tend to always say something ridiculous like, I was a SEAL, I was Delta bro, or at least an Army Ranger. Also, I have too many pictures of me in uniform that I could show someone if they really wanted to see them, although I know haters can say they were photoshopped. Anyway, it’s silly. I wouldn’t stand around arguing with someone about my military service. After all, they have no idea about your service record. So who cares? (On a “rotator” headed to Doha, before an onward trip to Baghdad. People who steal valor don’t usually claim service in a “cushy” service like the Air Force. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is it true combat veterans remain hyper aware long after their service? Is the brain rewired? What causes this hyper state, new synaptic connections?
Answer: Yes, combat veterans, but many veterans in general. As a Security Forces Airman, our job was to always be vigilant, to be ready to respond and react whether on duty or off duty. For the US Air Force, the Khobar Towers bombing in Saudi Arabia had been a watershed event in terms of how the Air Force viewed our security posture. (Khobar Towers, Saudi Arabia. Photo credit: US Department of Defense.) 19 airmen were killed when members of Hezbollah in Saudi Arabia detonated a vehicle borne explosive next to a building that was housing airmen for operations in Middle East. The actions of a couple of airmen prevented further casualties, but the point was made clear. There is never a time we could completely put our guard down. US forces would always represent a considerable target whether in combat operations, off duty, in transit, or inside a barracks or hotel. After 9/11, this kind of paranoid thinking was sent into overdrive. It was constantly drilled into our heads that every airman was responsible for security and that we all had an obligation to be vigilant and take action if necessary. We received some decent training that emphasized how to behave, dress, and what we should look for when selecting a secure location when traveling. Today, I still find this training useful and I implement it in my personal life, where I often travel to somewhat dangerous countries where things like kidnapping, robbery, and narco-terrorism aren’t all together unlikely. It’s better to be safe than sorry.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is scary for sure?
Answer: Fear is a valuable tool in steering us in the direction we should live our lives. I have written about this before here. Of all the fears, my biggest fear is not living life for myself. Pay attention, really pay attention to how those around you react when you come to them with an idea or for advice. You may be thinking of changing careers, studying art, living in a monastery in India, or leaving your spouse. Your friends or family may object to this “I don’t know…I wouldn’t do that if I were you.” Of course they wouldn't, because they aren't you. Yet, it is only you who has to live with the life you chose for yourself. You will make mistakes, but making mistakes is better than making regrets. However daunting, lonely, or scary the path, it is yours to take. You already know what it is you want to do, you’re not asking for advice, you’re seeking permission. Don’t do that. Take life by the horns and completely own both your successes and failures. You’ll be a better person for it. (After my mother died, I spent a few months on the road all alone around the Southwestern US living out of an SUV and a cheap Walmart tent. I know my mother would have approved. It was at times scary, but one of the most meaningful journeys I have taken in my life. Luckily, I had people in my life that always encouraged my independence. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why do the French dislike American tourists?
Answer: I’ve never gotten the impression that French people dislike American tourists. In fact, France isn’t even the least friendly country I have been to in Western Europe and certainly not the least friendly place I have visited in the world (I don’t want to open this can of worms again, so read through my other answers if you want to know). I did have a few interesting encounters with people in Paris, though. One of them I still laugh about when I think about to this day. Mind you, I don’t speak any French at all besides a few greetings. The morning I was due to leave Paris I went to the metro station to get the train to Charles de Gaulle airport. Unfortunately, I didn’t have any coins and needed change for the Euro notes I was carrying. It was early in the morning (probably around 6:30) and I noticed a man in the kiosk inside the metro station sipping coffee. I decided to go over and ask him for help. Me: Bonjour, parlez-vous anglais? Him: Yes. What do you want? Me: I need change for my money so that I can pay for my ticket to the airport. Him: I don’t open until 7 a.m. He then closed the shutters for his kiosk so that I would leave him uninterrupted. I was really anxious about getting to the airport since my flight left at around 9 a.m., so as a result, I didn’t wait until quite 7 a.m. before I returned to the kiosk to get change. It must have been 6:57 a.m. or so when I returned and knocked on the glass window. He opened the shutters again and then looked at his watch. “I already told you, I don’t open until 7!” He then waited until the exact moment his watch struck 7 a.m. before he opened the till and handed me my change. To this day I couldn’t figure out if maybe he couldn’t open the till before precisely 7 a.m. or if he was just being pedantic. My girlfriend and I got our tickets, however. As we stood on the platform waiting for the train to the airport, another Parisian man whipped out his penis in full view of all onlookers and urinated on the platform. Paris. (A duplicate of the torch from the Statue of Liberty in central Paris. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are the best ways to travel between Schengen countries once inside the area?
Answer: Train or airplane, usually. It’s pretty straight forward. You can use apps like Omio that will automatically compare prices between flight, train, and bus tickets. The thing is, flying is often as cheap or close to the price as taking the train, so it’s often times more appealing, although, of course, less environmentally friendly. One problem I encountered last year though, is that the train operators went on strike in Portugal to demand better wages. This meant I was forced to take the bus or plane during all of my travels in Portugal. (Boarding a Ryan Air flight for a short flight from Sevilla to Lisbon. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you believe the death penalty should be abolished in America?
Answer: In modern day America? No. There was a time when I think our justice system was prone to bias and lots of mistakes. For much of my life I was very much against the death penalty and I think that, given what I knew at the time, this made a lot of sense. Then I spent a lot of time living in a state, Ohio, which has the death penalty. After I saw how rarely and how deservingly the death penalty was applied, I completely agree with it. I have been tangentially connected to two death penalty cases in my time in Ohio. The first was in the death of a student of one of my friends. This sweet little 14-year-old girl was on her way to school one morning when she was kidnapped by a complete psychopath of a man. Not only did he rape her, but he tortured her using a power drill, before finally murdering her. He was already a registered sex offender and both his DNA and surveillance footage connected him to the crime. (Trigger warning: Only read this if you have a strong stomach.) The other case was one of the guards that worked as a contractor for the federal government in my office building in downtown Cleveland. This was a man I saw every morning as I went to work, not knowing he was capable of committing a horrifying and heinous crime. One night he got into an argument with his girlfriend and decided that he would take revenge by murdering her two teenage children with his service weapon. He then barricaded himself in their home for several hours before finally giving up. I believe both of these men deserve death, I don’t think that makes me callous. They were for the crimes they committed.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Who uses the euro?
Answer: A lot of countries. Interestingly enough, a few countries in the Americas use the Euro. When exchange rates were less favorable, this made vacations less enjoyable. These countries also tend to charge a rather high amount for currency conversion from the US dollar to the Euro. Some years ago I was in Saint Martin in the Caribbean and we went for a short day trip over to Saint Bart’s on a catamaran. It was a fun experience, but I remember stopping into some tourist shop and there was a man there with an obvious New York accent. He politely asked the shop attendant how much a T-shirt in the shop would cost. I think it was something like €25, but they wanted $35 if he was going to pay in dollars. He got incredibly upset. “This place is a third world country! You’re hardly suckin’ air. You would be NOTHING without America!” I was a bit embarrassed by my fellow American. But he was also right. The price was too god damned high for a simple t-shirt. (St. Bart’s. This island is a part of France, so they use the Euro. Don’t expect anything to be cheap in this playground for the rich and famous. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do Americans really avoid hospitals, even in serious situations because of the bills that follow after?
Answer: For me, this has never been an issue. When I was young and we had very little household income, we qualified for the state Medicaid program which usually covered most or all of the cost of going to a hospital. As an adult, I have been able to go to the Veterans Affairs hospital or to the nearest hospital to me in a serious emergency and they would cover the bill. Contrary to what a lot of people may say, my care at our veteran’s hospitals has almost always been at least good or excellent. I had some problems when I lived in an area with a lot of veterans (Phoenix), where I would get longer wait times for an appointment for routine medical care. However, in an emergency, it was never an issue to show up to the ER. In Cleveland, this isn’t an issue at all. In fact, I will often times travel back to the United States just for my medical appointments. At times, I get a same day appointment if I call and have an urgent, but not serious problem. I have absolute trust in my care team. I still have private insurance, but I haven’t used it in many years because I prefer to go to the Veterans Affairs hospital that has my entire medical history dating back to the age of 20. (Louis Stokes Veterans Affairs hospital. Not only have I liked my care here, but I really like my doctor who really pushed me to get into better shape and to take care of my health. Photo credit: VA.gov)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is an American man?
Answer: If we rely on the classical archetype, an American man is strong, courageous, adventurous. He is self-reliant, always respectful to strangers and women. Not unwilling to engage in violence, but since he is not a bully, he never strikes first. (Alan Ladd as the titular character Shane. Photo credit: Flicks.) Shane, for example, embodies everything an American man is supposed to strive to be. He is courteous, gentlemanly, handy, but also dangerous. In Quentin Tarantino’s retelling of the classic western in Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, however, we are told that the archetype of the American man is largely a myth created by dime store novels and western movies from the 50’s and 60’s. (Brad Pitt as notorious stuntman, Cliff Booth. Photo credit: Quentin Tarantino Wiki.) Cliff Booth is strong and courageous, but he misses the mark with politeness and is sometimes a bully. It’s strongly suggested that he has killed his wife. Yet, he comes off as very typically American. So, what is an American man? It depends on who you ask.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What makes a great guest experience in a restaurant?
Answer: When most things are better than average and a few things are excellent. I am no stranger to eating at low-brow establishments, but when I eat at those places it’s because the food is excellent and that’s the reason I am there. When I am spending a considerable amount of money on dinner it’s not just for the food, but also the experience. A neatly dressed and courteous waitstaff, a nicely decorated restaurant, a dining room with a view, an excellent list of wines and spirits, and a few dishes using fresh and superb ingredients. (Out for dinner at DonDoh in Bogotá. This place has most of the things I mentioned above. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you think technology is making us more disconnected from each other?
Answer: Yes, especially politically speaking. Online political rhetoric, in my opinion, is responsible for the highly charged political atmosphere we all live in today. It’s hazardous to become “friends” on Facebook or other social media with co-workers, friends, and even some family members. Some time ago, one of my friends told me that her niece blocked her uncle on Facebook because he wouldn’t stop posting pro-life material, something she feels very strongly against. Now they rarely speak in person anymore either. Just a couple of decades ago, no one had a platform to constantly badger others with their political beliefs. Politics was something people talked about much more rarely. Maybe just a few times a year. Everyone eventually had some laughs about it around the dinner table or the bar and went home more or less unscathed. That kind of polite discussion around politics really isn’t possible anymore.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are the worst experiences as a USA soldier on deployment?
Answer: Barring death or dismemberment of yourself or those close to you, the worst things are usually the things that happen far away from a service member’s watchful gaze. These are the things happening at home that give him worry or evoke the fear of missing out. Particularly, in my squadron, three of us, including myself, had one of our parents die while we were deployed. We were given leave to sort out their affairs, but expected back in Baghdad in just a couple of weeks. My squadron executive officer had his wife diagnosed with cancer and was permitted to go home. A few people had their girlfriends or spouse leave them. These things are pretty much guaranteed to happen on every deployment. (Pictured here, I am pointing to the closest city on the sign post to my hometown of Detroit, which was East Lansing. Ironically, after returning from deployment I would attend graduate school at the University of Michigan. As a rule, Michigan graduates are required to hate East Lansing, since it is the home of our rival university. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do you define the American Dream?
Answer: My definition of the American dream is probably a bit interesting. When I was young, it meant growing up to live a life of adventure, financial stability, and a fair amount of violence. In that I succeeded, mostly. In the 1990’s we grew up on adventure and spy flicks. We always knew who the bad guys were, even if they didn’t always wear black hats. Americans were confident and self-assured and always the hero. (Three Kings. A movie of my childhood fantasies. Image credit: Amazon.) To me, achieving the American dream, ironically, meant leaving America. It meant going to interesting places, learning the local culture, and appreciating the food. Americans, by nature, are explorers (despite what you might hear here on Quora). After all, we are the people who conquered the West, traveled to Antarctica, and landed on the moon.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Younger guys, do you like older women?
Answer: Yes, almost exclusively. I get made fun of sometimes by my buddies, but I have never enjoyed dating women my own age. There is something more enigmatic, intoxicating about older women. Furthermore, they are almost always straight to the point. If an older woman doesn’t like you, she tells you. She doesn’t have time to waste. There is also something incredibly beautiful about the body of a woman who has lived her life. Scars, gray hairs, wrinkles. The signs of a life well-lived. An older woman can tell you where you’re headed, because she has already been there. (Jennifer Coolidge. To people my age she will always be known as Stifler’s mom. A generation of young men lusted after her. Photo credit: Buzz Feed.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you still use cursive handwriting?
Answer: Sure. This is mostly true when I write in my journal. This is because no one has to try to decipher my terrible penmanship. So yes, I write in cursive, but it’s not really legible to anyone but myself. (My journal that has traveled with me for many, many miles. The pages can be replaced once they are filled. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What city has an underrated food scene?
Answer: In the United States, it’s easily Minneapolis. People don’t think of going to the cold Midwest for good food, but I would put Minneapolis up against NYC, San Francisco, or Miami any day of the week. Want Vietnamese? They have that! (Pho Hoa. A must try if you are in Minneapolis.) Want Middle Eastern? They have that! Want Ethiopian? They have that! Want Mexican? They have that! (Los Ocampo. You have to try the beef cheek tacos here or your life will not be complete.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Which country has the worst cuisine?
Answer: That I’ve been to? Canada. I’m just kiddin’. I like you poutine-munching cretins. Iceland though, seriously. Motherfuckers tried to feed me fish for breakfast and I don’t see how any American could square with that. (Pickled herring. No red-blooded American would eat this for breakfast. Image credit: Reddit.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: In what ways are you a political hypocrite?
Answer: I’m a little nervous to write this answer because I know it will make some people upset. However, I just want to get this out of the way. I have fervent political beliefs. I’m fiercely patriotic. While I will call the country of my birth out about its flaws, I still think it’s one of the best, if not the best nation on earth. Heck, I haven’t even spent much time there over the last five years or so, because I have preferred my life abroad. Still, I am unmistakably, unapologetically American. What I like about America is the idea of America. I know some people like my sweet neighbor, Maria, who have come to America and made an incredibly good life for themselves and it makes me immensely proud. I still have hope and faith in our country and its system of governance. All of that said: I don’t vote. (Voting booth. You won’t catch me in one of these. Image credit: Voting Source.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do I cook a thick steak without burning the outside?
Answer: I love to cook big pieces of ribeye (entrecôte for you Europeans) and then eat them. My favorite method is incredibly simple. I heat the oven 250F/121C and place the steak in the oven for approximately 15–20 minutes depending on thickness. I finish the steak on a really hot grill, preferably charcoal or wood. I sear it for just a couple of minutes on each side for a medium doneness. Let the steak sit for five minutes or so before serving. Enjoy. (Get the grill started well in advance so that the charcoal or wood is already very hot when it’s time to take that steak out of the oven. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is your favorite restaurant to eat at and why?
Answer: I, the man known as a notorious food snob among my friends, hold a terrible secret. One of my favorite restaurants is actually a chain restaurant. The Mexican steakhouse chain Sonora Grill. While I still would say that I can make a better steak than them, it’s a pretty good option when I don’t feel like cooking or want to have a nice night out. The food is always consistently better than average. They serve good, freshly made salsas and have a nice variety of options like ribeye, bone marrow, cow tongue, and steak tacos. All of their restaurants are nicely appointed and have a fun vibe. I’ve never had a bad experience in one of their joints. Note: all photos are my own.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: In combat, is it common for soldiers to “finish off” a dying comrade?
Answer: In the US military, no. This would be considered murder and you could expect to be brought up on charges. Things like this only happen in dystopian militaries like the mobile infantry in Starship Troopers or the armed forces of Russia. (Rico, our favorite alien fighting Argentinian. Without hesitation he kills his badly wounded commanding officer. We’d better hope the ballistics can’t be traced back to his weapon or he’s in trouble.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why do I look down on veterans?
Answer: Because you don’t know us. Most of us are ordinary people with very ordinary lives. If you were ever at my place we would have beers, cigars, and grilled steaks and talk college football. How do you think the Wolverines will do this year?

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is your favourite breakfast?
Answer: Easy. Longaniza de Valladolid with eggs and a side of really hot habanero salsa. A Yucatecan speciality that makes life worth living. (Longaniza de Valladolid is a smoked and savory sausage from the Yucatán region of Mexico. Here it is paired with eggs and pickled onion. A Seville orange for flavor. It makes the perfect breakfast. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Can a dead body look like it’s still alive?
Answer: Yes, especially in the heat of battle, like close quarters combat. Moreover, dead bodies can still make noises. When I trained with the Green Berets they asked me to not use the phrase “huah” (a common military saying) anymore while doing building clearing. The reason being is that dead bodies sometimes expel gas and air. It can sound remarkably like “huah” under the right circumstances.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are biggest misconceptions about London?
Answer: That everyone speaks the King’s English, takes a Routemaster to work, and lives on a steady diet of nothing but fish and chips and blood sausage. Or that London has nothing to offer from a culinary perspective. (London Eye on the Thames at night. Photo by author.) London is one of my favorite big cities in the world and a lot of people have probably guessed that if you have followed me for a bit. It’s just as diverse as its American counterpart (New York), has limitless good food options, a cool pub culture, and is a good lookin’ city with tons of history and interesting architecture. If you visit you just might fall in love! (Doner kebab in London. 🤤 Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What makes people hate you even if you are not doing anything wrong?
Answer: It’s called envy. I can think of a couple of cases where this affected me. Once, as a federal employee, I applied for a job with a new agency that was a GS-12 position, which is a pay grade that most federal employees hope to achieve, but sometimes can take years. Others will never obtain such a pay grade. I felt confident since I had a graduate degree and four years of civilian service under my belt. After a rigorous board interview, I was notified a couple of weeks later that I’d been selected for the position. Little did I know that the fiscal officer at my new agency had also applied for the position, but was not selected. I believe that in part, she felt it was incredibly unfair that a much younger and less experienced federal employee was selected for the position over her. Any time I interacted with her she was curt and quick to point out any perceived shortcomings on my part. She also used to enjoy CC’ing my boss on any emails when she felt I made an error. This is the ultimate F-U for federal employees. We hate having our boss CC’d and our bosses hate it too. Usually the things that she had a problem with were minor and things she could have come directly to me about instead of sending an email. Despite her behavior, I was always amicable. It was many months before word got back to me that she’d applied for the same position that I took and then it all made sense. (Me as a desk jockey for the government. Photo by author.) Another case was a person I actually called my friend that backstabbed me for years. We’d both worked for the same agency and in similar positions, so it wasn’t that which got him envious. Instead he had an incredibly unhappy life with a marriage he didn’t want and a life he didn’t want. He wasn’t just envious of my girlfriend, my house, my car, or my exotic vacations. He wanted my entire life and felt he deserved it more than me. For years he’d trash talked me to mutual friends and co-workers all while pretending to be my friend. It took years for me to see his true character and for someone to finally speak up and tell me the truth about him. It turns out he is what it is called a narcissist and these people make terrible friends.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How long does it take people to stop hating everyone from a country they fought a war against?
Answer: To be clear, I never felt our fight was against the Iraqi people, but against the insurgency that had come to be by the time I was deployed to Iraq (2009). However, I could also clearly see that the insurgency was a direct result of American intervention in Iraq and that had it not been for our presence, they wouldn’t exist. The insurgents were also not all Iraqis. Some of them came from as far away as Chechnya for the opportunity to kill us. That said, I always thought the situation was a bit unfair. The insurgents could pull up alongside our base and lob rockets and mortars at us and then take off. They weren’t doing this because we were a direct threat to them, rather it seemed like a pastime they engaged in when they were bored on a Tuesday night. Their actions resulted in very real casualties and rarely were any of the perpetrators caught. The Iraqi military was mostly a pleasure to work with. Many of them had absolutely horrifying stories of death and survival that could not even be imagined by your average westerner. One guard from the Iraqi military managed to tell me in his broken English that his wife and kids had all been wiped out in a single bombing. He joined the military to get revenge. (Off duty in Baghdad. Photo by author.) That said, I never trusted anyone from the Iraqi military. I never turned my back on any of them when I had to work with them. Whenever I passed through an Iraqi military checkpoint I always unholstered my pistol and had it ready to fire. So to answer the question, I never hated any of the Iraqi people and never harbored any ill will towards anyone except for the insurgents that tried to kill us.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is something that you're one of the few people to ever see?
Answer: A terrorist attack might be one of those things. One morning in Baghdad I was just leaving my post and heading back to my quarters to get some sleep. Suddenly, I heard the sound of an enormous blast followed by a mushroom cloud I could clearly see on the horizon. Unforgettable. Apparently there was a vehicle borne explosive set off in downtown Baghdad. The vehicle was packed with hundreds of pounds of explosives and something like 200 people were killed (I learned this later from CNN). Sure, I didn’t see it up close, but it’s one of those things that’s forever stuck in my memory knowing that I was witness to a moment where hundreds of people were wiped out in an instant. (The area formerly known as the Victory Base Complex (VBC), Baghdad, Iraq. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are some ways to tell if someone is a veteran? How can you tell that someone has served in the military from their appearance, behavior or speech patterns/accent?
Answer: A lot of the time I can tell if someone is a veteran just by their general demeanor. Sure, things like tattoos and haircuts help, but on a deeper level, being a veteran is something that makes you behave differently. In general, I don’t wear anything associated with the military, nor do I have any military tattoos. I also am bearded and don’t wear a military style haircut. Last year I stopped by the Starbucks near my home for a coffee before going on a walk. I walked in and the barista behind the counter took one long look at me and said, “Jesus Christ, you have some big arms, man. You were in the military, weren’t you?” I was a little embarrassed and said, “yes.” He then thought about it for a minute and then said “let me guess which service…you were in the Air Force, weren’t you?” Again, I smiled and said “yes.” Now, I am someone who prides themselves in being a veteran that tries not to look or dress like a veteran. But still, within 30 seconds a barista was able to intuit that not only was I a veteran, he was even able to deduce my branch of the military. Maybe he was a psychic, or maybe we really are built just a little different. (I am forever a fan of Starbucks, but I really wish they would spell my name right. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are sad facts of life?
Answer: I wrote another answer a while ago that became incredibly popular on Quora. I wrote about how intelligence, self-determination, and grit are characteristics that assure success in modern America. As popular as that answer was, I received a fair amount of pushback. That’s not completely unwarranted. (Egipto slum, Bogotá, Colombia. Photo by author.) A sad fact of life is that the great majority of people born today are born in circumstances that are not changeable, no matter how hard one might try. A few years ago, I was sitting on the beach in Rio de Janeiro when a man approached me selling souvenirs. He spoke good English and explained to me that he was from Senegal and had come to Brazil after being smuggled there on a cargo ship. He told me that while he liked Brazil, he was applying for a visa to go to the United States where he hoped to start a new life. My heart sank knowing that there was zero chance this young man without a stable career or any marketable skills would ever be approved for a visa. Yet, he was hopeful and even smiling just speaking about the opportunity to do so. We sat there, separated by inches, but living worlds apart. For those of us lucky enough to be from a developed nation with the opportunity to realize our hopes and dreams, it comes with a downside. It is the guilt we feel knowing that we’re privileged mostly by chance and circumstance. We could have easily been born in a different place, in a different time. The way we make amends for our privilege is to lighten the load for others whenever we have the opportunity. I didn’t need or even want to buy a bracelet that day, but I was happy to do so. (Bracelet bought on the beach in Rio. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Have you ever saved someones life? If so, where did they end up today?
Answer: Yes, maybe. Two years ago I was home for the summer in Cleveland, Ohio. I was bored and, uncharacteristically, I decided to go out downtown at night for a walk. It was probably about 1 a.m. and I was actually having quite a good time. To be perfectly honest, I was under the influence of some really good legal marijuana from my home state of Michigan. (Downtown Cleveland at night, photo by author.) I was walking down St. Clair when I noticed a disturbance. A tall (honestly), beautiful red headed woman was struggling to get away from an also very tall Black guy in leather pants and an interesting shirt. He had his arm around her and was trying to lead her to a parking lot. I could tell that she was struggling just to stand, but she had the conscience of mind to at least say out loud “please leave me alone! I don’t want to go with you!” What was interesting is that the street was full of people leaving bars and clubs. It’s unbelievable, but not a single other person on the street said a fucking thing, even though it was clear this woman was in distress and trying to get away from a would-be kidnapper. I was nervous and I too nearly kept walking, but my conscience got ahold of me. I had to do something. Finally, as I saw the man leading the woman down an alley, I said “hey man! Leave her alone. Do as the woman said and let her go!” He tried to ignore me and keep going. At this point I actually started to follow them down the alley. “Hey motherfucker! I am talking to you! Let her the fuck go!” Finally, he turned around and looked at me. He mumbled some words to the effect of “hey man, why you hatin’?” This was enough of a distraction that the woman threw his arm off from around her shoulder and took off running. At this point, the man also took off running in a different direction. At first, my instinct was to follow the woman to ask if she was actually okay, but I realized that she’d just survived an almost terrible ordeal and following her would have probably freaked her out. I watched as she put a lot of distance between us and I felt confident that she got away safely. I don’t know where she ended up, but I am glad that somewhere inside me I found the courage to say something. Please, if you ever see something untoward happening to a person on the street, don’t be a bystander. Do something!

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is it true that all Canadians are friendly? What about those living in Quebec?
Answer: I’m going to disagree with other people. Having lived and spent a considerable time in southern Mexico, I can tell you that the opinion of Canadians here, particularly French Canadians, is rather mixed. There is a large population of Quebecois who live here either full time or part time to escape the Canadian winters. (Our friendly neighborhood cat that lived at the bar. Photo by author.) Story time: during the COVID-19 pandemic, Mexico was subject to rather severe restrictions. To our endless annoyance, nearly all bars and restaurants were restricted to closing at 10 pm for all of 2021 and even part of 2022. One night I was at my local bar run by a friend of mine in Merida. It must have been 9:50 or something close to that. Just as my friend was ready to close the bar a group of French Canadians showed up to the bar. My friend regretfully informed the group that he could not serve them since the bar would be closing in just 10 minutes. In short order they expressed their outrage. My friend, ever polite, didn’t want to do anything to offend them. I sat merely observing the entire ordeal. Finally, one of the men took out a $500 peso note and slammed it on the bar “this is Mexico! You will open this fucking bar!” Unbeknownst to these idiots, the fine for staying open during COVID restrictions was at least $10,000 pesos. Not nearly enough money to break the law. At this point I said what my friend was thinking: “you don’t have enough money, so get the fuck out of here!” They did as I said. It felt good to do a little justice in the world. After living in Mexico I have always joked that Canada is a polite country because they make all the jerks leave. You can often find them in the Yucatán region of Mexico.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is convicted felon Donald John Trump capable of kindness, mercy, and empathy?
Answer: Yes, he is. For all of his flaws, Trump is still a human being. I remember being nearly moved to tears when he pardoned Alice Johnson and spoke kindly of her in his 2019 State of the Union Address. For those not in the know, Alice was a convicted drug trafficker who had been sentenced to life without possibility of parole. President Trump not only invited her to the 2019 State of the Union Address, he actually managed to humanize her with kind words about her character. To me, it was a bizarre moment in American politics. A Republican president pardoned a Black woman who trafficked drugs and made her seem like an ordinary person. Could you imagine Ronald Reagan doing the same? Or even Obama for that matter? Unreal. (Alice Johnson at the State of the Union Adress. Photo credit: whitehouse.gov.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What do soldiers say when they salute?
Answer: The greeting of the day is always rendered to an officer when saluting. E.g.: “Good morning ma’am!” It’s funny to do it when officers are standing around talking to teach other. Usually it is rude to interrupt people during a conversation, however, military courtesy requires that we salute and give the greeting of the day. Not saying we do this all the time, but sometimes we enlisted members actually go out of the way to walk past an officer just so we can salute them and receive a salute in return. After a while they’ll understand that they shouldn’t be standing outside having a conversation unless they want to be interrupted every few minutes by someone giving a salute and greeting.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What was your first experience of being under artillery fire like?
Answer: In Iraq it was always inconsistent. Generally, the insurgents liked to use rockets that were fired from the back of a truck. They would take off as quickly as possible because they were aware that we could easily calculate the point of origin (POO) and return fire or send out a patrol. (Counter rocket, artillery, and mortar (C-RAM) system. We used these to keep us safe from enemy artillery fire. Photo credit: Wikipedia.) That said, my very first night on duty in Iraq we came under a rather sustained rocket and mortar attack. For whatever reason the C-RAM didn’t activate and quite a few things around the base got blown to bits. Luckily, no one was killed or injured. This wouldn’t be the case for our entire deployment, however, where the insurgents sometimes got some lucky shots. One night several people were killed in just one attack on the Victory Base Complex. I will never forget the sight of their coffins being loaded onto a C-130 draped in American flags.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do I avoid bad language?
Answer: If I knew, I would tell you. Generally, I’m quite profane, certainly much more than my posts here on Quora would let on, even though I don’t shy away from using profanity here either. I hate to admit that in some ways I am a product of my environment. I grew up in Detroit and served in the military. Two things that don’t lend well to strictly speaking the King’s English. I find ways to tone it down when I am around my sweet older neighbor, Maria. My other neighbor, a septuagenarian from Cleveland, swears more than I do. Still, I have only accidentally let myself slip around her a few times. Ironically, my neighbor who swears a lot asked me to no longer swear in my Facebook posts. I have tried to comply as best as I can. (Whenever I am in a bad mood I watch videos of George Carlin’s standup. This certainly doesn’t help me in avoiding foul language. Photo credit: Britannica.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is it like to throw a grenade?
Answer: In one word: awesome! To start the day that we went to the grenade range, our instructors took us on a trail that went up the side of a small mountain at Camp Bullis, Texas. They didn’t tell us why we were on the trail or what was going to happen. After some time, we halted our patrol on a part of the mountain overlooking a small valley. Briefly, we saw a flash of light and then the sound of an enormous explosion which reverberated off the nearby hills. My first thought: holy shit! They took us to a gunnery range to watch the F-16 fighter jets drop a bomb! But no, it was just one of our instructors throwing an M68 fragmentation grenade. Needless to say, at least a few of us were quite terrified of actually throwing grenades after that little preview. I think that was the point of the demonstration. “Don’t fuck around when throwing these grenades, ya hear?” (Throwing practice grenades at Camp Bullis. Photo by author.) Thankfully, we first got to warm up by throwing practice grenades before moving on to the real thing. I never played much baseball, but I am rather good at throwing grenades. I find that having several ounces of explosive in your hand with a kill radius of 5 meters is plenty of motivation to make a good throw.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What was the worst thing you got in trouble for as a kid? How did it play out?
Answer: I’m laughing just thinking about this, but at the time it probably wasn’t so funny. It was 1999 and to give some context, it was just a few weeks after the unfortunate Columbine Massacre. Early one morning one of my friends showed up at school and had a surprise for me. (McMichael Middle School, Detroit, Michigan. Image credit: X.) “Hey man, I got these firecrackers. Will you hold these for me until lunch time?” I was hesitant, but eventually said yes and stuffed them into my socks. At lunch time, after getting some courage, he suggested that we light the firecrackers in the school lobby and throw them into an empty locker. Of course, we did it. It caused absolute mayhem as students, teachers, and administration believed that the school was under attack. People ducked, dove for cover, and nearly shit their pants. We took off running, believing we could get away with our crimes. The school was essentially locked down and thorough interrogations took place. It didn’t take long before my co-conspirator was found out and he also gave me up under intense questioning. I was given a suspension from school for an entire week, which to me, wasn’t a real punishment. You mean I get to stay home and watch Jerry Springer for a week and don’t have to go to class? I think my aunt was so angry she didn’t even bother to give me an ass whipping as was her custom. She just wanted me out of her sight. What I did learn though is that if you ever commit a crime with someone else, they’ll always give you up if they think it would help them.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you still remember being bullied as a child?
Answer: Yes, but I wouldn’t say I was traumatized by it. People used to mess with me because I wore glasses and I was, in fact, quite nerdy. I was into reading sci-fi and watching Star Trek. When teachers asked a question in class, I almost always knew the answer and would raise my hand. (Steve Urkel from the show Family Matters. I was always called Urkel in school because of the ugly glasses I used to wear. Photo credit: today.com.) Looking back, I probably could have kept a lower profile. Yet, the same things that made me the object of bullying in junior high, made me more or less respected in high school. People wanted to study with me or ask me questions. I also got into weightlifting my junior year and after that no one ever messed with me. The last time I got into a fight in school was my sophomore year. One of the jocks on the football team walked up to me and hit me directly in the groin without warning. Not sure what would have provoked him to do so. I immediately gave him my best right hook (by this time I had years of kick boxing experience). Even though he was taller, bigger, and stronger than me, my response was clearly unexpected. He was startled and backed away. What was more embarrassing to him is that a sizable crowd saw this happen in the hallway of the school. Naturally, he promised to beat my ass after school. He met me right outside the doors of the school where a crowd had gathered to watch me get my ass kicked. I put up my guard in a fighting stance and told him to come at me. He laughed and said “man, get out of here, I’m not going to beat your ass in front of all these people.” He then walked away. I feel certain my bully probably ended up in a prison or worse. So I will have the last laugh.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What do veterans think of being used as a prop for political arguments?
Answer: I think it’s a bad idea to use your military service as a shield when making political arguments. (Senior Airman Brian Kolfage. Photo credit: Tucson Sentinel.) Meet one of my fellow Air Force Security Forces Airmen, Brian Kolfage. Most of us within the career field knew about him due to his prominence on social media and, of course, due to the severe injuries he suffered during a deployment to Iraq. Brian is a triple amputee, having narrowly survived a rocket blast at Balad Air Base. For many years, Brian used his status as a wounded veteran to espouse his political beliefs on his popular Facebook page. Eventually, he drew the attention of some notable Republicans when he campaigned to build a wall on the southern border of the United States. He started a GoFundMe page that raised millions of dollars for his effort, which he conducted jointly with notorious political strategist Steve Bannon. (Brian and his wife aboard his fishing boat, Warfighter. Photo credit: Daily Mail.) Unfortunately, Kolfage also saw this as an opportunity to enrich himself and he devised a scheme to surreptitiously transfer the funds from his campaign to his personal accounts. In a short amount of time he was caught. He is now serving a 51 month prison sentence in a federal penitentiary. His co-conspirator, Steve Bannon, was pardoned by president Trump. Don’t be like Brian.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What's the weirdest question you've been asked when crossing an international border?
Answer: I was transiting the United States a few years ago (not staying, just catching a connecting flight). I was flying from London to Cancun, Mexico, but I had a stop in Newark, New Jersey. I imagine this is a rare occurrence since most Americans probably don’t find themselves in this situation. However, I was a Mexican resident at the time and traveling with a US passport. The customs officer took a look at my passport and my Mexican visa. Him: “Where are you headed today, sir?” Me: “I’m headed to Cancun, Mexico” Him: “why?” Me: “I live in Mérida, Mexico.” Him: “Sir, so you’re just going to abandon America then?” Me: “no, I’m not abandoning America, I still have a home here in fact, it’s just that I live somewhere else right now.” He looked at me incredulously again, shook his head, and handed me my passport. He simply couldn’t believe there were Americans who wanted to live outside of the United States, I guess. (The international airport in Madrid. European countries never give me as much trouble as the border guards in my own country. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Which foreign actors influenced Germany's ban on nuclear power plants?
Answer: We know that the KGB/Stasi at least attempted to influence the German Green Party. There is endless debate on the effectiveness of their influence campaign. The Green Party investigated itself and concluded that the Soviets had very little impact on their policy directives. Is it hard to imagine that, after the end of the Cold War, Russia had a vested interest in seeing that the Germans moved away from nuclear energy? Of course the FSB was doing everything they could to make that a reality. That part isn’t really debatable in my book. The only question is how much they influenced Germany. We’ll likely never know.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why do you think there is growing support for far-right parties in Europe?
Answer: (Giorgia Meloni and Marine Le Pen. The faces of Europe’s Far Right. Photo credit: New Statesman.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What factors prevented a Civil War from occurring in Mexico and other Central and South American countries?
Answer: But a civil war did happen in Mexico. Except it wasn’t called a civil war, but the Mexican Revolution. It lasted 10 long years and a million people were killed. Mexico had one of the deadliest, bloodiest civil wars in history, lasting from 1910 - 1920. (General Tomás Urbina, General Pancho Villa and General Emiliano Zapata during the Mexican Revolution. Photo credit: Latino USA.) After the civil war, a low intensity conflict continued for decades, particularly the so-called Dirty War that took place from the 1960’s all the way until the 1980’s. Similar events occurred in other Latin American nations like Colombia during a period simply called La Violencia. (Bombing during the El Bogotazo in Bogota, Colombia in 1948. Photo credit: Colby.edu) Most Latin American nations experienced civil wars or long periods of civil unrest and violence, particularly during the Cold War when left wing guerrilla factions were common all throughout Central and South America. The leftists enjoyed moderate support from the Soviet Union, while the United States supported right wing governments/dictatorships with Operation Condor. Notable examples being Augusto Pinochet in Chile and Jorge Rafael Videla in Argentina.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do most of the people you know own guns?
Answer: Most of the people I know in the United States own guns, yes. I’m from Michigan and I have lived in Arizona, Ohio, and Minnesota. All places with a deeply ingrained gun/hunting culture. Additionally, I’m a military police veteran and previously worked for a police department. If you wanted to put together a resume for a person likely to own guns in America and to know many gun-owning people — it would be someone like me. To people from other parts of the world and even to some people who live in my very liberal Ohio suburb, this is shocking. They believe that all gun owners sit around and masturbate to the newest edition of Guns and Ammo. (Quesadillas with pumpkin salsa. A regional speciality from Yucatán that I learned to cook during my time there. Photo by author.) Maybe this applies to other people, but owning guns is not a part of my identity or anything like that. I have a couple of university degrees, careers in several disparate industries. I also love to run, hike, cook, paint, travel, and write. Most of those things interest me more than shooting. Why is it that once I tell someone I own guns that it often becomes the defining aspect of my personality? Weird. I think they’re more obsessed with guns than I am.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Which airline is the worst you've traveled on?
Answer: Sky Airlines, which operates in Peru and Chile. Terrible customer service. What should have been a short and uneventful flight from Lima to Cusco, turned into an entire ordeal at check-in. I paid extra to skip the line and I paid for a larger seat in the front of the aircraft. When I arrived at check-in they actually made me wait until every single other person in line had checked-in because they said they couldn’t find my reservation. I showed it to them on my phone, but that wasn’t good enough. I also didn’t get the seat I paid extra for. Sky is a poor excuse for an airline and I hope they go out of business. (Sky airlines A320. Screw this airline! Image credit: Wikipedia.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why does Mexico have so much more colonial architecture than does the United States of America?
Answer: This is just a guess, but the Spanish in Mexico built their buildings out of really sturdy stuff. Pretty essential in a place that has hurricanes as frequent visitors. Something cool about Mexico is that sometimes you get to stay in really, really old buildings. One time I stayed in a bed and breakfast in a building that was over 200 years old and once belonged to an author of some note. Pretty ordinary experience in many parts of Mexico. (Center of Campeche. Pretty well preserved and doesn’t look much different than it did a few hundred years ago. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the hottest club you have been to?
Answer: Clubbing in Mexico City is insane and really cool. I went to some club in Roma Norte on the recommendation of others with five or six (mostly)Australians that were hanging with me. The clubs there stay open until 4 or 5 a.m. and sometimes beyond. Absolutely packed to the gills. The best part to me though: you can find an excellent taco stand outside when you’re extremely drunk and hungry. Mexico City clubs: 10/10. I highly recommend! (Out clubbing in Roma Norte, Mexico City. I don’t really go to clubs anymore these days, but there was a time. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is your favorite show or movie?
Answer: The Knockaround Guys is unquestionably my favorite movie. There’s something about this American coming-of-age tale that I have always identified with. It also has a lot of star power. John Malkovich, Dennis Hopper, Vin Diesel, and Barry Pepper fill out the cast. It’s a movie that makes you laugh, makes you cry, and makes you think.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What was it like to grow up in the United States in the 1990s?
Answer: I grew up in the 1990’s in Detroit. Today it almost feels like Detroit was a part of a different country back then. Here’s what I remember: (Depending on who you asked, Mayor Young was the biggest bully of them all. Photo credit: Bridge Detroit.) (Downtown Detroit as seen from Belle Isle. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: You are faced with a dilemma: Live another 50 years, but in crushing poverty, or live just 25 years more, but in comfortable affluence. Which do you choose, and why?
Answer: I’ve been 39 for just over a month now. That means I’ll make it to 64 and live in affluence the entire time? I think that’s a pretty good deal. Consider that less than a century ago, even in a country like the United States, men didn’t typically live that long. Life expectancy didn’t reach age 64 for men until the mid-1940’s. So basically, I will live in affluence and also live longer than probably 99% of all human males that have ever come before me in history. Yes, I will take that deal in a heartbeat if it means never being poor again. (Life expectancy just 100 years ago was much shorter.) Source:

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Restaurant employees who vocally ask customers in the beginning or on the billing about how much would they like to tip, how would you say this isn’t an unprofessional behavior?
Answer: In Mexico tipping is common in a lot of places too. When I get the bill at a nice restaurant, the credit card reader will give three options: 10%, 15%, or 20%. The waiter will then ask, “how much would you like to tip?” You can say no tip, if you want, but as a red-blooded American this is against my nature. By default I always say 15% unless the service was above and beyond, then I’ll say 20%. I am not offended by the waiter asking, because that’s just how things work here. I adapt to wherever I am. In the US, it would be unusual for a waiter to directly ask though. Yet, it still wouldn’t stop me from giving a tip, I would just think it odd. (Pulpo at one of my favorite restaurants in Campeche, Mexico. Tipping is common in more than just the US, but in many other countries too. However, there are nuances to tipping that you only pick up after a while in other countries. Here in Mexico it is also common to tip the person who bags your groceries, which isn’t a thing in the US. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Are celebrities actually nice?
Answer: Sure. I have met a few celebrities in my time and 100% of them were pleasant around me. It’s important to remember that celebrities are just people though and sometimes they’ll have an off day or a day where they just don’t feel like dealing with fans. People tend to latch onto those stories versus the thousands of interactions they’ve had with others. The most memorable time I met a celebrity had to be Danny Glover. I was actually having kind of a bad day, because I somehow managed to miss my flight to Colombia and I had only a 5 day vacation planned, so right off the bat I missed an entire day. Naturally, since I had the day off, I decided to go to a bar in my neighborhood and get a little silly. I even brought a flask my girlfriend had given me for my birthday. I was sitting on the patio in front of my favorite neighborhood bar, sheepishly taking sips out of my flask and lamenting my day of missed vacation when I noticed a gray SUV pull up to the curb. Before I knew it, people were surrounding the car and taking photos. Now, I have always loved the Lethal Weapon movies in particular and once I noticed that the person in the car was Danny Glover I was shocked, but I still wasn’t going to get up to try to squeeze through all of the people taking photos. But, Danny didn’t really give me a choice. After a few minutes he spotted me sitting on the patio alone, half way crying into my drink and said “Hey! You! Come here, I want to talk to you!” Me: “me?” Danny: “yeah, you. I want to talk to you for a second.” (I took the most awkward selfie, because I was pretty nervous. Photo by author.) Let’s just say we actually ended up speaking for nearly half an hour on a number of topics, some of them political which I won’t delve into here. The important thing was that he left me with the impression of being a very well-grounded and normal guy. It’s weird to meet one of your childhood heroes and walk away from it without a bad taste in your mouth. So yes, sometimes it’s okay to meet your heroes.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you think that Michelin star restaurants are overpriced?
Answer: It’s all relative, but no. Typically you can get some pretty good stuff for a relatively low price at the right time. A few years ago I was in London and wanted to grab lunch at Alain Ducasse at the Dorchester (three Michelin Stars). It was, I believe, something like £230 for the prix fixe menu for two for lunch. That’s the cost of just a few outings at Applebee’s for us ‘Mericans, but the experience is much more of a once-in-a-lifetime thing. At a three star restaurant you can expect a stunningly beautiful dining room, top notch service, and obviously, excellently prepared dishes. At Alain Ducasse there were technically only three courses, but a few more tastings were brought out as compliments of the chef. They made sure that we left more than completely full. (Three star Michelin restaurants are as much about the experience and presentation as they are about the quality and food. Photo by author.) In addition to high-priced options like Alain Ducasse, there are quite a few humble establishments like Taquería El Califa de León here in Mexico, that won’t even come close to breaking the bank. (Tacos from El Califa are some of the best of Mexico City, but will only set you back a few bucks. Photo credit: Google Reviews.) The days of all Michelin star restaurants being stuffy and expensive French joints are over, but you can still find those places too if you look for them.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What was your first experience after returning home from a war zone?
Answer: I went straight to Pizza Papalis in downtown Detroit for deep dish pizza. This was worth living for! (Deep dish pizza from Pizza Papalis in Detroit. Italians of Quora, avert your eyes! Photo credit: Click on Detroit.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you split the bill when you go on a date? Why?
Answer: Sometimes. This mostly happens when I am in the US or Europe, where often times women will volunteer to split half the bill with me.
