If they do, I typically don’t refuse, because arguing just makes things awkward. In Latin America this is never a concern: men are expected to pay for dates the great majority of the time. However, the important thing is that no matter where I am going on a date, I am always prepared to pay for the entire date/meal. (Studying the menu carefully at Restaurante Les Présidents in São Paulo, Brazil. If for some reason your credit card is declined here, they employ giant bouncers that will crush your bones! Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How long did it take for you to readjust to civilian life or decompress after returning from combat?
Answer: Let’s start with the fact that I am not really a “combat” veteran, although I did serve in Iraq. I am not trying to steal valor from my Marine, Army, and Navy comrades (Coast Guard, where you at?). Yes, the time I spent in Iraq came with its own kinds of unique stress and circumstances. Yes, I was in danger at times, but not the same level of danger many other less fortunate troops were exposed to. (The commute to work is much more fun in a humvee. Photo by author.) When I got back home and was released from active duty I had very little time to sit around and think about things. A month later I was back in college to finish the last two classes for my bachelor's degree. While I was deployed I’d already sent in my application package to the University of Michigan for graduate school. A couple of months after I returned home I found out that I’d been accepted. Once I finished my bachelor’s degree I had only another couple of weeks off until graduate school started. I spent it camping and hiking in northern Michigan. (Sleeping Bear Dunes, where I spent part of my summer camping and hiking after deployment. Photo by author.) All of my friends, my girlfriend, and family were there for me as they had been throughout my entire deployment. It essentially felt like I’d never left. Those two years that I spent in graduate school immediately after deployment were some of the best of my life because I had a lot of money, I had few responsibilities, and no job. My only job was to get my graduate studies done and find a job for after graduation. I didn’t hit any difficulty until I was nearly finished with my degree and absolutely no job offers were rolling in. That’s when I started to panic and question everything. I started to drink heavily and worry if everything I’d done was a mistake. Luckily, just a few weeks before graduation I finally got an interview for a position with the federal government and a job offer. I’d be moving to Phoenix, Arizona and starting a new job with decent pay and benefits. Phew! I spent the next eight whole years in a career that was mostly tolerable, but had a lots of ups and downs. I still feel lucky about my time in the military and my time after. Things could have turned out much worse. I’m not religious or anything, but maybe someone, somewhere was looking out for me.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What was a really racist situation you have been in, and what did you do about it?
Answer: I must have been about 14 or 15 when this happened. I was leaving tae kwon do classes in Dearborn, Michigan, and waiting for the bus to take me back to Detroit. The bus stop was in front of an optometry shop on Michigan Avenue. Just a few feet away from the bus stop (probably illegally parked too close to the stop actually), was a new looking Land Rover. It was a nice car, but I didn’t think too much of it. (Dearborn police headquarters. Funnily enough, I ended up going to graduate school with the future chief of police of the department some years later. Photo credit: City of Dearborn.) After a few minutes of standing and waiting for the bus, a rather rotund white woman came out from the optometry shop and lit a cigarette. She looked directly at me for a moment, then when she finished her cigarette, she flicked it onto the sidewalk. She then went back into the optometry shop. A few minutes pass and I am still waiting for the bus (our transportation system in Metro Detroit sucks). The same woman comes out and then gets into the Land Rover and pulls it just a few feet forward, so that it is clearly more visible from the front window of the optometry shop. She then went back into the shop. A few more minutes pass and this is when the Dearborn police arrive. They pull up in front of me in their squad car and ask me what I’m doing just hanging around there. Of course, even as a young teenager I think this is a stupid question. I slowly move my gaze upwards to the sign that says “bus stop” and then I point with my finger. “I’m waiting for the bus.” Luckily, I wasn’t dealing with cops that were idiots and they just said “ok” and left, deciding that they had better things to do. I found it interesting that they found the time to even respond to a 9–1–1 call about a Black kid standing at a bus stop close to a luxury vehicle though. To this day I wonder what she could have said to get the police to come out on the call. I did nothing whatsoever to indicate I was going to steal her car besides just standing there. I also felt a little sad for a woman that lived in such fear for her material possessions.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do you live a simple lifestyle?
Answer: This depends on who you ask. On one hand I get to spend a large amount of my life traveling, which is a privilege to be sure. On the other hand, I own few physical possessions, particularly in comparison to others my age from my country. I own only a small apartment, no car, no TV. For the majority of the year I am happy living out of two bags that carry both cold weather and warm weather clothing. I’m usually ready to travel just about anywhere at a moment’s notice from anywhere else in the world. Having few physical possessions is incredibly liberating. Here’s the catch: living a minimalist lifestyle is, more often than not, something that very few people can actually afford. It takes money to have less. Most people, for example, couldn’t live in the US without a car. I am easily able to do so for the few months I spend there every year.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What part of life gives you the most trouble?
Answer: Relationships, bar none. This applies equally to my romantic relationships and friendships. I think it is a result of the rugged independence I was imbued with from the time I was a young child. I have rarely needed anyone as an adult and I think that, perhaps, an essential part of any relationship is a sense of need. A sense that, if I lose this person my life will be worse without them. I have rarely felt that way towards anyone. The few times that I did, it completely blew up in my face. Even now I am feeling rather guilty because I have gone nearly two weeks without speaking to my best friend, for no particular reason except that I felt slighted in a conversation we had a couple of weeks ago. I didn’t say anything. I simply stopped sending messages or calling. When I finally got a message asking what was up, I said that I would appreciate not being bothered for a while. Sure, on my part it is likely that I have an aversion to being vulnerable and to confrontation. This is something that I continue to work on to this day. Despite everything I have been through in the realm of relationships, I am actually still really optimistic. I don’t want to grow old completely alone. I think that there’s still a chance I can find that person out there that will accept my quirkiness and desire to still spend time alone. Fingers crossed. (Don’t push me ‘cause I’m close to the edge. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How difficult is it to strangle someone from behind using tools or bare hands?
Answer: I don’t know about tools, so I will tell you how to do it with your bare hands. You want to get the person in a blood choke. This is the most effective technique you can use in my opinion and I have used it in grappling/martial arts several times. This means getting one arm looped around the neck while the other arm holds it in place and grasps the head. Now the person can writhe around a lot and try to hit you. This is why I always recommend taking the person to ground if possible and using your body weight to lay on top of them. Of course, the odds of doing this successfully on a person much taller and larger than you are low. However, if you are the same weight or larger than your opponent, the odds of them getting out of the hold become much lower. Something I was always taught is that you want to have the fold of your elbow line up with their chin if you don’t want to kill the person. This prevents you from inadvertently crushing their windpipe. (This soldier demonstrates perfect technique with a blood choke. Photo credit: US Army.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why do soldiers tend to keep their personal lives private while deployed? Is there a specific reason for this?
Answer: I’m not sure who told you this but they are pulling your chain! Often times when you’re deployed, depending on your job, you can be stuck with the same person all day or night. In Baghdad, when we were posted to an overwatch position for security, you’d sit in an observation post for 12+ hours with the same guy. Sometimes you’re literally locked inside a small space with machine guns and a radio. (.50 caliber machine gun overwatch position. Camp Sather, Baghdad. Photo by author.) As our instructors said to us during technical training: you can be in an observation post (OP) with your worst enemy. By the end of your shift you’ll be best friends. We trade stories about every single aspect of our lives, some with great embellishment, I am sure. It’s actually great when you’re in an OP with a great story teller, because it really helps to pass the time. They’ll tell you about the time they got into a gunfight on another deployment, about the first girl they “scored” with. The one time they participated in an orgy in Las Vegas, or a bar fight they got into on leave in Topeka, Kansas. Not only will you learn the name of his girlfriend, but that she has a tattoo that you can see only when she is completely naked. The other issue though, is that wives talk to each other and then wives talk to their husbands who are deployed. This means that if your spouse is back home misbehaving, it’s only a matter of time before that news makes it to her husband who is deployed. This makes it impossible to keep some aspects of your life private. Trigger warning: (this is a story about suicide). First, I want to be clear that this is not something that I witnessed, but something one of our instructors told us about during training. When one of my instructors was deployed to Saudi Arabia, it soon became news that one of the men on his team had an unfaithful wife back home who was cheating on him with several men. Other wives living on base had seen several men visiting his home and told their husbands who were deployed with him. In true military fashion, they made fun of him relentlessly. Of course, he was several thousand miles from home with nothing he could do about it. One night the airman was posted in an armored booth alone at an entry control point. When my instructor went around to do a post check they found they he’d taken his pistol and killed himself. Even more unfortunate, the entry control point was vital to the security mission. After a short investigation by Office of Special Investigations (Air Force version of the FBI) and some cleaning, the post had to be re-opened mere hours later. He spoke about how much of a mind-fuck it was to have to work in the same booth where one of his colleagues had killed himself only a few hours prior. The moral of the story was this: be careful about razzing someone when they’re going through difficulties. You never know how truly upset they are and things can quickly turn homicidal or suicidal, since we’re always armed.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is your opinion on modern Greece and its people? Did your experience visiting there or reading about it differ from your initial expectations?
Answer: I’ve been to Greece only once in 2011 and it was only my second time in Europe. I had only been to Italy in Europe before, so it was my only basis for comparison. I thought Rome and Athens would be very similar in that they are both modern cities dotted with ancient architecture and artifacts. While this is true, Athens is a bit rougher around the edges. This not a criticism so much as it is an observation. However, in regard to the ancient architecture there is so much to take in. It seemed that in downtown Athens everywhere you go there is something to see. (Lively streets of Athens. Photo by author.) The metro in Athens is the cleanest I have seen anywhere. Some of the metro stops are practically museums since they display the ancient artifacts found when they tunneled to build the metro. If you go to Greece in the summer it’s hot. I mean really hot! It reminded me of some of the Middle Eastern countries I have been to. In the week I spent there I don’t think the temperature ever dropped below 100F/37C during the daytime. (Some students giving out free hugs in Athens. Photo by author.) The people were friendly and seemed very welcoming to tourists just about everywhere I went. The only exception was one taxi driver. First he stopped to buy cigarettes and kept the meter running. Then when we arrived at our hotel, he quickly turned off the meter which clearly displayed €12. He then demanded €15. I paid it since I didn’t want any trouble, but I’ll always remember that guy. Asshole! Overall, my impression of Greece was very positive and I think I’ll be returning soon, I really want some Greek food in Greece again. (The Greek countryside is rugged, but very beautiful. This is the scenery from above the ruins at Delphi. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How did your life change after moving abroad?
Answer: Once you remove all of the people you know from the equation, the only constant is you. I could tell you that I learned self-reliance and mental toughness, but growing up in Detroit and the military had already given me those characteristics. Instead, what I learned was how to truly be alone. I have a twin, so even in the womb I was never alone. My entire childhood I had a “shadow.” Nor did I ever really get to be alone during college or the Air Force. Moving abroad in my mid-thirties meant I got to spend a lot of time alone for the first time. I had only my own thoughts and a few possessions to keep me company. Books and writing became my friends, especially when traveling alone in other countries. I spent many, many hours waiting around in bus stations, airports, and train stations. Many hours more on buses, planes and trains. That leaves a lot of time for introspection. Your life changes because you learn certain truths about yourself, not all of them good and comforting. If you’re lucky, the things you learn can be the impetus for change. (Waiting for the train in Cusco, Peru. Some journeys you need to take alone. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What surprises you about people?
Answer: Just how irrational and impulsive we can all be. About a month ago I had my friend come visit me in Rio de Janeiro from Bogota. He decided to stay for a week. The weather was rather pleasant and for the most part, we had a good time. However, he told me before he left “Dennis, I really don’t like this place. I can’t ever imagine myself coming back here ever again! I’m very disappointed!” So, imagine how surprised I was to receive a message from him a couple of days ago saying that he was returning to Rio de Janeiro for a week. It turns out that one evening he met a nice girl and he decided that he wanted to go back to visit her. Now just a few days later he has told me that he is thinking of moving to Rio de Janeiro. Mind you, my friend isn’t an idiot or a typically impulsive person. In fact, he is a highly educated doctor (anesthesiologist) that has continuously demonstrated the kind of intelligence and discipline to get where he is in life and his career. For this, I have always looked up to him and been impressed by his intellect and resolve. Yet, if even people like him can fall prey to impulsive behavior, what hope do the rest of us have?

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: If you could talk to somebody who has died, who would it be and what would you say?
Answer: It was March 2020 and the beginning of the health crisis thay would affect all of our lives. I was in Medellin, Colombia, at the start of what was supposed to be a trip that would last for the next six months or so. I had actually received some really good news that morning about some pending business that had finally been resolved in my favor. It also happened to be my aunt’s birthday, so I gave her a call. She was at my mother’s house in Detroit. I was wishing my aunt a happy birthday when I heard my mother’s voice in the background, asking me what I planned to do. It seemed that COVID was getting serious and she wanted to know if I was going to come back to the United States. I told my aunt to tell her that yes, I would be returning to the US soon. Particularly since I’d been notified that my travel insurance would not cover me in the event that I contracted COVID. Little did I know that hearing my mother’s voice in the background of my call with my aunt would be the last time I would ever hear her voice. The very same day I booked a flight back home to Cleveland. It was a chaotic experience on all ends. The airport in Medellin was packed with people trying to get out of Colombia. When I landed in Fort Lauderdale for my connecting flight, it was the same. Thousands of people waiting to be processed through customs to get into the country. By the time I landed in Cleveland I was exhausted and I went home and uncorked a bottle of scotch, not thinking much about anything else. I spent the next few days listless. Then I received a call from my sister telling me that my mother was in the hospital and seriously ill. She ended up spending more than a month in the hospital sick with COVID. She wasn’t intubated at first, so I could have called her to speak with her, but for whatever reason, I didn’t. I sent her a few messages and then some flowers. By the time I decided I wanted to speak with her it was too late. Her conditioned has worsened and she was on a respirator. She held on for many weeks. I celebrated my 35th birthday while she was in the hospital and while we were all under COVID restrictions. My mother died at around 3 a.m. the day after my birthday. I like to think that she held on so that I wouldn’t have to experience the horror of having her die on my birthday. If I could speak to her I would simply tell her that I love her and forgive her for everything that happened when I was younger. That, despite everything, she is still and will always be my personal hero.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why should I not complain in life?
Answer: Mind you, this isn’t true 100% of the time, but usually we shouldn’t complain because almost everyone that you might complain to has something they could complain about too. These last few years it’s incredibly rare to know someone who hasn’t suffered some kind of personal tragedy or endured some period of hardship. People with a sick parent or spouse, the loss of a close loved one, the ending of a marriage, or long term relationship. Personal financial or health difficulties. When we complain it’s often times because we have failed to take stock of all the things in our life that have gone right. Express gratitude for the things you have right now, even the small things. Especially if you woke up with a roof over your head, food to eat, and in relatively good health (which is actually no minor thing).

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: If you have a chance to have a drink with any historical figure, who would you choose and what would you talk about?
Answer: I had to think about this, my first instinct was to say Churchill or Eisenhower. However, when I thought about it, I’d have to go with Marcus Aurelius. He’d probably prefer to have wine, but if he was open to it, I’d share a bottle of a single malt scotch with him. I’d ask him about being a good leader, his favorite foods, and why his son, Commodus, is such a dick.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do I deal with rejection from women?
Answer: In short, gracefully. Change your perspective a bit; rejection has more to teach you than acceptance. Maybe she will tell you why you don’t match up, or maybe she won’t. Life means learning to process all of our emotions and not just the pleasant ones. I also bet that if you look hard enough at yourself, you can find something to work on that will improve your odds in the dating game. Become a better conversationalist, hit the gym, work on your posture, learn how to tell a joke, and how to put the people around you at ease. Begin a hobby that truly interests you so that you have something to talk about other than school or work. Most of us can also stand to be better read. Be a man for all seasons. Busy yourself with those things and before you know it, rejection will play a smaller part in your life. Most importantly, learn when to fold ‘em and move on. Life’s too short to go around wanting those that don’t want you.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do you make sure you can live an action-packed life at all times?
Answer: You don’t and even if you could, you wouldn’t want to. Take for example, the movie Top Gun, with Tom Cruise who plays the role of our hero pilot, Pete Mitchell. In the span of a 110 minute movie we get to see our hero tango with evil commies over the Indian Ocean in a fighter jet, ride motorcycles, play volleyball with the bros on a picturesque beach, make love to a beautiful woman, get into an aircraft accident where he loses his friend, and finally (in a very unlikely scenario) called from training to take a mission of utmost importance to go fight the evil commies again. He gets into a dogfight where he successfully blows up several enemy aircraft with missiles. All within a 110 minute movie. (Pete Mitchell can only exist in a fantasy world. There is no real life equivalent of him and there never will be. Image source: Reddit.) Supposing the events depicted in Top Gun were actually possible for one pilot to experience in a short amount of time. There’s tons the movie doesn’t show you! The movie doesn’t show you that Pete Mitchell has to attend four boring years of college to be eligible to be a pilot. During that time he is in Navy ROTC, where he must do boring things like shine shoes and boots, perfectly iron his uniform, and take many exams and memorize mundane facts about Naval history. He then has to attend undergraduate pilot training after graduating college, where he will then spend an enormous amount of classroom time learning about the technical aspects of flying an aircraft, navigation, and radio communication, all before he ever handles the controls of an aircraft. After a couple of years of training and being certified as a pilot, Mitchell will then be sent to the fleet where much of his time will be attending briefings and waiting around for something, anything to happen. When actually flying, probably 90% or more of his flights will be completely uneventful. After Mitchell actually does get to experience action a few times, he ends up extremely traumatized due to the death of his friend and RIO, Goose. He has screaming fits of PTSD which sometimes wake him up at night. And oh, he still has an unresolved case of the clap he picked up on a port call in Hong Kong one time. He carelessly gives it to his instructor-girlfriend, Charlie, who later unceremoniously dumps him. He’s also been ticketed by the MA’s for not wearing a helmet while riding a motorcycle on a Navy installation. Eventually he has his motorcycle impounded after repeated offenses. You get the point. Life is not a movie or an adventure novel. No matter how bold or daring you might be in life, much of your life will be spent doing mundane and uninteresting things, just for the 10% or (likely) less of the time you actually get to do things that excite you. Then some of the things that excite you have a not-so-insignificant chance of terrifying you. By all means, lead an adventurous life, I approve of it. However, there is no way to lead a life that is action-packed at all times in reality. That’s just a fantasy best left to Hollywood.

Answer: (Somewhere in the Andes mountains in South America. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How are you doing today? I hope you are doing great out there.
Answer: Great! I am in Playa del Carmen, Mexico. I had an amazing dinner with a beautiful Italian woman who was gracious enough to laugh at my jokes. I was also happy that she understand my Spanish, since she only spoke Spanish and Italian. Even though I’m pretty much fluent in Spanish, my pronunciation can be rough and not always understood. It was funny because she understood everything I said during our hour long date. Our Mexican waiter…not so much. At the end of our date I asked her if she would see me again. She said yes, but I am not so sure. All I can do is cross my fingers. If you see this, pray for me! 🥹 (It’s summer and the rainy season in Playa. Still…it’s one of my favorite places on earth. I’m thinking of spending the entire summer here this year, instead of going back to the States as usual. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: If you could do it all over again, would you serve in the military knowing what you know now?
Answer: Not only would I say “hell yes”, I would have enlisted sooner and served for longer. When I was very young I was afraid of not going to college, because my parent put an enormous amount of pressure on me to get a good education, since I was the first generation of my family that really had the opportunity to go right out of high school. For the most part, a university education was a mistake. I didn’t really need it for today’s job market. Being sharp between the ears is more than enough to sustain you, much more so than a piece of paper. This has proven to be true since I have used the knowledge from my degrees almost never in my professional life. Nor were my degrees a prerequisite for any job I held. The military, on the other hand, offers some of the most practical and valuable life skills you can hope to obtain. Most importantly, the military will teach you not to give up and give you a mental toughness that most civilians will never possess. For most of us, the opportunity to serve in the military was a privilege and one that continues to heap rewards onto me for years after I left service. (Doing army training, but as an airman. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Could you bring the elite down by killing 99.99% of their country?
Answer: You don’t need to kill anywhere near that many people. Some people make the argument that the UK became a more egalitarian society after the World Wars, specifically because those wars wiped out a large part of the aristocracy. This was because in those days aristocratic men made up a large part of the officer corps of the British military. (Churchill during WWI. Photo credit: Wikipedia.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Would bodybuilders make good soldiers in the army?
Answer: Like many things in life, the answer depends. But particularly since your question included the word “good” and not the best soldiers, I can say that in some cases, yes, bodybuilders can make good soldiers. This is even more possible on the modern battlefield in militaries like the United States where modern fighting is often times more akin to what would have been mechanized infantry in WWII. In other words, you’re more likely to spend a good deal of your time doing mounted patrols. Every military unit has at least few guys (and even gals) that are into bodybuilding. There were a couple of bodybuilders in my unit. One was a man in his early 30’s at the time, and one of our first sergeants, a woman, who was nearly 40 years old. Both were about 6ft tall and well over 200lbs. The thing is, you actually can be rather big and still have good endurance, if you train for it. Of course, we’re also not talking about professional bodybuilders, but amateurs, who, although they will be larger than average, won’t be beating Ronnie Coleman at Mr. Olympia. Now, a lot of people here on Quora will tell you that special operations personnel tend to be thin and wiry. This may be true during their initial ascension training, but, in-country, many SOF soldiers would come to our gym, since naturally, the Air Force had the best gym. At least a few of them were definitely on the bigger side of normal and enjoyed weight lifting. That a few were on PED’s, was obvious, in my opinion. These were the guys mostly going out on snatch and grab missions at night in Baghdad while mounted on humvees or other vehicles. Hardly a job that required the endurance of a marathon runner. (Arnold in his prime. He would likely at least make a good soldier in today’s US Army. Photo credit: Wikipedia.) Edit: just as a case in point, Taylor Cavanaugh, a rather infamous Navy SEAL, was kicked out of the teams specifically because of his PED use. Later on he became a member of the French Foreign Legion. (Taylor Cavanaugh, former SEAL and Legionnaire. Photo credit: Taylorcavanaugh.com.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why do some rich people claim to be "miserable" despite having better lives than literally 99% of the population?
Answer: Rich people can be just as miserable or in some cases, more miserable than your average person. Now, let’s not completely buy into the myth that money can’t buy happiness on some level. If you’re a subsistence farmer in Afghanistan and suddenly find your way into enough money to move to a western nation, to live in a comfortable home with a refrigerator stuffed with all of your favorite Afghani snacks and an iPhone with all of your favorite Afghani songs — you will almost certainly be happier than you were before. However, after all of your basic needs are met, the relationship between money and happiness is less clear. (Christina with her father, Aristotle. Photo credit: El Mundo newspaper.) Take for example, Christina Onassis. Christina was the only daughter of Greek shipping magnate Aristotle Onassis. Within a short period of time, Christina had both of her parents and her older brother die, leaving her with a fortune worth hundreds of millions of dollars at only age 24. So, by the time she inherited her personal fortune, she had already suffered through some incredibly difficult circumstances. Additionally, she went on to develop a prescription drug problem, suffered from constant issues with her weight, and bouts of depression. Furthermore, her love life was a complete mess and she married (and divorced) a total of four times all before the age of 37. By the time she was 37, the effects of her chaotic and miserable life had taken its toll on her and she died of a heart attack. Wealth can buy you a very nice chateau, yachts, and ski vacations in St. Moritz. What it can’t guarantee you is that you will lead a life free or misery, or that you will have good health, or even that you will live a long life.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How good or bad is food in the military?
Answer: US Air Force perspective: very good! Now of course, the military chow walls won’t be winning any Michelin stars or anything like that, but your average airman eats very well pretty much every day of the week. Even our meal rations are very good. (The excellent chili mac MRE. You can always trade this bad boy for anything else if you happen to get it. Of course, in the field you’re not allowed to dig through the box and choose your MRE, this impolite practice is called “rat-fucking” and strictly prohibited.) Additionally, our bases always have a few restaurants, mostly chain stuff like Burger King or Popeye’s. However, there was one meal I had while I deployed that I will always remember. It was at a restaurant run by a local Iraqi man on the Victory Base Complex (VBC), and served some local Iraqi fare. What was interesting is that the restaurant didn’t have a hook-up to the power grid, so was without electricity for the majority of the day. Whenever customers would drop by he had to turn on an expensive diesel generator to power the restaurant. I can only assume he kept all of the food on ice or something. When you’ve been deployed, after a while you stop asking these kinds of questions and just relish the opportunity to eat something different. Both my wingman and I ordered the lamb, rice, fries, and I think there was a salad involved too. After waiting for what seemed like an eternity, the owner reappeared from the kitchen with our food. After months of eating pretty standard American fare from the chow hall, how delighted were we to bite into the juiciest, tastiest, most succulent lamb chops that we’d ever had! All in the middle of a war zone from a restaurant without a steady source of electricity. We both downed our plates rather quickly and then ordered seconds. I don’t know what happened to the man who ran this restaurant after coalition forces withdrew from Iraq, but I’d like to think he is still out there serving up the best lamb chops in the world. Thank you, sir! (My wingman and me waiting for our food at the restaurant. Can you tell I was hungry? Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Have you ever had a good time in an American town or city that most folks wouldn't think of visiting? Where was it, and what did you do?
Answer: Yes! One of my favorite towns to visit whenever I am in Arizona is Jerome, Arizona. It’s half way between Phoenix and Sedona, Arizona, so many people probably pass it on the highway without thinking of stopping. (Jerome, Arizona, in winter. Photo by author.) Until the 1980’s it was the site of a copper mine, but when the copper in the area was depleted, industry left and so did nearly all of its residents. Today it continues to survive on a modest amount of tourism. (One of the few occupied homes left in Jerome. Photo by author.) The town now has a few bars, restaurants, a winery, a really neat hotel, and some boutique bed and breakfast spots. There is also a museum dedicated to the history of the town. It’s a great place to stop if you have ever wanted to stay in a uniquely Southwestern US town, with surprisingly good restaurants, bars, and shops. (Playing pool at a bar in Jerome. Photo by author.) (One of the uniquely cool restaurants of Jerome. Photo by author.) If you are ever in the area I recommend Jerome as a place to stop, if only for a nice lunch on the way to Sedona, but if you wanted to stay the night, I wouldn’t blame you.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is it possible to receive health benefits from only doing one type of exercise, such as walking?
Answer: Walking is one of the healthiest forms of exercise one can do, in my opinion. Especially if you are unable to do a more difficult exercise such as weight lifting or running. When I decided that I needed to lose weight a few years ago, I started with a modest goal of simply walking 10,000 steps a day. From there, and whenever I had time I would see if I could double or triple that amount. It took me a few years, but eventually I lost enough weight thay I felt comfortable beginning to run again. I’ve never really looked back. If you know you need more exercise in your life, but don’t know where to start, going for a walk every day is a good place to make that start. (Most days I walk at least 10,000 steps. Of course, some days I greatly exceed that number.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: As a soldier in an army, what are your thoughts on berets?
Answer: Not a soldier, but an airman. In the U.S. Air Force, only a handful of career fields are authorized the wear of a beret when in uniform. All of those career fields are combat-oriented career fields, so they are a source of pride and distinction. For security forces airmen like me, you aren’t allowed to wear your beret until the day of graduation, at which point it is a great relief to never have to wear the french fry cap again (flight cap). In the field, we switch to wearing a patrol cap just like everyone else. The same is true for deployed locations where we aren’t allowed to wear berets, even when on base. Something unique about security forces, is that we are authorized to keep our beret on when indoors, if we are armed and on duty. This is just another way of letting the general public on base know that we are on duty and they can come to us if they have a problem. (Okay, not actually on duty here, but I was in my own house and about to leave for a ceremony. Most SF airmen are proud of having earned the right to wear a beret. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Would the military actually shoot at people trying to storm Area 51 or would they try to arrest them?
Answer: The military does not have a license to kill. People trespassing on federal installations are apprehended as long as they are not using force. Although we do have signs on our installations stating that deadly force is authorized, what it really means is that deadly force is authorized if you yourself are armed and threatening or attempting to cause harm at the level of grievous bodily harm or above. We aren’t going to open up on you with fully automatic gunfire if you’re caught jumping a fence. With national security assets there are special circumstances, but these are rare. If you are attempting to steal an aircraft or nuclear weapon, all bets are off. We actually deal with trespassers pretty regularly on military installations. If they aren’t in the military we aren’t allowed to “arrest” them. Instead they are held in detention until they can be handed over to the appropriate civilian authority, usually the US Marshals or local police. (USAF Security Forces. Photo credit: US Air Force.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Can you recommend a hidden gem place in Europe that you have visited and why is it your favorite?
Answer: Define hidden gem? I will say this. It’s not the most popular destination in Europe, but one of the best weekends I have had in Europe was just a quiet weekend in Dover, England. (The first time I tried fish and chips in the UK was in Dover. Photo by author.) It was surprisingly sunny every day, the townsfolk friendly. Nice pubs and a few good restaurants. Every day I woke up to the sound of the sea and I was relaxed and well-rested. Of course, there are the white cliffs that really enhance the scenery. What more could anyone ask for? (Sunset in Dover. Highly recommended. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are the best amazing tourist places with unique attractions in Mexico? Why are they the best tourist places?
Answer: I’m partial to the places that are a little off the beaten path, mostly in Yucatán region. Here are some of my favorites: Mucuyche. Small pueblo in Yucatán region. There’s a hacienda here that used to belong to the doomed Emperor Maximilian I of Mexico. Amazing, authentic food nearby, some of the best cenotes (underground rivers) in all of the Yucatán. This is an experience that should not be missed. (Hacienda at Mucuyche, photo by author.) Mérida. The capital of Yucatán state. It gets some tourism, but lives in the shadow of the more popular cities in the region like Cancun. Visit here to experience life in a culturally rich part of Mexico with food that is unique to the region. Be sure to visit the cathedral in the historic center. Get some cochinita pibil at a market and hangout at a cantina. (The incredibly popular La Negrita cantina. Get here early. Photo by author.) Campeche (City). Just one of my absolute favorite places in Mexico. I used to go here a lot when I just needed some peace and quiet and to eat good seafood. Some really nice boutique hotels near the city center. The historic center is very well preserved. (Historic center of Campeche. Photo by author.) (One of the hotels I used to frequent in Campeche. Photo by author.) Valladolid. A small town surrounded by jungle in Yucatán region. This town is famous for its unique smoked sausage. That alone is a reason to visit. Some nice hotels and a few historical buildings, but mostly a quiet and relaxing to visit. (City center of Valladolid. Photo by author.) Puerto Escondido. Popular beach town on the Pacific coast with surfers and some European tourists. Visit here if you like or want to learn to surf especially, but also if you want to go to a beach town that is still quite rustic and cheaper than most other beach towns in Mexico. Also, there are thousands of dolphins in the bay, they don’t mind if you swim with them. (Sunset in PE. Photo by author.) Izamal: Another small town in Yucatán that is almost entirely yellow. A very photogenic place. Visit the monastery and eat at the market. It’s not too far from Chichen Itza and worth a detour. (The monastery in Izamal. Photo by author.) Telchac Puerto: A sleepy town on the Gulf of Mexico with some of the best seafood. I would travel here many weekends just to eat the fish. You can also find a property directly on the beach for the weekend if you are so inclined. The prices are always reasonable. (Center of Telchac Puerto. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do I become mentally strong?
Answer: When I was young, probably 16 or 17, I received the best advice I have ever gotten in my life. I was speaking to my mother about something I either didn’t want to do or was afraid to do. Now my mother and I had not always been close and we spent many years apart, but at that moment, she made up for all the years of her absentee parenting. My mother gave me this look and said “son, the things you are afraid of are the things you need to do.” Since then I have always taken that advice to heart. At every stage of my life, no matter how unbearable that fear might be, I learned to embrace it and move in the direction of that fear. This has been true for both big and small things in my life. Like when I went to college, asked out my first girlfriend, when I decided to volunteer to deploy to Iraq. When I (quite foolishly to many observers) gave up a good paying career, packed my things in a single bag and moved to Mexico City. Embracing your fears will not only make you a stronger, confident, more durable person; it will set you free from the type of rumination that comes with regret. Chance will favor the bold. (When I was already in my 30’s, I decided to learn to rock climb. Why? As you may have guessed, I’m very afraid of heights. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why does everyone love rare/medium rare meat so much?
Answer: Of course this can never be anything but an opinion subject to endless to debate, but it’s the best way to eat your steak. Anything else is simply a waste of good meat. Imagine buying a good cut of ribeye and cooking it until it’s dry in the middle. I call that a waste of money. (A steak I prepared just the way I like it. Potatoes are optional. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Has racism ever worked out in someone’s favor?
Answer: Yes. I can think of a couple of ways in which it has worked out in my favor: (Out and about in Bogotá. I felt much less likely to be a victim of crime there than my friends. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: You are helicoptered into a remote location. The pilot dies, the radio doesn't work, and you have never flown anything. Would you attempt to fly the helicopter?
Answer: Absolutely not. I actually don’t even like flying on helicopters, despite my military service. I made a promise to myself I’d never even get on a helicopter again after leaving the Air Force. I really don’t enjoy it. So the miracle is how someone convinced me to get on a helicopter again in the first place. Even someone like an experienced fixed wing pilot would likely not be able to pilot a helicopter if they have never done so before. For someone who has no clue about helicopters it would be impossible. Stay close to the helicopter and wait for rescue. (Helicopter at the top of Urca, Rio de Janeiro. I climbed instead of taking a helicopter, because there’s no way you’d get me on that thing willingly. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why do Americans love cheese singles so much?
Answer: I can only speak for myself, but I am not sure this is even true. I like the good stuff for burgers and sandwiches especially. Easily available from my local Aldi. (Cheddar from Aldi. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Are Americans shocked when they first go to Europe?
Answer: I wouldn’t use the word shocked. More like impressed. I am from a rust belt city, Detroit, and my first trip to Europe was in 2011 to Rome for a week. At this point I had never been to any really big cities, not even New York. It was nice to be able to take the metro or bus everywhere in the city. Everything was a little expensive for me as a graduate student, but I don’t remember having any bad meals. What’s interesting is that I had two really memorable meals that I’ll never forget. The first was carbonara at our hotel, which was unlike any Italian food I had eaten in the US. The food seemed very simple, but the ingredients and flavor top notch. I also remember tipping our waiter, Muhammad, who seemed shocked (I think it was only something like €10 on a €50 meal, which is the bare minimum in the US.) Every night after that he was happily waiting for my girlfriend and me to return to the hotel to usher us into the restaurant. The second meal I had that I absolutely loved was actually Chinese food at a simple restaurant in the middle of Rome. I had no idea “Chinese food” is quite different in every country and takes on the tastes of the local culture. I think the fried rice is still some of the best I have ever had in my life. The other part is that so much beauty and history is in one place. People from Italy go about their day, live, work and dine, all in the shadow of places like the Colosseum or the Roman Forum. I can’t imagine being around so much ancient history every day and regarding it as just part of the scenery. Again, it’s impressive. (Monument to Vittorio Emanuele II, my tour guide said that many locals hate this monument, but to me as an American, I thought it was rather impressive. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Can you describe a typical day in basic training for an airman in the US Air Force? How long does it usually last and what are some activities that take place during this time?
Answer: Okay, it’s been nearly twenty years for me, but I am pretty sure not too much has changed. So here’s what a typical day might look like: 0445: rise and shine, get your physical training gear on get ready to train. 0500: morning PT formation. PT will either be calisthenics or running for the first part of basic training. During the latter weeks you’ll do both. 0600: return to the dorm for the triple S (shit, shower, and shave.) 0700: breakfast. This will last only 15 minutes individually, the rest of the time you will study your airman’s manual, do laundry, or shine boots. 0800: classroom instruction or medical/dental appointments. This will last all the way to noon. 1200: Lunch 1300: more classroom instruction. At this point you’re going to already start to feel sleepy, but stay awake! Otherwise you have to maintain the seated position without your chair if caught dozing off. 1700: you’ll be released back to your primary training instructor. Dinner time. 1800: learning military drill and marching and/or cleaning the dorm. 2100: bed time. At some period during the night you may also have guard duty for an hour. You’ll be violently shaken awake for your shift. Of course, all of this can vary and some days will last much longer. You shouldn’t ever actually count on getting anywhere near eight of hours of sleep, in reality. Basically, every moment of your day will be accounted for and you’ll never really get any time to relax or chill out unless you get sick and have to go to the hospital (which will probably happen at least once during basic.) (Newly minted Airman First Class, Watson. I was able to get promoted to A1C right out of basic since I already had two years of college.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: You are given 1 year of paid vacation - what do you do?
Answer: I took an entire year away from work in 2019, which was very fortunate, since the next year the illness of unspecified origin swept the world and travel would be completely changed for nearly the next three years. I backpacked Latin America for the first time at age 34. It was a thrilling and liberating experience to both have so much time away from a desk/computer and also to get to spend enough time in foreign countries to feel fully immersed in another culture. I rapidly improved my Spanish speaking ability, I got to try all of the local foods over many months spent between Mexico City all the way to Montevideo, Uruguay. I was so far away from home. I remember that at times I felt incredibly lonely, other times like I was in an adventure movie akin to Indiana Jones. It’s my firm belief that everyone should take at least a year away from work to travel while still young, if at all possible. It will change your perspective on many things. Particularly if you have never spent a great deal of time outside of your native country. (Hanging out on the beach with sea lions in Viña Del Mar, Chile. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How much alcohol did Winston Churchill consume? Was he a big drinker?
Answer: We can get a peek into how much Churchill drank since the White House butler, Alonzo Fields, wrote about Churchill’s drink requests in his memoir. Not long after Churchill arrived at the White House in December of 1941, he pulled Mr. Fields aside and said the following: “Listen, Alonzo, when I leave here we want to depart as friends, right? I’ll have no whistling in the hallways in the mornings. Now, I must have a tumbler of sherry in my room before breakfast, a couple of glasses of scotch and soda before lunch and French champagne, and 90-year-old brandy before I go to sleep at night.” This was not inclusive of everything Churchill drank during the day, however, it was just a starting point. Essentially, Churchill drank for a good part of his waking hours every single day. His drinking sessions were known to last until 2 a.m. or 3 a.m. every night, wherein he kept President Roosevelt up to talk shop. This exasperated the First Lady, who was at least a little pleased to see him go at the end of his three week trip to Washington. Churchill maintained his heavy drinking and smoking lifestyle all while leading his nation through a war and as a renown public speaker and author. He still managed to live to age 90. Good genetics. (Winston Churchill. Photo credit: biography.com)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What was a blend/kind of sausage you only tried once but will never forget?
Answer: A smoked Argentinian sausage in Buenos Aires. One night amidst a heavy drinking session with some of my buddies from England and Wales, I suddenly remembered I hadn’t eaten anything at all that evening. Overcome with both inebriation and hunger, I wisely decided I’d better get something to eat. I stopped in a rather humble diner. I ordered the sausage and steak. Never have I had a sausage that was such a good combination of smoked flavor, spice, and juiciness. It could have also been that I was extremely hungry and drunk. I still remember that meal nearly five years later though. (One of the things I like about Argentina is that you can order a meal completely devoid of anything healthy like vegetables and receive no judgment at all. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What countries have female special forces soldiers and how are they selected?
Answer: I’m not sure if they were considered special forces, but Gadaffi famously had an all female guard force. I’m not sure at all if they were selected for their operational skills. As you probably know, Gadaffi was quite brutally and publicly killed.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is it true that Green Berets only train foreign militaries?
Answer: No, I had the pleasure of spending many days in Iraq training with the Green Berets as an airman in the US Air Force. This was because my chief was a former Green Beret and he went over to their camp and asked them to conduct firearms training with us on a regular basis. For several months, at least once a week we would go over to the SF camp and train shooting drills. They also let us do cool stuff like blow up claymores. It was a privilege to learn from some of the best soldiers in the world. I still remember and use the techniques they taught me to this day. (Training at Green Beret camp in Baghdad as an airman in 2009.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: If someone is fatally wounded, should you tell him?
Answer: I’m not a medic, so it’s actually not my job to tell someone if they’ll make it or not. I usually didn’t know for sure. In my military career I would say I encountered a few people who were obviously going to die, but I didn’t say anything. I think they already knew anyhow. You comfort the person as best as you can and wait for the medics. (Air Force tactical casualty care. Photo credit: US Air Force.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the worst country you have ever visited?
Answer: Besides an obvious country like Kuwait, the worst country I have visited was Argentina. The people were cold, unfriendly. I was anxious my entire time there. I spoke Spanish as best as I could with anyone that would listen. From the moment I landed at the airport in Mendoza I was detained by the police, I was interrogated and asked where I was coming from and where I was going (I believe they thought I was Venezuelan.) When they realized I was from the US, they let me go. I think it’s regrettable I had such a poor experience in Argentina, because Buenos Aires and Mendoza are very beautiful cities. I would still go to Argentina again probably, but now I am more prepared to receive an unfriendly welcome. I am hesitant to blame the poor time I had in Argentina on my dark skin, but I believe it probably played a part. Oh well. (Downtown Buenos Aires. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do I fix a weak squat? I have been training at the gym for a year and 8 months. I’m 14, 5 foot 5, weigh 148 lbs. I can bench 195, deadlift 295 lbs and leg press 455 lbs for 7 reps, but can’t even squat 225, but can rep 215 lbs on squat.
Answer: I think the problem is thinking there’s something wrong with your squat. For your age, weight, and experience, I would say that your squat is right on point. Keep lifting with dedication young grasshopper. You’re doing just fine.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is life really unfair?
Answer: Of course. I am not even sure where we got the notion that life is fair. For those of us, for example, that were born in a western nation, we hit the jackpot right out of the gate. We’ll never truly worry where our next meal is coming from. If we get hit by a car, we’ll certainly be treated for our injuries. If we become disabled we’ll get a pension. Compare that to the developing world. I often feel anxiety vicariously for my Mexican and Colombian friends, many of whom I love dearly. They deal with a level of uncertainty that will never be experienced by those of born in the United States. I am not just talking about my friends who are store clerks or who work as nannies. I am talking about my friends from the developing world who are engineers, architects, nurses, and physical therapists. They hang on to life by a thread, simply because the world they were born into offers no guarantees. In my estimation it’s bullshit, because their hard work has no guarantee of bearing the fruit they so rightfully deserve. If you are lucky enough to not have to worry about these issues, give thanks. You are a part of the global elite, usually by happenstance.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why don't men like big women?
Answer: Actually, we do. It’s not that we always like bigger women specifically, it’s that we like women with nice facial features and a good personality that are uncomplicated. If you have that combination of things most, but not all men are open to dating you, as long as you don’t veer too much towards the morbidly obese. I have dated women of nearly every phenotype and body type. Some of the best women I have dated have been overweight, but had really cool personalities. If you aren’t getting a lot of dates or attention from men, work on your personality. It’s the most important thing once we get to know you. Cheers! (Actress Dana Gourrier. She is very beautiful in my opinion, but more than that, her personality seems really amazing. I want her to know that I am single and available! Photo credit: X.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is your favorite military equipment to operate?
Answer: This is kind of surprising, but in my experience, I had a ton of fun with the M203 grenade launcher. I was deadly accurate with it and I could easily put a grenade through the window of a house or skip it under a vehicle. The recoil is also not too bad. It’s an incredibly fun weapon system once you get used to it. (A soldier operating an M4 with an attached M203 grenade launcher. This weapon system is incredibly easy to operate and very cool to use. Photo credit: US Army.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: If you could have a 30-second conversation with a Trump supporter, what would you say?
Answer: This happened to me in Sedona, Arizona, a few years ago. I was getting ready to go to a bar when a man noticed me get out of my car with my camera around my neck. It was an awkward moment because I was actually unloading the Glock 23 I had on my hip and putting it into the lockbox that I kept in the back of my car. I was carrying my pistol because I was worried that I might encounter javelinas on the trails, which can be incredibly dangerous. This isn’t so unusual in Arizona. The man was dressed head to toe in a jumpsuit that had Trump’s face all over it. He wanted to know what camera I was using and what I was taking photos of. I told him I had been hiking the trails with my Nikon and taking photos while doing so. After a few moments we said goodbye. He was a pleasant fellow all around, so there was no reason to be upset or outraged. I thought it a bit funny that he only asked about my camera and that he wasn’t at all startled by me having a gun, though. Trump supporters made up approximately half the country in the last couple of elections. Most of them are pretty normal people like your neighbor, your mailman, or the cop patrolling the streets of your town. (Me on the trails during my trip to Sedona. I looked like the quite the mountain man. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do modern soldiers fight carrying so much weight?
Answer: Generally, we will carry a lot of weight if going on a long patrol in the field, but if you know you will be performing a raid, for example, you’ll drop a lot of your gear and only take essentials. An element will stay behind to guard your rucksacks and additional gear. If you’re ambushed while carrying a lot of gear, you un-ass it as quickly as possible so that you don’t sacrifice your mobility. A basic load out and your body armor and Kevlar helmet actually aren’t too difficult to fight in, although the heat of the desert or jungle can complicate things. Modern gear is actually very good in my opinion and loads better than what soldiers had in Vietnam or even the first Gulf War. (a soldier about to cop some Z’s in full “battle rattle.” Photo credit: Task and Purpose.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Have you ever been threatened on Quora? If so, what happened?
Answer: I took a number of years away from Quora and only recently have I decided to actually try my hand at writing again. Mostly because I think at this point in my life I need to work on my creativity and writing, in general. Additionally, I find writing here cathartic. In the last month or two I have written almost daily and to my great surprise it didn’t take long before I received a few death threats. Some of them direct and a few in a roundabout way “If I wanted to I could find you!” I think these threats are quite laughable. I don’t worry about them and simply delete them. I think that if my content offends you that much, you could simply choose not to read it. What’s so difficult about that? I’m not at all afraid of people who threaten me online. I use my real name, I’m not too hard to find. I’m not invincible either, but if you come looking for me in real life (which I seriously doubt), you should know that I don’t make for easy prey.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What the craziest situation you've encountered being in the military?
Answer: Let me paint you a picture. It’s sometime around midnight on Sather Air Base, Iraq. The year is 2009. There is a port-a-potty set up right next to our entry control point (ECP) to the air base. This ECP is right next to the end of the active runway, with only a chain link fence separating us from the runway. (C-17 Globemaster. Image credit: US Air Force.) Most of us are relaxing, playing cards and hoping that no one from command comes around and pesters us with stupid questions. One of our Ugandan security contractors gets up and goes to the port-a-potty. Just as he is doing so a huge C-17 cargo aircraft pulls to the end of the run way. The aircraft then turns 90 degrees, so that the rear of the aircraft is pointed directly at our ECP. While our unfortunate security contractor is inside taking a dump, the aircrew decide to do a run-up of all four of the aircraft’s powerful engines, directing the blast right at us. Sons of bitches! It kicked up a lot of rocks and debris, and made a metric fuck ton of noise. But most unfortunately, it manages to flip an entire port-a-potty with our 160lb Ugandan comrade inside! The port-a-potty is now lying flat on the ground with the door side facing up, thankfully. Hearing the muffled screams emanating from inside, we rush over to open the door to let our friend out. Unfortunately, a funny situation then arises, because as much as we want to help the man up, he’s now covered in blue water, urine, and shit. No one wanted to touch him. After some time someone had the courage to grasp his hand and lift him up. We sent him directly to medical for evaluation. He was okay, physically. I’m sure that no matter what else happened during his deployment, that was the most traumatic thing he experienced. (Port-a-potties at a deployed location, Baghdad. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the general attitude of locals towards tourists in your country? Why do you think your country is a popular tourist destination?
Answer: The United States is a very large country with a very diverse population. It would be difficult to state if there is a general attitude about tourists that applies to every region of the country. I have never lived in New York or San Francisco, for example, so their ideas about tourism are probably a bit different than someone like me, who is from the midwest. Generally, in the midwest we like tourists as long as they aren’t rude. Having kept my home in Cleveland for the last 10 years, it’s not all that common that we get a lot of tourists. Those that we do get usually come to see the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Every four years the Hall of Fame induction is actually held in Cleveland (the other years it’s done in Los Angeles). This is usually one of the times when we get the most tourists. I usually think of it as a pretty fun time, you get to meet people from all over the country and even the world. The other tourists we get are actually medical tourists from different parts of the world who come to Cleveland to receive treatment at Cleveland Clinic. A few times I have met some pretty rich people from the Middle East who came all the way to Cleveland for medical treatment. Interesting folks. If you come to a place like Cleveland or Detroit as a tourist, you’re most likely to draw a lot of curiosity because people will want to know what brought you there. (Sunset on Lake Erie, Cleveland. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is it considered acceptable to not leave a tip if you were dissatisfied with your meal at a restaurant? If so, how can this be communicated politely without causing offense?
Answer: In the United States, no. Not leaving a tip for a waiter is seen as almost borderline psychopathic behavior. It will always cause offense. If the meal was not acceptable it’s totally fine to leave feedback. Managers are often interested in knowing if the quality of your meal is not up to par. It’s never acceptable to not tip the waiter for service though.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why do Americans tend to view their country's current state as the best in history, rather than objectively?
Answer: If you have to ask this question you haven’t spent much time around Americans. Americans, as a group, are some of the most self-critical people I have ever been around. Our universities, for example, are almost universally critical of the US government, our institutions, and the structure of our society. Our media, even so-called conservative platforms, like Fox News, make their money from telling people exactly how screwed-up we are as a nation. I have, for many years now, taken the opposite view. Americans have very little appreciation for how good they have things relative to a lot of the world as it actually exists. Most of my liberal-leaning and college educated friends tend to buy into the idea that Europe is a haven on earth that has managed to right all the wrongs that exist in America. “They have free healthcare! They have walkable cities! There’s no racism over there!” Even if all of these things were true about Europe (they aren’t, universally), they forget that Europe and other OECD nations make up a rather small fragment of the people on earth. There are billions of other people who live in objectively worse conditions than your average American. There’s a lot of work still to be done in the US of A, but I question the validity of arguments that compare us to countries like Sweden or Denmark.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the worst US city to live in?
Answer: Rust belt cities like Detroit, Buffalo, Cleveland, Gary, Flint. They have all suffered from flight to other areas, brain drain, shrinking tax revenues, poor education systems, poor public services, poor public transit, high crime, high drug use, and general desperation and malaise. Yet, it’s the region I call home. I will always love it. (I’m a Detroiter who has lived in exile in Cleveland for much of my adult life. Both cities perfectly embody the spirit of America. They simply just won’t die. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do you evaluate the Iraq War?
Answer: Poorly. In fact, we are still dealing with the repercussions of invading Iraq to this day. Not only that Iraq is an incredibly unstable country that has become an Iranian proxy. Not only that its economy has never flourished. Not only that it lead to the rise of ISIS and greater political instability throughout the region. What I mean, specifically, is the war in Ukraine. Putin, uses Iraq as an example as to how great powers actually don’t need to follow international law and that a rules-based order is just another myth used by the West when it is convenient to do so. In effect, might makes right. It’s impossible not to see hypocrisy in the actions of the United States when they call Russia out for invading a sovereign nation. The invasion of Iraq continues to handicap American foreign policy and calls into question the legitimacy of the West in enforcing a rules-based order. (Mural of Saddam Hussein near Baghdad International Airport. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is America still considered a superpower? If not, what factors contribute to their global influence?
Answer: Yes. There’s this kind of hilarious meme I have seen floating around on social media recently: (In typical American fashion, we can deploy artery-hardening, diabetes-inducing restaurants to any corner of the globe to sustain our troops. Photo credit: Twitter.) However, the US military is only one aspect of America’s superpower status. Its economic might is arguably more powerful, such that merely restricting other nations from using the US dollar system can doom their economies (e.g. Venezuela, Cuba). US-based technology platforms also dominate the landscape in much of the world (Facebook, Google, YouTube, Airbnb, Uber, etc.). This level of reach and influence is so far unsurpassed by any other nation on earth and there really doesn’t appear to be anyone seriously challenging the US for that role. While China’s rise, at first, appeared to be stratospheric, its trajectory doesn’t look so clear anymore. As a nation, the Chinese are facing steep demographic decline and aging. Their economy isn’t as robust as it appeared years ago. It’s leadership and military prowess, questionable. Furthermore, they seem to have lost the trust and confidence of their neighbors like Vietnam and the Philippines, which at one time seemed to be inching closer to the Chinese sphere of influence. So, yes, America is still a superpower for now. And in fact, the lone superpower. I think the only country that can ruin its superpower status is America.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is New York City worth it for foreigners?
Answer: I wrote an answer earlier this morning comparing some aspects of the UK to the US. It was interesting that a lot of people commented speaking about their experiences in New York. I couldn’t relate to them because even though I’m American, I have actually only spent one long weekend in New York City and that was 15 years ago. I absolutely hated it. Mind you, I stayed in Manhattan like a typical tourist, but I found many aspects of the city very unpleasant. The dirty subway, people that are rather rude to each other, not to mention tourists (I witnessed a really bad case of road rage), extremely high prices, and surprisingly mediocre food in many places. Sure, it could be a cool place to visit once, to experience it. That entirely depends on you. I am much more partial to our capital, Washington, D.C., however. You could be asking the wrong person since I happen to be an American that has spent much more time in London, Rome, Madrid, and even Bogotá than New York City, and I like all of those cities much more. (Times Square. I found this part of the city chock full of American chain restaurants and endless advertising very unimpressive. Photo credit: Wikipedia.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do soldiers tell their weapons apart when deployed? Does it even matter?
Answer: In addition to the serial number, our weapons had a 3 digit number taped on the buttstock right below the charging handle. That number is also on your weapons card. Your weapons card is presented to the unit armourer prior to the beginning of each shift and left in the armory until you return the weapon. It absolutely matters, since your weapon is zeroed for your eyes only. The optic and back-up sights are fickle, but very accurate, as long as you’re the one who zeroed the weapon during your last qualification with it. If another person picks it up, it won’t fire as accurately. (Bumping guns is strictly prohibited, you don’t want to mess up the zero on your optic! Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Have you ever changed your political opinions?
Answer: Yes. Not long ago, I was watching a video on YouTube by the author Mark Manson, who wrote the book “The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck.” He spoke about his experience living in South America and how, when he returned to the US, he had become more conservative. I could only nod my head in agreement as I listened. While I have always had libertarian leanings and leaned left on most social issues (as many libertarians tend to do), I find that living in a developing nation with much weaker rule of law suddenly made me more grateful for the positive aspects of the United States. Although I have indeed had some rather unpleasant interactions with the police in the US, not ever have I been pressured to, or would I feel inclined to offer to pay a bribe. I have never been stopped in the US and asked to show my documents by soldiers wielding assault rifles (also expecting a bribe). Also, I have never been to any place in my country where I have seen gang members carrying AK-47’s and selling drugs out in the open for all to see, without fear of any intervention by the police. Of course, I have experienced all of these things while living and traveling in Latin America. While most parts of the developing world are still very welcoming and livable, there is often a stark contrast with how the law works compared to the place where I am from. I am much more in favor of preserving the rule of law and order than I used to be.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do American cops differ from British ones? Is one system considered better or worse than the other?
Answer: American cops are VERY hesitant to interact with people on the street. Just approaching a cop on the streets in the US in 2024 feels a little risky, because they don’t know who you are, if you’re armed, and if you have bad intentions. A couple of years ago I remember that I was going to a football game (American football, of course), and as I approached the stadium there were several SWAT officers and a tactical vehicle parked in front. I remember that I went for my wallet to retrieve my ticket and one of the officers placed his hand on his gun as a precautionary measure. I was just an ordinary football fan, but I was aware of the fact that if I had likely moved too rapidly or alarmingly, the officer would have blown me away. In the UK I knew that, on the Tube, for example, if I got lost, it would be totally fine to approach an officer from the British Transport Police or The Met and let them know that I was lost and needed help getting back to my hotel. This is exactly what happened one night. The officers were extremely courteous and gracious. I don’t think this is something that is even possible in the US, the police in the US have a different attitude because it’s a different level of danger and a more dangerous culture. I think the British method of policing is a model for the entire world to follow though. Just my opinion. (Officers of the British Transport Police. If you get lost in London, let them know, and they’ll help you out. Photo credit: Daily Mail.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What television show is the most realistic when it comes to depicting (public) schools?
Answer: For someone who went to Detroit Public Schools, The Wire, was the perfect representation of public schools in my experience. There are students dealing with all kinds of issues ranging from parents who are in jail or prison, many, many single mothers. Children who are abused or generally neglected. All against the backdrop of living in an incredibly violent city with widespread drug abuse and gangs fighting for turf to meet the demand for those drugs. There were no heroes coming to save us. The world was sometimes a startling a frightening place. Then there’s the teachers. Most hampered by an uncaring administration, many are ineffectual. Some are suffering from burnout and are riding out the time to retirement. A few, usually young, rookie teachers actually care. Although, it’s usually not long until they too fall victim to burnout. The Wire deserves every accolade and then some for shedding light on what it’s like to live and grow up in an urban area in the United States. Especially one that has fallen victim to decay and the withdrawal of industry that plagued Rust Belt cities in the 1990’s. (Scene from The Wire. Roland "Prez" Pryzbylewski is the new teacher who hasn’t burnt out yet, but one day, in the not-distant-future he will. Photo credit: HBO.)
