Name: Dennis Watson
Question: If cops carry a gun in their belt at all times, I assume it’s on safety to keep it from going off. How do they turn the safety off so quick when they pull it out?
Answer: As others pointed out, most duty weapons that cops carry don’t have a manual safety. The Glock 17, a very popular police firearm the world over, doesn’t have any safeties to worry about. In my military police unit, we carried the M9 Beretta, which was standard issue for the entire military at the time. It does have a manual safety, but it was never engaged when on duty. This is because the M9 is a double action/single action pistol. The first trigger pull requires a very heavy and intentional pull on the trigger to fire. This was considered safe enough that regulations didn’t require us to have the safety switched on, while on duty. Any subsequent shots after a first shot are very light and require significantly less effort. Whenever we were on the firing range, the safety is also used as a de-cocker. Activating the safety and switching it off again meant that the hammer is then safely lowered, so that the gun will fire in double action again for your next shot. The manual safety feature on the pistol was mostly important for when we turned in our duty weapons to the armory. You switch the safety on before unloading at the clearing barrel to prevent a negligent discharge. (Beretta M9. Note the red indicator on the slide, when the safety is in this position the pistol is ready to fire. We always carried in this manner during law enforcement duty in the military. This pistol is heavy and it was almost universally hated by those of us that carried it. Image source: Wikipedia.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How did the "cool kids" from your high school turn out?
Answer: Class president: an Air Force pilot with wife and kids. Jock friend #1: went to the same college as me for a couple of years to study engineering. Dropped out. Went back to college, dropped out again. Went back a third time and graduated. He is now an engineer in the automotive industry. Two kids, is now divorced. Jock friend #2: I call him a jock here because he was our star football player, but he was a very well rounded student. He also played in jazz band with me and was a gifted student. He played football for a while in Division 1, but nothing ever came of it. I believe he manages an auto parts store, is now married with one kid. Nerdy but popular kid: He is now a physician. Never married, no kids (surprisingly, even in high school he was already a bit of a womanizer). Don’t let the nerdy kids fool you! Bully: the last time I saw him was when I was in graduate school at the University of Michigan. My friends and I went to downtown Detroit to a bar and he was the bouncer there. Even just ten years removed from high school, he looked rough. Prom King: Not sure what he does for a living, but I think he still lives in the same neighborhood in Detroit. Prom Queen: Same as above. Sweet, innocent girl: She became an engineer, has a husband and kids. Sweet, innocent girl #2: first, I have to say that in high school I was convinced I was in love with her. I helped her study hard for our college entrance exams. She got into the college she wanted to go to (Michigan State), but instead she didn’t attend, got married, had kids, and became a military wife. She has since divorced.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Is crime a major issue in Sao Paolo and Rio de Janeiro? Is it safe for tourists to visit these cities?
Answer: Yes, I would say so. You still likely won’t encounter crime as a tourist, however. You’ll likely stay in nicer neighborhoods and won’t venture too far off the beaten path. Obviously, if it’s your first time in Brazil, you shouldn’t go anywhere near any favelas (slums). This is not to say that I have never been to any favelas, but never without a local. You need to keep your wits about you at all times and be cognizant of when you use your phone. Generally, it’s never a good idea to use your phone on the streets. Always dress plainly and the best practice is not to wear any jewelry whatsoever. (Pedra do Sal, Rio De Janeiro. This neighborhood is a big tourist attraction, but it can get incredibly dangerous rather quickly if you wander off at night. Always exercise caution in Brazil. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Are your twenties really the best years of your life?
Answer: Fuuuuck no. In my twenties I was a premature father, in the military, college, then graduate school. After that I was in an entry level government job making $20 an hour while living in Phoenix, Arizona (a very expensive city) and trying to pay back student loans while paying child support. I’d say that my late 20’s, specifically, were the worst years of my life. I’m much happier to be 39, free to travel the world and being my own boss. I’m also in better shape, have fewer financial obligations and making more money. Growing older is fine if you do it right. There’s nothing to be afraid of. (I turned 39 a month ago. Oh the horror!)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Are the Spanish really anti-tourists? It seems they want to bite the hand that feeds them.
Answer: I spent two months in the Iberian Peninsula last year. My feeling is actually that Lisbon had the most complaints about Airbnb’s and tourism. I went to a bar and the bartender read me the riot act about how we Americans were ruining the city, raising the rent, ruining the local culture, and that we could fuck off. No one got that upset with me in Spain. Overall, I still like Portugal better though. That was one of the only negative interactions I had. Hahaha. (Lisbon. This neighborhood has been completely overtaken by Airbnb’s. The locals HATE this. My experience in Spain was much more generally cold though, but no one ever specifically gave me problems like in Portugal. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are the most common crimes committed against tourists in Barcelona, Spain?
Answer: Pickpocketing. Particularly on the metro and maybe near tourist attractions like Sagrada Familia. I just wore a money belt everywhere and kept an eye on my phone. No problems. We even went to some pretty rough bars in some working class neighborhoods. It was all a lot of fun. (Walking the streets of Barcelona late at night. I didn’t feel nervous or afraid at all. Photo by author.)

Question: What happens if an American tourist is injured or killed in Mexico?
Answer: It’s reported to the consulate or embassy. The family is then contacted to arrange repatriation of the injured or dead citizen to the United States. (Cancun, Mexico. You have some of the best chances of being injured or killed here, even though it’s a large resort city. I usually avoid it. Photo by author.)

Question: How dangerous is Spain for American tourists? How many have been murdered?
Answer: Spain is 0% dangerous for Americans. I think even the criminals there are actually afraid of us. (Walking the mean streets of Toledo, Spain, at night. You won’t find much crime here. Photo by author.)
